services.name: backend
services.description: FastAPI-based home network monitoring backend exposing 13 route prefixes for devices, events, mesh nodes, cellular routers, Alexa, signal boosters, alarms, and speed tests. Persists state in SQLite (WAL) with Fernet-encrypted credentials and pushes real-time updates via SSE.

violations.title: Public API routes lack version prefix
violations.content: All backend route prefixes use `/api/<resource>` (e.g., `/api/devices`, `/api/deco`, `/api/chester`, `/api/alexa`, `/api/hiboost`, `/api/alarm-com`, `/api/speedtest`, `/api/settings`, `/api/sse`, `/api/digest`, `/api/network`) without a version segment such as `/api/v1/`. The React frontend and the AWS Lambda Alexa skill in `lambda/lambda_function.py` consume these endpoints, so any backwards-incompatible change forces every client to update simultaneously with no migration window.
violations.fixPrompt: Introduce a `/api/v1/` prefix for all public route modules in `backend/routes/` and `backend/main.py`. Mount the existing routers under `/api/v1` while keeping `/api` as a temporary alias if needed for backwards compatibility, then update `frontend/src/hooks/useDevicePolling.js` and any `fetch`/`axios` callers in `frontend/src/components/` and `frontend/src/pages/` to target the versioned paths.

violations.title: Frontend missing an `api` layer between components and backend
violations.content: The frontend service is reported with only a `service` layer. The central data hook `frontend/src/hooks/useDevicePolling.js` mixes SSE wiring with multi-tier polling, and individual components/pages call backend endpoints directly across 13 route prefixes. Without a dedicated `api` layer (typed client modules per resource), URL paths, error handling, and auth headers (`X-API-Key`) are duplicated across the codebase.
violations.fixPrompt: Introduce an `api` layer under `frontend/src/api/` with one module per backend resource (e.g., `devices.js`, `deco.js`, `alexa.js`, `hiboost.js`, `alarm_com.js`). Centralize base URL, `X-API-Key` header injection, error normalization, and response parsing there, then refactor `frontend/src/hooks/useDevicePolling.js` and components in `frontend/src/components/` and `frontend/src/pages/` to call the api modules instead of `fetch` directly.

violations.title: Chatty polling hook drives multiple sequential requests per refresh
violations.content: `frontend/src/hooks/useDevicePolling.js` is described as the central data hook combining SSE with three polling tiers (15s/30s/60s) across 13 route prefixes (`/api/devices`, `/api/events`, `/api/deco`, `/api/chester`, `/api/alexa`, `/api/hiboost`, `/api/alarm-com`, `/api/speedtest`, `/api/digest`, `/api/network`, etc.). Rendering the dashboard requires many small endpoint calls that could be aggregated, increasing latency and failure probability.
violations.fixPrompt: Add an aggregate endpoint such as `GET /api/v1/dashboard` (or `/api/v1/snapshot`) in `backend/main.py` / a new `backend/routes/dashboard.py` that returns devices, events, deco topology, chester cellular status, hiboost RF, alarm partitions, and health score in a single response. Update `frontend/src/hooks/useDevicePolling.js` to call this aggregate for initial loads and reserve per-resource polling for tabs that need fine-grained refresh.

violations.title: Inconsistent route prefix conventions
violations.content: Route prefixes mix hyphenated (`/api/alarm-com`) and non-hyphenated (`/api/speedtest`, `/api/hiboost`) styles, and the OAuth router uses `/oauth` instead of `/api/oauth`. This inconsistency leaks into client URL construction and response handling, making it harder to apply uniform middleware (auth, versioning, error envelopes) across the surface.
violations.fixPrompt: Pick a single naming convention (e.g., lowercase, hyphen-separated) for all route prefixes in `backend/routes/` and `backend/main.py`. Move `/oauth` under `/api/v1/oauth` so it shares the same middleware stack and rename inconsistently styled prefixes like `/api/alarm-com` → `/api/v1/alarm` (or `/api/v1/alarm-com` if kept) consistently. Update the Alexa skill in `lambda/lambda_function.py` and `frontend/src/api/` callers accordingly.

violations.title: God function: `startup_event` orchestrates 20+ subsystem initializations
violations.content: `main.startup_event` in `backend/main.py` is 207 lines and 47 statements. It instantiates `Database`, `OUIService`, `NetworkDeviceService`, `DeviceSearchService`, 4 repositories, `EventService`, `DecoClient`/`DecoService`, `ChesterClient`/`ChesterService`, `CorrelationService`, `AlexaClient`/`AlexaService`, `AlarmComClient`, `HiBoostClient`/`Service`/`Scheduler`, `SpeedTestService`/`Scheduler`, `DigestService`, `NetworkHealthService`, `PollingServiceManager`, and `RetentionScheduler`, then wires them together via setter functions. Validation, credential loading, dependency injection, scheduler startup, and error handling are all in one body — impossible to test or reuse any individual subsystem wiring.
violations.fixPrompt: Split `startup_event` in `backend/main.py` into focused factory functions per subsystem (e.g. `build_device_pipeline`, `build_deco_stack`, `build_alexa_stack`, `build_alarm_com_stack`, `build_speedtest_stack`, `start_schedulers`). Each helper should return its wired services so `startup_event` becomes a short composition root that calls them in order.

violations.title: God function: `get_topology_graph` is 420 lines with 7 levels of nesting
violations.content: `deco.get_topology_graph` in `backend/routes/deco.py` spans 420 lines at nesting depth 7. It calls `DecoService.get_nodes_with_details`, `CorrelationService.get_merged_clients` (implied), `ChesterClient.get_system_info`, `TSLPPacket.decode` (twice), opens `Database.get_connection`, closes it, and apparently builds a Response payload — combining topology fetching, cellular enrichment, raw protocol decoding, DB access, and HTTP serialization in a single route handler.
violations.fixPrompt: Extract the topology graph assembly out of `get_topology_graph` in `backend/routes/deco.py`: move the node + client + cellular merging into `DecoService` (or a new `TopologyGraphService`), keep `Database` access inside a repository, and let the route only validate the request and return the assembled payload.

violations.title: God function: `scan_and_update` orchestrates ARP, DHCP, Deco, Chester, and event recording in 264 lines
violations.content: `NetworkDeviceService.scan_and_update` in `backend/services/network_device_service.py` is 264 lines at nesting depth 7. It calls `ARPScanner.scan_subnet`, `DHCPParser.parse_dhcp_leases`, `_merge_arp_and_dhcp`, repository CRUD (`get_device_by_mac`, `create_or_update_device`, `update_device_metadata` 8×, `mark_offline`, `mark_online`), `OUIService.lookup_vendor`, `_record_device_event` (which records events AND creates alerts), `DecoClient.get_client_list_local`, `DecoClient.get_topology_local`, `TSLPPacket.decode`, and `ChesterService.get_router_status`. Five orthogonal scan sources are fused inline with persistence and event emission.
violations.fixPrompt: Break `scan_and_update` in `backend/services/network_device_service.py` into discrete steps: `collect_arp_devices`, `collect_dhcp_leases`, `collect_deco_clients`, `collect_chester_devices`, `merge_sources`, `persist_devices`, `emit_status_change_events`. Have `scan_and_update` only orchestrate by calling them in sequence.

violations.title: God function: `generate_insights` (275 lines) mixes querying, statistics, classification, and persistence
violations.content: `SpeedTestService.generate_insights` in `backend/services/speedtest_service.py` is 275 lines, 15 statements at nesting depth 4. It calls `get_all_history`, `get_hourly_averages`, and `store_insight` seven times — performing data fetching, threshold-based classification (degradation, spikes, time-of-day patterns), and persistence in one body.
violations.fixPrompt: Refactor `generate_insights` in `backend/services/speedtest_service.py` into named insight detectors (e.g. `detect_throughput_degradation`, `detect_latency_spikes`, `detect_off_hour_drop`), each returning an insight or `None`. Let `generate_insights` iterate detectors and call `store_insight`.

violations.title: God function: `_authenticate_local` performs RSA exchange, AES setup, signature, and retry in 118 lines
violations.content: `DecoClient._authenticate_local` in `backend/services/deco_client.py` runs 118 lines / 25 statements. It instantiates `DecoEncryption`, performs `rsa_encrypt`, `aes_encrypt`, packet `TSLPPacket.encode`, `get_signature`, `aes_decrypt`, and even calls `DeviceSearchService.search` from an auth path — combining crypto orchestration with persistence search.
violations.fixPrompt: Split `_authenticate_local` in `backend/services/deco_client.py` into `_negotiate_keys`, `_exchange_password`, and `_finalize_session` helpers on `DecoClient`, and remove the `DeviceSearchService.search` call from the authentication path entirely.

violations.title: God function: `get_alexa_devices` is 136 lines at nesting depth 5
violations.content: `alexa.get_alexa_devices` in `backend/routes/alexa.py` is 136 lines deep in 5 levels of nesting and only delegates two real service calls (`get_all_devices_with_state`). The rest is response normalization, classification fallbacks, and error handling that belongs in `AlexaService` rather than the route.
violations.fixPrompt: Move the response shaping and classification logic out of `get_alexa_devices` in `backend/routes/alexa.py` and into `AlexaService`. The route handler should only call the service, map errors to HTTP responses, and return the result.

violations.title: God function: `import_alexa_mac_addresses` is 148 lines combining web scraping, correlation, and persistence
violations.content: `alexa.import_alexa_mac_addresses` in `backend/routes/alexa.py` spans 148 lines / 15 statements at nesting depth 5. It calls `AlexaClient.get_all_device_macs`, `AlexaClient.get_echo_devices_web`, and then performs correlation and DB writes inline — three distinct responsibilities (Alexa fetch, MAC correlation, persistence) in one route handler.
violations.fixPrompt: Extract three helpers in `backend/services/alexa_service.py` (or a new `AlexaMacImporter`): `fetch_alexa_macs`, `correlate_macs_with_network_devices`, `persist_mac_correlations`. Have the route in `backend/routes/alexa.py` only orchestrate them.

violations.title: Divergent change: `backend/routes/alexa.py` mixes auth, device, smart home, Lambda, and sync concerns
violations.content: The `alexa` route module is 1999 lines with 35 methods spanning OAuth (`start_alexa_auth`, `alexa_auth_callback`), cookie auth (`set_alexa_cookies`), device listing (`get_alexa_devices`, `get_alexa_device`), control (`send_device_command`, `control_smart_home_device`), Echo discovery (`get_echo_devices`, `import_alexa_mac_addresses`), match suggestion (`suggest_matches`, `apply_alexa_name`), identification (`identify_start/complete/associate`), and a Lambda passthrough surface (`lambda_store_token`, `lambda_accept_grant`, `lambda_discover`, `lambda_refresh_cache`, `lambda_get_state`, `lambda_command`). Five+ unrelated stakeholders share one file.
violations.fixPrompt: Split `backend/routes/alexa.py` into `routes/alexa_auth.py` (OAuth + cookies), `routes/alexa_devices.py` (devices, control, echo), `routes/alexa_correlation.py` (import/suggest/identify/associate), and `routes/alexa_lambda.py` (Lambda passthrough). Mount each under its own subpath.

violations.title: Divergent change: `backend/main.py` hosts 29 unrelated route methods plus startup wiring
violations.content: `main` in `backend/main.py` is 967 lines with 29 methods covering startup/shutdown, root/health, device CRUD, polling configuration, manual scans, device groups (create/list/get/update/delete plus membership add/remove), events, alerts, event stats, and the SPA catch-all. New features in any of these areas force edits to the same file, and the routes overlap with dedicated route modules (`routes/events.py`, etc.).
violations.fixPrompt: Move device CRUD, polling/scan, and device group routes out of `backend/main.py` into `routes/devices.py`, `routes/polling.py`, and `routes/device_groups.py`. Leave `backend/main.py` with only app construction, startup/shutdown, root/health, the SPA catch-all, and router registration.

violations.title: Divergent change: `backend/routes/deco.py` is 1450 lines covering nodes, clients, WiFi, QoS, mesh, and topology
violations.content: The `deco` route module has 19 methods spanning node lookup/refresh/auto-name, client listing/import/rename/merge/sync, WiFi config get/update, QoS, client-node mapping, mesh assignment, network optimization, topology, and topology graph rendering. Changes to any of these surfaces (e.g. adding a WiFi field, tweaking topology output) force edits in the same large file.
violations.fixPrompt: Split `backend/routes/deco.py` into `routes/deco_nodes.py`, `routes/deco_clients.py`, `routes/deco_wifi.py`, and `routes/deco_topology.py`. Group setter helpers and shared dependencies into a small `routes/deco_deps.py` module.

violations.title: Excessive fan-out: `backend/main.py` imports 47 internal modules
violations.content: `main` imports 47 internal modules — including 12 Pydantic models, every repository, the route modules, and most services. This makes `main.py` tightly coupled to nearly every backend component, so any rename or signature change ripples back here.
violations.fixPrompt: Move the Pydantic request/response models out of `backend/main.py` into the route modules (or a shared `backend/models/api.py`). Replace direct repository/service imports in `backend/main.py` with a single `build_app()` factory in `backend/app_factory.py` that wires dependencies, so `main.py` only imports `build_app`.

violations.title: Excessive fan-out: `SettingsPage` imports 3 modules but contains 50 statements across 808 lines
violations.content: `SettingsPage` in `frontend/src/pages/SettingsPage.jsx` is 795 lines with 50 statements and `useToasts` and `buildUrl` are called 12+ times. While the file's import count is low, the page concentrates state, fetch logic, validation, and rendering for Deco, Chester, HiBoost, and Alexa credentials all in one component.
violations.fixPrompt: Split `frontend/src/pages/SettingsPage.jsx` into `DecoCredentialsForm.jsx`, `ChesterCredentialsForm.jsx`, `HiBoostCredentialsForm.jsx`, and `AlexaCredentialsForm.jsx` subcomponents, each with its own state and submit handler. Have `SettingsPage` only render tabs/sections.

violations.title: Component too many responsibilities: `SpeedInsightsPage` is 749 lines with 34 statements
violations.content: `SpeedInsightsPage` in `frontend/src/pages/SpeedInsightsPage.jsx` is 759 lines with 34 statements and calls `buildUrl` 8 times. It performs data fetching, history aggregation, insight rendering, and chart presentation in a single component body — far over the 200-line threshold.
violations.fixPrompt: Extract data fetching into a `useSpeedInsights` hook in `frontend/src/hooks/`, split the page into `<SpeedHistoryChart>`, `<HourlyAveragesChart>`, `<InsightsList>` presentational components, and have `SpeedInsightsPage` only compose them.

violations.title: Component too many responsibilities: `DeviceTable` is 698 lines with 19 statements
violations.content: `DeviceTable` in `frontend/src/components/DeviceTable.jsx` is 705 lines, calls `buildUrl` 6 times, and renders devices in both card and table modes, handles search/filter, edit actions, and group membership. It mixes data mutation, fetch, and complex rendering.

violations.title: Business logic in component: insight derivation lives in `SpeedInsightsPage`

violations.title: Middleman class: `ChesterService._safe_call` only wraps `ChesterClient.api_call`
violations.content: `ChesterService._safe_call` in `backend/services/chester_service.py` and the thin `get_router_status` / `get_cellular_status` / `get_lte_band_config` / `get_lte_traffic_stats` methods exist mostly to forward to `ChesterClient.api_call` / `get_dashboard` / `get_system_info`. violations.title: Missing abstraction: route handlers in `routes/deco.py` open raw `Database.get_connection`
violations.content: `deco.set_deco_service`, `deco.auto_name_deco_nodes`, `deco.import_deco_client_names`, `deco.rename_deco_client`, and `deco.get_topology_graph` all call `Database.get_connection` directly inside the route module instead of going through a repository. violations.fixPrompt: Move every direct `Database.get_connection` call out of `backend/routes/deco.py` and `backend/routes/hiboost.py` into dedicated repository methods (e.g. `DecoNodeRepository.upsert_alias`, `HiBoostHistoryRepository.list_recent`). Routes should only depend on services and repositories.

violations.title: Temporal coupling: every route module requires manual `set_*` calls before use
violations.content: Route modules (`alarm_com`, `alexa`, `chester`, `deco`, `digest`, `events`, `health`, `hiboost`, `settings`, `speedtest`) each expose `set_*` setters (e.g. `set_db`, `set_deco_client`, `set_chester_service`, `set_alexa_service`) that must be invoked from `main.startup_event` before any route works. If a setter is missed the route silently throws `AttributeError` at request time. Nothing enforces the call order or completeness.
violations.fixPrompt: Replace the module-level `set_*` globals in `backend/routes/*.py` with FastAPI dependency injection. Define a `Dependencies` container (e.g. via `fastapi.Depends`) holding services and have each route declare what it needs. This removes hidden ordering requirements and makes missing wiring fail at import time.

Refactor `deco`, `chester`, `alexa`, `alarm_com`, and `hiboost` to implement it, and have `backend/routes/settings.py` iterate registered integrations instead of duplicating per-integration endpoints.

The singular name `alert` strongly implies a single alert object, but the next line iterates over it (`for a in alert`) revealing it is actually a list. The misleading name obscures that this is a list and also masks a likely bug — the `limit=1` query will almost never contain the alert matching `alert_id`, so `alert_found` will usually be `None`.

violations.title: `get_device_with_state` writes to the database despite `get_` prefix
violations.content: `get_device_with_state` reads like a pure accessor that returns a device with its current state, but it also mutates the cached device dict (`last_state`, `state_updated_at`, `is_stale`, `parsed_state`) and writes to the database via `_save_device_state_to_db` (line 234-235). A caller looking for a read-only lookup would not expect a DB write on every call, which makes the function unsafe to invoke from read-only contexts or hot paths.
violations.fixPrompt: Either rename `get_device_with_state` in `backend/services/alexa_service.py:216` to something that signals the side effect (e.g. `refresh_device_state`), or split the function into a pure read (returns the device + fetched state) and a separate persistence step the caller invokes when they want the DB to be updated.
violations.snippet:
def get_device_with_state(self, endpoint_id: str) -> Optional[Dict[str, Any]]:
        """Get a single device with its current state"""
        devices = self.get_devices()
        device = next((d for d in devices if d["endpoint_id"] == endpoint_id), None)
        if not device:
            return None

        # Fetch fresh state
        state = self.alexa_client.get_device_state(endpoint_id)
        now = datetime.now()

        device["last_state"] = state
        device["state_updated_at"] = now.isoformat()
        device["is_stale"] = False

        # Parse common state values for easier frontend consumption
        device["parsed_state"] = self._parse_state(state, device["capabilities"])

        if self.db:
            self._save_device_state_to_db(endpoint_id, state, now)

        return device

violations.title: `get_nodes_with_details` writes to the `network_devices` database table
violations.content: The method `get_nodes_with_details` is named like a pure getter, but it has the side effect of mutating the `network_devices` table via `_sync_online_nodes_to_devices`. The sync runs both when serving the cached value (line 97) and after a fresh fetch (line 154), and inside it `self._device_repo.mark_online(device['device_id'])` is called for every Deco node whose MAC matches a known device. Callers who reasonably assume `get_*` is read-only will be surprised that simply reading node details writes to SQLite — especially on cache hits. Either rename the method to reflect the side effect (e.g., `refresh_nodes_and_sync_status`) or move the DB-sync call to an explicit method invoked by the caller, leaving `get_nodes_with_details` purely read-only.
violations.fixPrompt: In `backend/services/deco_service.py`, remove the side-effecting `_sync_online_nodes_to_devices` calls from `get_nodes_with_details` (lines 97 and 154) and expose the sync as a separate explicit method that callers invoke when they actually want the DB to be updated. Alternatively, rename `get_nodes_with_details` to something that signals the write side effect, such as `refresh_and_sync_nodes`, and update all callers accordingly.
violations.snippet:
def get_nodes_with_details(self) -> List[Dict[str, Any]]:
        """
        Get list of Deco nodes with enriched details

        Returns:
            List of node information dictionaries with enriched details:
            - node_id: Unique node identifier
            - node_name: Human-readable node name
            - firmware_version: Current firmware version
            - uptime_seconds: Node uptime in seconds
            - connected_clients: Number of connected clients on this node
            - signal_strength: Signal strength indicator (0-100%)
            - model: Node model name
            - status: Node operational status
            - last_updated: Timestamp of last data update

        Raises:
            InvalidCredentialsError: If not authenticated with Deco API
            APIConnectionError: If API request fails
        """
        # Check if cache is still valid
        if self._is_cache_valid():
            logger.debug("Returning cached node list")
            # 2026-03-10: Still sync on cached returns in case device_repo wasn't ready on first call
            self._sync_online_nodes_to_devices(self._nodes_cache)
            return self._nodes_cache

        try:
            # 2026-03-14: Use get_topology_local() exclusively — it uses _local_api_lock
            # and a fresh temp client, avoiding session races with the persistent deco_client.
            # get_node_list() / get_client_list() called directly on the persistent client
            # bypassed the lock and caused "Empty data field" session conflicts.
            logger.info("Fetching fresh node list from Deco API (via topology local)")
            topology = self.deco_client.get_topology_local()
            raw_nodes = topology.get("nodes", [])
            node_clients_map = topology.get("node_clients", {})

            # Aggregate all clients across nodes into a flat list for compatibility
            local_clients = []
            for clients in node_clients_map.values():
                local_clients.extend(clients)

            # Build clients_by_node index from the per-node topology data
            clients_by_node = {}
            for node in raw_nodes:
                node_mac = node.get("mac", "")
                if node_mac in node_clients_map:
                    clients_by_node[node_mac] = [self._extract_client_details(c) for c in node_clients_map[node_mac]]

            # Build set of node MACs that have clients connected (from topology local data)
            nodes_with_clients = set()
            for node_mac, clients in node_clients_map.items():
                online_clients = [c for c in clients if c.get("online", True)]
                if online_clients:
                    # node_mac from topology is in AA-BB-CC-DD-EE-FF format
                    nodes_with_clients.add(node_mac.upper().replace("-", ":"))

            # Enrich nodes with additional data
            enriched_nodes = []
            for node in raw_nodes:
                enriched_node = self._enrich_node_data(node, clients_by_node)
                enriched_nodes.append(enriched_node)

            # Mark nodes online if they have clients (local API is authoritative)
            for node in enriched_nodes:
                if node["status"] == "offline":
                    node_mac = (node.get("raw_data", {}).get("deviceMac", "")
                                or node.get("raw_data", {}).get("mac", "")).upper().replace("-", ":")
                    if node_mac in nodes_with_clients:
                        node["status"] = "online"
                        logger.info(f"Node {node['node_name']} marked online (has clients via topology)")

            # If local API returned clients but all satellites offline, mark all online.
            # Rationale: a mesh with many clients can't have only 1 node working.
            offline_satellites = [n for n in enriched_nodes if n["status"] == "offline"]
            if local_clients and len(local_clients) > 10 and len(offline_satellites) == len(enriched_nodes) - 1:
                for node in offline_satellites:
                    node["status"] = "online"
                logger.info(f"Marked {len(offline_satellites)} satellite nodes online (mesh has {len(local_clients)} clients)")

            # 2026-03-10: Sync online Deco nodes to network_devices table
            self._sync_online_nodes_to_devices(enriched_nodes)

            # Update cache
            self._nodes_cache = enriched_nodes
            self._cache_timestamp = datetime.now()

            logger.info(f"Retrieved and cached {len(enriched_nodes)} nodes")
            return enriched_nodes

violations.title: Single `/api/health` endpoint with no liveness/readiness distinction
violations.content: The FastAPI app exposes only a single health endpoint `GET /api/health` in `backend/main.py` (plus `GET /api/network/health-score` in `routes/health.py`, which is a domain-level network score, not a service health check). There is no distinct readiness endpoint (e.g., `/ready` or `/healthz/ready`) versus liveness endpoint (e.g., `/healthz/live`), so container orchestrators and load balancers cannot differentiate between "process is alive" and "process is ready to serve traffic with all dependencies up". Given the long list of critical dependencies wired up in `startup_event` — SQLite (`db`), Deco client, Chester client, Alexa service, Alarm.com client, HiBoost service, speed test service, digest service, health service, correlation service, polling service, retention scheduler — a readiness check that verifies these subsystems are reachable is essential. The metadata also gives no indication that the existing `/api/health` handler queries the database or any external client; a health check that returns 200 without verifying dependencies will allow load balancers to route traffic to an instance whose Deco/Chester/Alexa integrations are broken, masking outages.
violations.fixPrompt: Add two distinct health endpoints in `backend/main.py` (or a dedicated `routes/health.py`): (1) `GET /healthz/live` that returns 200 as long as the process is running, with no dependency checks — used by orchestrators to decide whether to restart the pod; (2) `GET /healthz/ready` that performs lightweight verification of each critical dependency wired up in `startup_event` (a `SELECT 1` against SQLite via `db`, a status check on `deco_service`, `chester_service`, `alexa_service`, `alarm_com_client`, `hiboost_service`, and verification that schedulers like `polling_service`, `speedtest_scheduler`, `hiboost_scheduler`, and `retention_scheduler` are running) and returns 503 if any required dependency is down. Keep the existing `/api/health` as a backwards-compatible alias for readiness, but document the new endpoints and wire them into the deployment manifests / `docker-compose.yml` as `livenessProbe` and `readinessProbe`.

violations.title: Alarm.com route handlers do not import or propagate a correlation ID
violations.content: The `routes/alarm_com.py` module crosses a service boundary by calling the external Alarm.com cloud API (`login_alarm_com`, `request_otp`, `submit_otp`, `send_partition_command`, `send_lock_command`, etc.) but the imports list (`fastapi, pydantic, typing, logging, json, os, utils, utils`) does not include `services.correlation_service`, and none of the handler signatures accept a `Request` parameter to extract a correlation/trace ID header. As a result, security-sensitive operations like OTP requests, partition arm/disarm, and lock commands cannot be traced from the originating HTTP client through this backend to the upstream Alarm.com cloud. When debugging duplicate OTPs or false-positive lock commands, operators have no shared identifier linking the client request, the backend log lines, and the upstream Alarm.com audit log entry.
violations.fixPrompt: In `backend/routes/alarm_com.py`, import `services.correlation_service`, add a `Request` parameter to each handler that issues an external Alarm.com call, extract the `X-Request-ID` (or generate one if absent), bind it to a logging context via the correlation service, and pass it as a header to the Alarm.com client requests so it appears in upstream logs and in every `logger.info`/`logger.error` emitted during the call.

violations.title: `send_lock_command` lock/unlock has no idempotency protection
violations.content: `send_lock_command` dispatches a `lock` or `unlock` action to a physical smart lock with no idempotency key, no check of the lock's current state, and no deduplication window. A retried request — whether from a flaky network, an impatient user double-tap, or an HTTP infrastructure retry — will issue the lock/unlock command twice. Each command typically generates a push notification, an audit-log entry, and an audible chime on the lock hardware. Duplicate unlock attempts are particularly concerning because they appear in the security audit trail and can obscure genuine unauthorized access attempts. Worse, an `unlock` retry triggered after the user has already physically locked the door behind them would unlock it again.
violations.fixPrompt: Require clients to pass an `Idempotency-Key` header (or include one in the `LockCommand` body) and cache the first response keyed by `(lock_id, command, idempotency_key)` for a short window (e.g., 60 seconds). On a retry with the same key, return the cached response instead of re-issuing the command. Additionally, consider querying the lock's current state from `alarm_com_client.get_locks()` before dispatching — if the lock is already in the desired state, return a 200 with `already_in_state: true` rather than dispatching the duplicate command.

violations.title: `send_device_command` Alexa command dispatch is non-idempotent
violations.content: `send_device_command` calls `alexa_service.send_command(endpoint_id, cmd.command, cmd.params)` to issue arbitrary commands (including security-sensitive `unlock` with PIN — see lines 477-478) to Alexa-controlled endpoints with no idempotency key, no dedup of recent identical commands, and no check of the current device state. The function explicitly handles `unlock` commands, which when retried will attempt to unlock the lock a second time, generating duplicate audit-log entries and physical-device chimes. For commands like setting brightness, color, or thermostat setpoints, a retry can push the device to an intermediate value and back, briefly visible to occupants. Because Alexa's upstream API has variable latency, client retries are likely.
violations.fixPrompt: Add an optional `idempotency_key` field to `DeviceCommand` (or require an `Idempotency-Key` header). Cache `(endpoint_id, command, params_hash, idempotency_key) -> result` for a short TTL (60-120 seconds) and short-circuit retries with the cached response. For the `unlock` path specifically, also persist the `(endpoint_id, idempotency_key, timestamp)` to prevent duplicate audit entries on the alarm provider side.

violations.title: `control_smart_home_device` plug/light control is non-idempotent
violations.content: `control_smart_home_device` forwards arbitrary smart home actions (`turnOn`, `turnOff`, brightness/color changes) to `alexa_client.smart_home_control(entity_id, cmd.action, cmd.params)` with no idempotency key and no current-state check. The endpoint is mapped to plugs and lights (per `get_smart_home_controllable`), which means a retried `turnOff` request that succeeds upstream but times out at the HTTP layer could be retried by the client and toggle the device off → on → off, visibly flickering the light. For color/brightness commands, retries can briefly push the device through intermediate values. Because Alexa's web API is documented as flaky throughout this file, retries from the frontend are likely.
violations.fixPrompt: Add an optional `idempotency_key` to `SmartHomeCommand` (or accept an `Idempotency-Key` header) and cache `(entity_id, action, params_hash, idempotency_key) -> result` for a short TTL (e.g., 60 seconds). On a duplicate request, return the cached response and skip the upstream call. Alternatively, fetch the device's current state via `alexa_client.get_smart_home_devices()` before issuing the command and short-circuit when the device is already in the requested state.

violations.title: `optimizeNetwork` lacks retry on Deco mesh API failure
violations.content: `optimizeNetwork` calls `/deco/optimize-network` which proxies to the external Deco mesh router hardware. A single transient failure (network blip, Deco device temporarily unreachable) causes the operation to fail immediately and show an error banner. Since this interacts with external network hardware over the LAN that often has transient connectivity issues, the call should retry with exponential backoff before reporting failure.
violations.fixPrompt: Wrap the `fetch(buildUrl('/deco/optimize-network'), ...)` call in `optimizeNetwork` with retry logic — e.g., 2-3 retries with exponential backoff (500ms, 1s, 2s) on network errors or 5xx responses before showing the failure banner. Consider extracting a `fetchWithRetry` helper for reuse across Deco calls.

violations.title: `toggleClientMesh` lacks retry on Deco mesh control call
violations.content: `toggleClientMesh` POSTs to `/deco/client-mesh`, which the backend forwards to the external Deco router. The function rolls back on any failure but does not retry. Because Deco hardware calls have transient failure modes (temporary auth refresh, router busy), wrapping a single fetch and immediately reverting on first error degrades UX. The call should retry with backoff before rolling back the optimistic state.
violations.fixPrompt: Add exponential backoff retry (e.g., 2 retries) to the `fetch(buildUrl('/deco/client-mesh'), ...)` call in `toggleClientMesh` before rolling back the optimistic `setClientNodeMap` update. Only revert state if retries are exhausted.

violations.title: `setPreferredDecoNode` lacks retry on update failure
violations.content: `setPreferredDecoNode` issues a PUT to `/devices/${deviceId}` that ultimately drives a Deco mesh pin change. On any non-ok response or thrown error it immediately rolls back the optimistic update with no retry. Transient backend or Deco hardware errors will incorrectly flip the UI state back even when the user's intent could have succeeded on a second attempt.
violations.fixPrompt: Add a small retry loop (2 attempts, exponential backoff) around the `fetch(buildUrl(`/devices/${deviceId}`), ...)` call in `setPreferredDecoNode` before performing the rollback in `setDevices`.

violations.title: `handleOtpSubmit` lacks retry on Alarm.com 2FA submission
violations.content: `handleOtpSubmit` posts the OTP code to `/alarm-com/otp/submit`, which is forwarded to the external Alarm.com authentication service to complete a security-system 2FA flow. The call uses a single `fetch` with no retry-with-backoff on transient network or 5xx failures. Because OTP codes typically have a short validity window (often 30–60 seconds), a transient TLS/network hiccup forces the user to wait for a new code and re-submit — and may lock the user out if too many attempts are consumed.
violations.fixPrompt: Wrap the `fetch(buildUrl('/alarm-com/otp/submit'), ...)` call in `handleOtpSubmit` with a small retry helper that retries on network errors and 5xx responses with exponential backoff (e.g., 2 retries at 500ms and 1500ms). Do not retry on 4xx responses (invalid code), since retrying a bad code wastes attempts. Distinguish in the UI between `OTP failed` (4xx — bad code) and `OTP submission failed, please try again` (network/5xx — transient).

violations.title: f-string debug log embeds exception in `_decode_alias`
violations.content: `logger.debug(f"Base64 alias decode failed: {e}")` interpolates the exception into the message string via an f-string. Each failure produces a unique message line, which prevents log aggregators from grouping `_decode_alias` errors and discards the structured exception fields. The bare exception text also makes it hard to capture the original input that failed to decode. Prefer structured logging (e.g. `logger.debug("Base64 alias decode failed", exc_info=True, extra={"alias": alias})`) so the static message can be grouped and the exception/traceback captured cleanly.
violations.fixPrompt: In `backend/services/deco_client.py` line 553, replace `logger.debug(f"Base64 alias decode failed: {e}")` with a structured form such as `logger.debug("Base64 alias decode failed", exc_info=True, extra={"alias": alias})` so the message is static and the exception/inputs are emitted as structured fields.

violations.content: `get_presence_history` loops over `days` (default 7) and, for each day, filters the entire `events` list with `ts.startswith(date_str)` (line 388-391). This is O(days × events). With long retention windows or busy networks, the event list can grow large, and the same list is re-scanned for every day in the window. The same pattern is repeated for the hourly slot computation at lines 421-427. Build a single dict mapping `date_str -> list[(etype, ts)]` once (O(events)), then look up each day in O(1).

violations.title: Async `_poll_loop` calls blocking `_record_snapshot` directly on event loop
violations.content: `_poll_loop` is an `async` coroutine running on the asyncio event loop, but it calls `self._record_snapshot()` synchronously (line 53). `_record_snapshot` performs blocking HTTPS requests to the HiBoost cloud API (`get_device_list`, `get_rf_params`) via the synchronous `requests` library, plus synchronous SQLite writes including RSA/SHA-256 crypto during HiBoost re-auth (see `hiboost_client._rsa_encrypt`, `_sha256`). Every poll (default every 5 minutes) blocks the asyncio loop — and therefore the FastAPI request handlers sharing that loop — for the full duration of network + DB I/O and any token-refresh crypto. Offload via `await asyncio.to_thread(self._record_snapshot)` (or `loop.run_in_executor`) so the snapshot work runs on a worker thread.

violations.title: Repeated `devices.filter()` passes on every render
violations.content: `App` performs four separate full scans of the `devices` array on every render: `devices.filter(isNewDevice)` at line 69, `devices.filter(d => d.vendor_name)` at line 130, `devices.filter(d => d.status === 'online')` at line 133, and `devices.filter(d => d.status === 'offline')` at line 134. For a network-monitoring dashboard the device list can grow large, and each pass allocates a new array just to read its `.length`. These four O(n) traversals can be collapsed into a single loop (or a single `reduce`) that counts all four metrics in one pass, and the result should be memoized with `useMemo` keyed on `devices` so it does not recompute when unrelated state changes trigger a re-render.
violations.fixPrompt: In `frontend/src/App.jsx`, replace the four separate `devices.filter(...).length` expressions at lines 69, 130, 133, and 134 with a single `useMemo` that iterates `devices` once and returns `{ newDeviceCount, vendorNamesPresent, onlineCount, offlineCount }`. Memoize on `[devices]` so re-renders triggered by unrelated state (e.g. `showInsights`, `theme`, `currentPage`) do not re-traverse the list.

violations.title: Pure-Python P-256 scalar multiplication blocks the event loop
violations.content: `_ec_mul` implements P-256 elliptic-curve scalar multiplication in pure Python using a double-and-add loop over a 256-bit scalar, with each iteration performing `_ec_add` (modular inverse via `pow(a, -1, m)` plus several big-integer multiplications mod `P256_P`). This is many milliseconds of synchronous CPU work and `Spake2PlusClient.compute_share` invokes it four times (lines 379, 380, 393, 398, 401) on top of a 10 000-iteration `hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac` at line 371. The whole `TMPClient.authenticate` path runs synchronously and is called from the backend (`services/`), so it will block FastAPI's event loop for the duration of the handshake. The standard fix is either to use the `cryptography` library's `EllipticCurvePrivateKey` (already imported at line 209) for scalar multiplication, or to wrap the authenticate call in `asyncio.to_thread` / `run_in_executor` so the work happens off the event loop.
violations.fixPrompt: In `backend/tmp_client.py`, replace the pure-Python `_ec_mul` / `_ec_add` calls inside `Spake2PlusClient.compute_share` (lines 378-401) with `cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric.ec` primitives that delegate to OpenSSL. Additionally, any caller that invokes `TMPClient.authenticate()` from async code should call it via `asyncio.to_thread(...)` so the PBKDF2 at line 371 and the EC multiplications do not block the FastAPI event loop.

violations.content: `getGroupColor` and `getGroupName` each perform a linear `groups.find()` and are invoked twice for every entry in `device.device_group_ids` when rendering the group list (lines 341–349). violations.title: `getDeviceName` uses `Array.find` inside render loop
violations.content: `getDeviceName` is defined with `devices.find(d => d.device_id === deviceId)` and is invoked once per event/alert during render at lines 325 and 396 (inside `events.map(...)` and `alerts.map(...)`). For each render this is an `O(events × devices)` lookup that scales poorly: with hundreds of events (the default `limit` is 100 and max 1000) and dozens of devices the work is significant and runs on every render — including each filter change, pagination, or polling-driven prop refresh. violations.title: Repeated `smartDevices.filter` inside `deviceTypes.map` for counts
violations.content: For each device type in the filter-tab loop, `smartDevices.filter(d => d.device_type === type).length` is recomputed on every render. With `deviceTypes` derived from `new Set(smartDevices.map(...))`, this is O(N × M) where N is `smartDevices.length` and M is the number of distinct types. A single pass that builds a count map (e.g. `smartDevices.reduce((acc, d) => { acc[d.device_type] = (acc[d.device_type]||0)+1; return acc; }, {})`) yields O(N) and O(1) lookups per tab. The same pattern would naturally produce `deviceTypes` from the map's keys.

Render the tabs by iterating `Object.entries(typeCounts)` and read the count directly instead of re-filtering.

violations.title: Repeated `fallbackClients.filter(...)` for unnamed count
violations.content: `fallbackClients.filter(c => !c.friendly_name).length` is computed twice in the same render block (once for the conditional, once for the displayed count). Each call walks the full array. Compute the unnamed count once into a local `const` above the JSX and reuse it. With a long device list this is a small but avoidable cost; more importantly the duplicated traversal hints the structure should be summarized into a counts object alongside `getNodeStats`.

violations.title: Three repeated `devices.filter()` passes on every render
violations.content: `SmartHomePage` walks the `devices` array three times on every render — once for the filtered view and twice more to compute `lightCount` and `plugCount`. The two count traversals could be combined into a single `reduce` (or a single `forEach`/`for` loop that tallies kinds while filtering), giving O(n) work instead of O(3n). The counts are also recomputed each render even when `devices` hasn't changed, so wrapping them in `useMemo` (or inlining the tally into one pass) would also avoid redundant work on unrelated state changes (e.g. `actionLoading`, `identifyState`, `banner`).

Iterate `devices` once, counting `light` and `plug` items while collecting the filtered subset, so the array is only traversed one time per render and only recomputed when `devices` or `filter` changes.

violations.title: Inline handlers and helpers recreated every render in `App`
violations.content: `App` defines `isNewDevice`, `handleDeviceClick`, `handleDetailCardClose`, `handleDeviceUpdate`, `handleDeviceDelete`, `navigateTo`, and `formatDate` as inline closures on every render. These are then passed as props to `StatusStrip`, `SystemStatusCard`, `SpeedTestCard`, `DeviceTable`, `DeviceDetailCard`, etc. Because `useDevicePolling` updates `devices` and other state on every poll/SSE event, `App` re-renders frequently, and every child that receives these unstable callback props is forced to re-render too — even when nothing meaningful for that child has changed. Wrap these in `useCallback` (and `formatDate`/`isNewDevice` are pure utilities that could live in module scope), and memoize the leaf components with `React.memo` so stable prop references actually prevent re-renders.
violations.fixPrompt: In `frontend/src/App.jsx`, hoist pure helpers `isNewDevice` and `formatDate` to module scope (they only read their arguments), wrap the event handlers `handleDeviceClick`, `handleDetailCardClose`, `handleDeviceUpdate`, `handleDeviceDelete`, and `navigateTo` in `useCallback` with correct dependencies, and add `React.memo` to `StatusStrip`, `SystemStatusCard`, `SpeedTestCard`, `CellularCard`, and `DeviceTable` so they skip renders when their props are referentially stable.

violations.title: `DeviceTable` re-renders on every unrelated `App` state change due to prop drilling
violations.content: `DeviceTable` receives 17 props drilled from `App`, including freshly-allocated functions (`handleDeviceUpdate`, `isNewDevice`, `formatDate`, `handleDeviceClick`, `setScanning`) and many state slices returned from `useDevicePolling`. Whenever any unrelated `App`-level state changes — `theme`, `selectedDevice`, `showDetailCard`, `currentPage`, `mountedPages`, `showInsights`, `scanning`, or the banner — `App` re-renders, all of these inline functions are recreated, and `DeviceTable` (a heavy table component) re-renders even when its own data is unchanged. Consider colocating the device-table state (e.g. `clientNodeMap`, `homeStatus`) inside `DeviceTable` or a dedicated context, lifting only what `App` itself uses, and memoizing the component so stable references actually short-circuit renders.
violations.fixPrompt: In `frontend/src/App.jsx`, reduce the prop surface on `DeviceTable` by (a) moving `clientNodeMap`/`setClientNodeMap` and similar device-only state out of `useDevicePolling` into `DeviceTable` or a context provider scoped to the dashboard, (b) wrapping the callback props in `useCallback`, and (c) exporting `DeviceTable` wrapped in `React.memo`. Alternatively, expose the polling data via a `DevicePollingContext` so `DeviceTable` consumes it directly instead of receiving it through `App`.

<DeviceTable
          devices={devices}
          deviceGroups={deviceGroups}
          homeStatus={homeStatus}
          setHomeStatus={setHomeStatus}
          handleDeviceUpdate={handleDeviceUpdate}
          formatDate={formatDate}
          isNewDevice={isNewDevice}
          banner={banner}
          showBanner={showBanner}
          pollingConfig={pollingConfig}
          clientNodeMap={clientNodeMap}
          setClientNodeMap={setClientNodeMap}
          decoNodeMacs={decoNodeMacs}
          decoNodesMap={decoNodesMap}
          decoNodeDetails={decoNodeDetails}
          chesterInfo={chesterInfo}
          setDevices={setDevices}
          onDeviceClick={handleDeviceClick}
          onScanningChange={setScanning}
        />

violations.title: Inline `style={{ display: ... }}` objects recreated for every mounted page on every `App` render
violations.content: Each lazy-mounted page wrapper uses an inline `style={{ display: currentPage === '...' ? '' : 'none' }}` object that is freshly allocated on every `App` render. Because `App` re-renders on every device poll update via `useDevicePolling`, the wrapping `div`s and their children (`DecoTopologyPage`, `AlexaDevicesPage`, `SmartHomePage`, `SpeedInsightsPage`, `HiBoostPage`, `SettingsPage`) receive a new `style` prop reference and may re-render even though the visibility hasn't changed. Memoize these style objects (e.g. with `useMemo` keyed on `currentPage`) or use CSS classes toggled by `currentPage` so the page subtrees aren't re-rendered on unrelated state churn.
violations.fixPrompt: In `frontend/src/App.jsx` lines 252-257, replace each inline `style={{ display: currentPage === 'x' ? '' : 'none' }}` with a className like `className={currentPage === 'x' ? '' : 'is-hidden'}` (with a corresponding `.is-hidden { display: none; }` rule) so the style prop reference is stable across `App` renders. Then wrap the page components in `React.memo` to ensure they don't re-render when only `App`'s polling state changes.

violations.title: Per-device inline style and per-render helper allocations in topology card list
violations.content: Inside the `nodeGroups.map(...)` -> `devices.map(...)` loop, every device card receives a freshly allocated `style={{ backgroundColor: ... }}` object and calls `getDeviceIcon(device)`/`getConnectionBadge(device.connection_type)` on every render, returning new object literals. Combined with the parent's auto-refresh `setInterval` (line 139), the entire list of `topo-device-card` nodes re-creates these objects on every poll. Extracting the device card into a `React.memo`'d child component and/or memoizing the icon/badge lookups would prevent unnecessary re-renders of the unchanged device rows on each topology refresh.
violations.fixPrompt: In `frontend/src/components/DecoTopologyView.jsx`, extract the inner `topo-device-card` JSX (lines 486-512) into a separate `TopoDeviceCard` component wrapped in `React.memo`, passing only the `device` prop. Inside that component, compute `getDeviceIcon` and `getConnectionBadge` with `useMemo` keyed on the relevant device fields, and inline the `backgroundColor` style as a memoized object so it doesn't change across topology refresh polls when the device data hasn't changed.

violations.title: Inline `onClick` arrow re-creates closure per `DeviceCard` each render
violations.content: Inside the grid branch each `DeviceCard` receives `onClick={() => onDeviceClick(device)}`, a new function instance created on every render of `DeviceTable`. Because `DeviceTable` holds local state that changes on every keystroke (`deviceQuery`, `inlineEditValue`, `loading`, `optimizeLoading`, `sortConfig`), every keystroke or filter change re-creates these closures and cascades a re-render across the entire device list. `DeviceCard` itself is not wrapped in `React.memo`, so even if the closure were stable the children would still re-render. Combine `React.memo(DeviceCard)` with a `useCallback`-wrapped handler that takes the device as an argument (e.g. via `data-` attributes or passing the device id and resolving in the parent) so unaffected cards skip rendering.
violations.fixPrompt: In `frontend/src/components/DeviceTable.jsx` around lines 358-366, replace the inline `onClick={() => onDeviceClick(device)}` with a stable callback by wrapping `onDeviceClick` (or a local handler that accepts a device id) in `useCallback`, and memoize `DeviceCard` with `React.memo` in `frontend/src/components/DeviceCard.jsx` so it skips rendering when its props are referentially equal. Consider passing `deviceId` to the card and looking the device up in the parent to avoid closure capture.

violations.title: Per-row inline closures and inline-computed objects force full table re-render on every keystroke
violations.content: Each `<tr>` is built with inline `onClick`, `onKeyDown`, `onDoubleClick`, `onBlur`, `onChange` arrows and an IIFE (`(() => { ... })()`) that re-computes `nodeInfo`, `decoNodesMap` entries, signal levels, and JSX trees on every render. `DeviceTable` re-renders on every change to local state (`deviceQuery`, `inlineEditValue`, `loading`, `sortConfig`, etc.), so typing in the search field re-renders the entire table including all per-row inline computations and inline arrow closures. The `filteredDevices`/`displayedDevices` arrays at lines 212-249 are also recomputed every render with no `useMemo`. Extract each row into a memoized `DeviceRow` component receiving primitive props, wrap event handlers in `useCallback`, and memoize the filter/sort pipeline with `useMemo` keyed on the relevant inputs.
violations.fixPrompt: Refactor `frontend/src/components/DeviceTable.jsx` so each table row is a separate `DeviceRow` component wrapped in `React.memo`, receiving `device`, `clientNodeMap`, `decoNodeMacs`, `decoNodesMap`, `decoNodeDetails`, `chesterInfo`, `isNew`, and stable callbacks (`onDeviceClick`, `onPreferDecoNode`, `onToggleMesh`) created with `useCallback`. Memoize `filteredDevices` and `displayedDevices` with `useMemo` keyed on `devices`, `deviceQuery`, `deviceStatusFilter`, `sortConfig`, and `clientNodeMap`. Move per-row inline computations (`nodeInfo`, `signalLevel`, etc.) into the memoized row component.

violations.title: `DeviceCard` is purely presentational but not wrapped in `React.memo`
violations.content: `DeviceCard` is a pure render of `device`, `groups`, `isNew`, and `onClick`, but it is exported as a plain function component. Its parent (`DeviceTable`) re-renders on every keystroke and timer/poll update, which causes every `DeviceCard` in the grid to re-render even when its underlying `device` row is unchanged. Wrap the component in `React.memo` so referentially stable props short-circuit the render. This must be paired with stabilizing the inline `onClick` arrow at `DeviceTable.jsx:364` (see related finding), otherwise memoization will never hit.
violations.fixPrompt: In `frontend/src/components/DeviceCard.jsx` wrap the default export in `React.memo`, i.e. `export default React.memo(DeviceCard)`. Pair this with a `useCallback`-stabilized `onClick` from `DeviceTable.jsx` (currently inline at line 364) so referentially-equal props enable the memo bail-out.

violations.title: `AlertContainer` re-renders every `DeviceAlert` whenever any alert or `devices` array changes
violations.content: `AlertContainer` maps over `alerts` and for each alert runs `devices.find(...)` inline and renders a non-memoized `DeviceAlert`. Whenever the parent passes a new `alerts` or `devices` array reference (very common with polling/SSE in this app), every `DeviceAlert` re-renders even if its specific `alert`/`device` is unchanged. Memoize `DeviceAlert` with `React.memo`, and ideally precompute an `alertId -> device` map with `useMemo` so each iteration is O(1) and the per-alert `device` reference only changes when that device actually changes.
violations.fixPrompt: In `frontend/src/components/DeviceAlert.jsx`, wrap `DeviceAlert` in `React.memo` before the default export. In `AlertContainer`, build a `useMemo`'d `Map` of `device_id -> device` from `devices`, then look up the device by id inside the `.map` callback to avoid `find()` allocating per render and to keep the `device` prop reference stable.

violations.title: Event list rows re-render on every filter keystroke; `devices.find` runs O(events × devices) per render
violations.content: The events list (`events.map(...)`) renders inline JSX with `getDeviceName(event.device_id)` doing a linear `devices.find` for every row on every render. Since `EventLog` re-renders whenever any local filter state changes (`startDate`, `endDate`, `limit`, `selectedDevice`, etc.), the whole list re-renders and every row pays the O(devices) lookup. Extract the row into a memoized `EventRow` component receiving primitives, and replace `devices.find` with a `useMemo`'d `Map` keyed by `device_id`.
violations.fixPrompt: In `frontend/src/components/EventLog.jsx`, build `const devicesById = useMemo(() => new Map(devices.map(d => [d.device_id, d])), [devices]);` and use it inside `getDeviceName`. Extract the event row JSX (lines 315-333) into an `EventRow` component wrapped in `React.memo` that receives `event`, `deviceName`, and color primitives so changing filter inputs doesn't re-render unchanged rows.

{events.map((event) => (
{event.event_type} {getDeviceName(event.device_id)} {formatTimestamp(event.timestamp)}
{event.description && (

)}

{/* Pagination controls */}

)}

violations.title: `chartData` recreated inline every render defeats downstream `useMemo`
violations.content: `chartData` is built with `history.map(...)` on every render of `SpeedInsightsPage` without `useMemo`, producing a fresh array reference each time. It is then used as a dependency in the `useMemo` hooks for `bandCombinationData` (line 207) and `carrierHistoryData` (line 275), so those memoizations are effectively useless — the memo dependency changes on every render and the heavy `forEach`/`reduce`/`Object.entries` work re-runs even when `history` and `chesterInfo` are unchanged. The new array reference is also passed as the `data` prop to multiple `ResponsiveContainer`/`AreaChart`/`LineChart`/`BarChart` subtrees (e.g. lines 442, 491, 547, 568), causing the entire Recharts subtree to reconcile/re-render on every state change in this page (banner timeouts, polling intervals, toggle states). Wrap the array construction in `useMemo(() => history.map(...), [history])` so the reference is stable and the downstream memoizations and chart components can short-circuit.
violations.fixPrompt: In `frontend/src/pages/SpeedInsightsPage.jsx`, wrap the `chartData` construction (lines 167-171) in `useMemo`: `const chartData = useMemo(() => history.map(t => ({ ...t, time: formatTime(t.timestamp), dateTime: formatDateTime(t.timestamp) })), [history]);`. This stabilizes the array reference so the dependent `useMemo` calls for `bandCombinationData` and `carrierHistoryData` actually memoize, and the Recharts subtrees no longer reconcile on every parent state change.

violations.title: `hourlyChart` rebuilt with `Array.from` every render
violations.content: `hourlyChart` is computed with `Array.from({ length: 24 }, ...)` plus `hourlyAvgs.find(...)` on every render and passed as the `data` prop to the `BarChart` at line 514. Because the array is a new reference on every render, the chart subtree reconciles even when `hourlyAvgs` has not changed (e.g. when the banner timer toggles state or `setShowCellular`/`setShowCarrierTable` flips). Wrap in `useMemo(() => Array.from(...), [hourlyAvgs])` to keep the reference stable.
violations.fixPrompt: In `frontend/src/pages/SpeedInsightsPage.jsx`, wrap the `hourlyChart` construction (lines 174-183) in `useMemo` with `[hourlyAvgs]` as the dependency array, so the `BarChart` at line 514 receives a stable `data` prop and skips reconciliation when unrelated state changes.

violations.title: Inline `chartData.filter(...)` prop creates new array each render
violations.content: The CA-count `LineChart` at line 568 receives `data={chartData.filter(t => t.cellular_ca_count != null)}`, allocating a fresh filtered array on every parent render. Combined with the un-memoized `chartData` above, this forces the entire chart subtree to reconcile whenever any state in `SpeedInsightsPage` changes (banner timeout, toggle, polling tick). Extract this filtered list into a `useMemo` keyed on `chartData` and pass the stable reference.
violations.fixPrompt: In `frontend/src/pages/SpeedInsightsPage.jsx`, hoist the inline `chartData.filter(t => t.cellular_ca_count != null)` at line 568 into a `useMemo` such as `const caCountChartData = useMemo(() => chartData.filter(t => t.cellular_ca_count != null), [chartData]);` and pass `caCountChartData` to the `LineChart`'s `data` prop.
violations.snippet: <LineChart data={chartData.filter(t => t.cellular_ca_count != null)} margin={{ top: 5, right: 20, left: 0, bottom: 5 }}>

violations.title: `import_alexa_mac_addresses` re-fetches the Alexa devices-v2 list solely to count
violations.content: `import_alexa_mac_addresses` calls `alexa_client.get_all_device_macs()` on line 744, which (per the comment on lines 741–742) already iterates `devices-v2` internally to enumerate every Echo/Fire device. Then on line 759 it calls `alexa_client.get_echo_devices_web()` again — hitting the same `devices-v2` Alexa endpoint — just to compute `total_devices = len(raw_devices)`. The second HTTP round-trip to Amazon is redundant: `get_all_device_macs()` already saw the full device list and could have returned the count (or the list could have been deduplicated by having `get_all_device_macs()` return both the MACs and the source device list). This wastes an outbound API call and adds latency on every `/api/alexa/import-mac-addresses` request.
violations.fixPrompt: In `backend/routes/alexa.py`, refactor `import_alexa_mac_addresses` so the Alexa `devices-v2` list is fetched only once. Either (a) change `alexa_client.get_all_device_macs()` to return a tuple `(device_macs, raw_devices)` and use the returned `raw_devices` length for `total_devices`, or (b) call `alexa_client.get_echo_devices_web()` once at the top of the handler, pass the resulting list into a new `get_all_device_macs(devices=...)` overload, and use the same list to compute `total_devices`. Remove the redundant `get_echo_devices_web()` call on line 759.

violations.title: N+1 device lookup in `_enrich_event` over events list
violations.content: `get_events` calls `_enrich_event` once per event in a list comprehension (`[_enrich_event(event) for event in events]`). Each call to `_enrich_event` issues a separate `device_repo.get_by_id(event['device_id'])` lookup (line 96). For the default `limit=100` (max 1000), this means up to 1000 sequential DB round-trips that fetch essentially the same kind of row by primary key — a classic N+1 pattern. These per-row lookups could be batched into a single `SELECT ... WHERE device_id IN (...)` query and joined in Python, or pushed into the SQL query inside `event_service.get_events` via a JOIN against `network_devices`.
violations.fixPrompt: In `backend/routes/events.py`, replace the per-event `_enrich_event` calls in `get_events` and `get_device_events` with a single batched device fetch: collect the distinct `device_id` values from the returned events, call a new `device_repo.get_by_ids(ids)` (or run a single `SELECT device_id, friendly_name, mac_address FROM network_devices WHERE device_id IN (?, ?, ...)`), build a `dict[device_id] -> device` lookup, then enrich each event from that dict instead of querying per row. Apply the same change to `_enrich_alert` in `get_alerts` / `get_device_alerts`.

violations.title: N+1 device lookup in `_enrich_alert` over alerts list
violations.content: `get_alerts` (line 310) and `get_device_alerts` (line 423) enrich each alert by calling `_enrich_alert` in a list comprehension. Each enrichment does its own `device_repo.get_by_id(alert['device_id'])` (line 117), so a 50-item alert list triggers 50 separate device-by-id queries. These are identical-shape requests issued sequentially without deduplication and should be batched into a single query keyed by the set of distinct `device_id` values found in the alerts list.
violations.fixPrompt: In `backend/routes/events.py`, before enriching alerts in `get_alerts` and `get_device_alerts`, gather `{a['device_id'] for a in alerts if a.get('device_id')}` and fetch them in one shot (e.g. `device_repo.get_by_ids(ids)` or a single `SELECT ... WHERE device_id IN (...)`). Build a `dict[device_id] -> device` and have `_enrich_alert` accept that map instead of calling `device_repo.get_by_id` per alert. Same pattern applies to `_enrich_event`.

violations.title: Per-client DB queries in `get_topology_graph` client loop
violations.content: Inside the client-rendering loop in `get_topology_graph`, each Deco client triggers up to two independent DB round-trips against `network_devices`: `_get_node_friendly_name(raw_mac)` (line 1239) opens a connection and runs `SELECT friendly_name FROM network_devices WHERE LOWER(mac_address) = ?`, and the IP fallback at lines 1248-1254 opens another connection and runs `SELECT current_ip FROM network_devices WHERE LOWER(mac_address) = ?`. For a typical home with dozens of clients across all Deco nodes, this is dozens of nearly-identical point lookups issued sequentially with no deduplication. They could be replaced with a single `SELECT mac_address, friendly_name, current_ip FROM network_devices WHERE LOWER(mac_address) IN (?, ?, ...)` keyed by the set of client MACs before the loop runs.
violations.fixPrompt: In `backend/routes/deco.py`, before the `for node_mac, clients in node_clients.items():` loop in `get_topology_graph`, collect all normalized client MACs into a set. Run a single SQL query: `SELECT LOWER(mac_address), friendly_name, current_ip FROM network_devices WHERE LOWER(mac_address) IN (...)`. Build a `dict[mac -> (friendly_name, current_ip)]`. In the loop, look up `db_dev_name` and `ip_addr` from the dict instead of calling `_get_node_friendly_name` and opening a per-row connection.
