violations.title: Three endpoints independently call `get_topology_local()`
violations.content: `get_client_node_map` (line 652), `get_topology` (line 825), and `get_topology_graph` (line 1064) each invoke `deco_service.deco_client.get_topology_local()` from scratch on every request. The dashboard typically loads all three endpoints together (client-node map for the device table, JSON topology for the graph data, SVG topology for the rendered image), so a single page load triggers three identical expensive calls into the Deco LuCI local API for the same payload. While `get_topology` and `get_topology_graph` each have a private route-level cache (`_topology_json_cache` / `_topology_svg_cache`), the underlying `get_topology_local()` result is not shared across endpoints, so cold loads and `get_client_node_map` (which has no cache at all) still re-fetch it. A shared service-level cache for `get_topology_local()` (e.g. on `deco_service`) would let all three endpoints reuse the same payload.
violations.fixPrompt: In `backend/services/deco_service.py` (or wherever `deco_service` exposes the client), add a short-TTL (e.g. 30-60s) cached wrapper such as `get_topology_local_cached()` that stores the last result plus a timestamp and returns the cached value if fresh. Then replace the three direct `client.get_topology_local()` calls in `backend/routes/deco.py` (`get_client_node_map`, `get_topology`, `get_topology_graph`) with `deco_service.get_topology_local_cached()` so concurrent dashboard fetches share a single upstream call.

violations.title: `DecoWiFiQoSView` independently polls `/deco/wifi-config` already fetched by `DecoWiFiConfigEditor`
violations.content: `DecoWiFiQoSView` polls `/deco/wifi-config` every `refreshInterval` ms (default 10s) inside its own `useEffect`. The sibling component `DecoWiFiConfigEditor` also fetches the same `/deco/wifi-config` endpoint independently (in `fetchCurrentConfig` and inside `verifyConfigChanges`). When both components are mounted together on a Deco/Settings page, each fetches the same endpoint with no shared cache or deduplication, doubling the request volume. The data should be lifted to a shared parent (or a hook/context) and passed down to both components.
violations.fixPrompt: Hoist the `/deco/wifi-config` fetch into a shared hook (e.g., `useDecoWifiConfig`) or a parent component, so `DecoWiFiQoSView` and `DecoWiFiConfigEditor` consume the same result. Pass the config and a refetch callback as props instead of each component issuing its own fetch and interval.

violations.title: `DecoWiFiConfigEditor` fetches `/deco/wifi-config` independently of sibling `DecoWiFiQoSView`
violations.content: `DecoWiFiConfigEditor` calls `fetchCurrentConfig` on mount (and again from `handleReset`) hitting `/deco/wifi-config`. The sibling `DecoWiFiQoSView` polls the same endpoint on its own interval. Two components fetching the same endpoint without deduplication is exactly the redundant-fetch pattern the rule targets — the result should be shared.
violations.fixPrompt: Lift the `/deco/wifi-config` fetch to a parent component or a shared hook (`useDecoWifiConfig`). Have `DecoWiFiConfigEditor` consume the cached value and call the refetch function after a successful PUT instead of issuing its own GET.

violations.title: Sequential fetches in `DecoWiFiQoSView` could be parallelized
violations.content: Inside the polling `fetchData` callback, `/deco/wifi-config` is awaited before `/deco/qos` is requested. The two requests are independent and should run in parallel with `Promise.all` to halve the user-perceived latency on every poll tick (default every 10s). This is not strictly the same endpoint twice, but it is unnecessary serial network usage on a repeating interval.
violations.fixPrompt: Replace the two sequential `await fetch(...)` calls in the `fetchData` callback with `const [wifiResponse, qosResponse] = await Promise.all([fetch(buildUrl('/deco/wifi-config'), ...), fetch(buildUrl('/deco/qos'), ...)]);` then await each `.json()` in parallel as well.

violations.title: Duplicate `fetchEvents` calls from overlapping `useEffect` hooks
violations.content: Three `useEffect` hooks fetch events with overlapping dependencies, causing redundant requests to `/api/events`. When a filter changes (e.g. `selectedDevice`), the `fetchEvents` `useCallback` identity changes — this fires the effect at line 112 (calling `fetchEvents()`) AND the effect at line 128 (also calling `fetchEvents()` because `fetchEvents` is in its deps), producing two identical requests in quick succession. The same double-fetch happens on `activeTab` switching to 'events'. The middle effect at line 121 only resets `offset` and doesn't trigger a fetch itself, but it doesn't prevent the duplication either.
violations.fixPrompt: Consolidate the three `useEffect` hooks in `EventLog.jsx` (lines 112-132) into a single effect that calls either `fetchEvents()` or `fetchAlerts()` based on `activeTab`, depending on `[activeTab, selectedDevice, selectedEventType, startDate, endDate, limit, offset]` directly rather than the memoized callback identity. Reset `offset` in the filter change handlers (e.g. inside `setSelectedDevice`) instead of in a separate effect to avoid the cascade where one state change triggers multiple effects each issuing a fetch.

violations.title: SSE handler and `fastPoll` fetch the same endpoints without dedup or debounce
violations.content: The SSE `device_update` listener calls `getDevices()`, `getActiveAlerts()`, and `getHomeStatus()` on every push. The `fastPoll` interval (15s, line 306) hits exactly the same three endpoints (`/devices`, `/events/alerts`, `/network/home-status`). If the server pushes multiple `device_update` events in quick succession (e.g. during a scan), each push fires three parallel fetches with no debounce or in-flight deduplication, and a poll tick landing nearby triggers another identical round. There is also no guard against firing while a previous request is still in flight.
violations.fixPrompt: In `useDevicePolling.js`, debounce the SSE `device_update` handler (e.g. coalesce events for ~250ms before refetching) and add an in-flight guard around `getDevices`, `getActiveAlerts`, and `getHomeStatus` so a second invocation while the previous request is pending either returns the same promise or is skipped. Consider passing an `AbortController` to cancel stale fetches and resetting the `fastPoll` interval timer when the SSE handler triggers a refresh so the next poll doesn't immediately repeat the same request.

violations.title: `fetchFallbackClients` re-fires on every `fetchNodes` state transition
violations.content: The `useEffect` that calls `fetchFallbackClients` (which hits `/devices`) declares `[nodes, loading, error]` as its dependency array. Every call to `fetchNodes` mutates all three of these values (`setLoading(true)` → `setNodes(...)` → `setError(null)` → `setLoading(false)`), so a single refresh of the Deco nodes list triggers the `/devices` fetch multiple times in quick succession. With the 60-second auto-refresh interval, this causes 2+ redundant `/devices` requests every minute even though the underlying client list rarely changes during a single nodes refresh. The fetch could run once on mount (and on explicit user refresh) and share its result via cache or a less reactive dependency.
violations.fixPrompt: In `DecoNodesPage.jsx`, refactor the `useEffect` at lines 105–126 so `fetchFallbackClients` does not re-run on every `nodes`/`loading`/`error` change. Either (a) run it once on mount with an empty dependency array and have it refetch on its own interval, or (b) trigger it explicitly inside the `fetchNodes` success path so a single `/deco/nodes` refresh produces exactly one `/devices` call. Avoid coupling the fetch to transient `loading` toggles.

violations.title: `/hiboost/status` re-fetched every 30s just to look up `deviceId`
violations.content: `fetchData` always calls `/hiboost/status` first to discover `status.devices[0].id` before issuing the actual `/hiboost/devices/{id}/rf-params` (or `/refresh`) request. Because the polling interval at line 51 invokes `fetchData()` every 30 seconds, the `/hiboost/status` endpoint is hit twice as often as needed for the entire lifetime of the page, even though the device ID does not change between polls. The component already stores the device ID inside `rfData.device_id` (used by `handleMgcSave` and `handleRfSwitch`), so the status round-trip is redundant after the first successful load.
violations.fixPrompt: In `HiBoostPage.jsx` `fetchData` (lines 18–47), cache the discovered `deviceId` (e.g. in a `useRef` or state) after the first `/hiboost/status` call and short-circuit subsequent polls to skip `/hiboost/status` when the ID is already known. Only re-fetch status when the cached ID is invalidated (e.g. on auth failure or explicit retry), so each 30-second poll issues a single `/hiboost/devices/{id}/rf-params` request instead of two requests.

violations.title: `/chester/system-info` re-fetched whenever `historyHours` changes
violations.content: The `useEffect` depends on `[fetchAll, fetchChester, fetchHiboostHistory]`. Both `fetchAll` and `fetchHiboostHistory` are `useCallback`s with `[historyHours]` as a dependency, so their identities change every time the user clicks a different time-range button (6h, 12h, 24h, …, 1y, or Custom). That re-triggers the effect, which clears and recreates all three intervals AND calls `fetchChester()` immediately even though `/chester/system-info` has no relation to `historyHours`. As a result, `/chester/system-info` is hit redundantly on every time-range change in addition to its 30-second interval. The Chester fetch could be moved into its own `useEffect` whose deps do not include the history-window callbacks.
violations.fixPrompt: In `frontend/src/pages/SpeedInsightsPage.jsx` around lines 97-105, split the single `useEffect` into separate effects so that `fetchChester` is not re-invoked when `historyHours` changes. Place `fetchChester()` and its `setInterval(fetchChester, 30000)` in their own `useEffect` with deps `[fetchChester]`, and keep `fetchAll`/`fetchHiboostHistory` (which legitimately depend on `historyHours`) in another effect. This prevents redundant calls to `/chester/system-info` every time the user changes the history time-range button.

violations.title: `sendCommand` swallows fetch errors with no user feedback
violations.content: The `catch` block in `sendCommand` catches a broad `err`, logs it via `console.error`, and then continues execution as if nothing happened. The `finally` block clears `sending`, but no error state is surfaced to the user — they see the button re-enable and assume the Alexa command succeeded. Additionally, the success path only calls `onStateChange` when `response.ok` is true; a non-ok response (e.g. 500) is silently ignored with no `else` branch, so the function returns a misleading success-like outcome for both network and HTTP failures.
violations.fixPrompt: In `sendCommand` (lines 45-67 of `AlexaDeviceCard.jsx`), add user-visible error handling: introduce an `error` state, set it in the `catch` block (preserving `err` and any HTTP status), and also handle the `!response.ok` case by reading the response body and surfacing the error. Render the error in the card UI so command failures are visible rather than silently logged.

violations.title: `fetchGraph` silently swallows fetch errors
violations.content: The `catch` block in `fetchGraph` logs the error via `console.error` and then falls through to `finally` without updating any error state or notifying the caller. The non-ok branch at line 126 also only emits `console.warn`. The component continues as if nothing failed — `graphSvg` stays at its previous value (or remains `null`) and the user sees the generic 'Failed to generate graph. Try refreshing.' message regardless of whether the cause was a 500, a network outage, or an auth failure. This is the classic 'log and continue' anti-pattern that hides real failures from both the user and the existing `error` UI surface used by `fetchTopology`.
violations.fixPrompt: In `fetchGraph` (lines 118-133 of `DecoTopologyView.jsx`), surface failures: set an error state (or reuse the existing `error` state) with a meaningful message that distinguishes between HTTP failure (`response.status` / `response.statusText`) and network/exception failure (`err.message`), instead of silently logging.

violations.title: `pollChanges` resolves promise on error, returning misleading success
violations.content: Inside `verifyConfigChanges`, the inner `pollChanges` `catch` block calls `resolve()` after any error during verification, with the comment 'Don't reject on verification error, just proceed'. This returns a misleading success value: the caller (`confirmAndSubmit`) then sets `setSuccessMessage('WiFi configuration updated successfully!')` even when verification GETs were failing the entire time. The user is told the change was applied and verified, when in fact verification could not be performed. A failed verification poll should either retry, reject so the caller can branch, or set a distinct 'verification failed' state — not silently masquerade as success.
violations.fixPrompt: In `verifyConfigChanges` (lines 189-263 of `DecoWiFiConfigEditor.jsx`), change the inner `catch` to either `reject(err)` so `confirmAndSubmit` can show a verification-failed message, or set a dedicated state like `setVerificationMessage('Verification could not complete — please refresh manually')` before resolving. Do not let the outer success path run unchanged after verification errors.

violations.title: `handleDismiss` logs dismiss failures with no user feedback
violations.content: The `catch` block in `handleDismiss` catches a broad `error`, logs to console, and only resets `isDismissing`. The alert stays visible and the user has no indication their click failed — they will likely click again, repeating the failed POST. Either the alert should remain with a visible 'Could not dismiss' state, or the failure should be surfaced via the `onDismiss` callback or a toast. Logging-and-continuing here looks like success from the user's perspective.
violations.fixPrompt: In `handleDismiss` (lines 23-45 of `DeviceAlert.jsx`), add a `dismissError` state set in the `catch` and render it inline in the alert (e.g. 'Failed to dismiss — retry?'), or call an `onDismissError` callback so the parent can surface the failure. Avoid silently logging while leaving the alert visually unchanged.

violations.title: `confirmAndSubmit` catch discards original error context
violations.content: The `catch` block stringifies only `err.message` into `setError(`Failed to update WiFi configuration: ${err.message}`)`, discarding the original `Error` object (its `stack`, `name`, and any custom fields like the HTTP `status` from the throw at lines 150-153). The error reported to the user collapses three different failure modes — network failure, non-ok HTTP from the PUT, and verification failure inside `verifyConfigChanges` — into one generic prefixed string, and the original error is never stored for diagnostics. This is the `err.message`-only pattern that loses stack and type.
violations.fixPrompt: In `confirmAndSubmit` (lines 124-187 of `DecoWiFiConfigEditor.jsx`), preserve the original error: store the full `err` object in component state (e.g. `setErrorDetails(err)`) alongside a user-friendly message, and include `err.stack`/`err.name` when logging. Consider wrapping with `new Error(message, { cause: err })` if you must re-throw, so the original cause chain is retained.

violations.title: `fetchTopology` catch stores only `err.message`
violations.content: The `catch` in `fetchTopology` calls `setError(err.message)`, dropping the original `Error` (its `stack`, `name`, and the distinction between the two different thrown errors at lines 100 and 101). Downstream consumers of `error` cannot tell whether the failure was a 401 auth error, a non-ok HTTP status, or a network exception, because only the message string survives. The stack trace useful for debugging is gone after this assignment.
violations.fixPrompt: In `fetchTopology` (lines 94-115 of `DecoTopologyView.jsx`), keep the original error: store the `Error` instance (or at minimum include `err.name` and `err.stack` in logs) and consider an additional `errorKind` state populated from `response.status` so the UI can branch on auth vs. transport failures rather than relying on a stringified message.

violations.title: Silent catch in `fetchPresence` swallows all errors
violations.content: The `fetchPresence` async function in `DeviceDetailCard.jsx` catches all errors with `catch (err) { /* silent */ }`. The error binding `err` is never used and there is no logging or user feedback. Network failures, JSON parse errors, and unexpected exceptions are all silently swallowed, making it impossible to diagnose presence-history fetch failures. This is the textbook case of logging-the-error-but-continuing — except even the log is missing.
violations.fixPrompt: Replace the silent catch in `fetchPresence` with at minimum `console.error('Failed to fetch presence history:', err)`, and consider surfacing a non-blocking error state so the UI can render a fallback for the presence heatmap instead of leaving it indefinitely null.

violations.title: `handleSaveField` returns generic error message regardless of cause
violations.content: In `handleSaveField`, the catch block always sets `error` to `'Failed to save changes. Please try again.'` regardless of the actual failure mode. The block also catches `throw new Error('Failed to update device')` from a non-OK HTTP response (line 98) along with arbitrary network/JSON errors. A 400 validation error, a 401 auth failure, a 500 server error, and a network outage all surface identically to the user, making it impossible for them to know whether retrying is appropriate or what to correct.
violations.fixPrompt: In the catch block at `DeviceDetailCard.jsx:100-102`, differentiate by error cause: read the response status and body when available (move parsing inside the try and throw an Error containing server detail), then in catch include `err.message` in the user-facing error. Also pass the server response body forward as the Error's `cause` so context is preserved.

violations.title: `new Error('Failed to update device')` discards response details
violations.content: Line 98 throws `new Error('Failed to update device')` without capturing the HTTP status, response body, or any server-returned error code. When the catch at line 100 runs, the original failure context (status code, server message) is lost and only the generic string remains. There is no `cause` option, no inclusion of `response.status` or `await response.text()`, so debugging requires inspecting the network tab.
violations.fixPrompt: Replace `throw new Error('Failed to update device')` with `throw new Error(\`Failed to update device: ${response.status} ${response.statusText}\`, { cause: await response.text().catch(() => null) })` so the original response context propagates to the catch block.

violations.title: `handleDelete` catches all errors without binding and shows generic message
violations.content: In `handleDelete`, the catch block is `catch { ... }` with no error binding, so any thrown value — network error, fetch rejection, programming error — is collapsed into the same `'Failed to delete device'` message. The original error is never logged or inspected, so there is no way to tell what actually went wrong. This catches too broadly and silently transforms diverse failures into a single misleading status.
violations.fixPrompt: Change to `catch (err) { console.error('Delete failed:', err); setError(\`Failed to delete device: ${err.message}\`); setConfirmDelete(false); }` so the original error is logged and its message is exposed to the user.

violations.title: `setCustomName` logs error but UI behaves as if rename succeeded
violations.content: In `setCustomName`, when the PUT request throws or returns a non-OK status, the catch block logs to console but the function returns normally with no state update and no user feedback. The user sees the inline edit dismiss as if the rename succeeded, but `devices` is never updated. This is the classic 'log the error but continue execution as if nothing happened' anti-pattern — additionally, the non-OK branch (when `res.ok` is false) has no handling at all and silently does nothing.
violations.fixPrompt: In `setCustomName`, surface failures to the user: add a non-OK branch that throws (or returns an error) and a catch block that calls a banner/toast helper. Also rollback any optimistic state changes if added in the future. Consider passing `showBanner` as a prop and calling `showBanner('Failed to rename device', 'error')` on both the non-OK and catch paths.

violations.title: `triggerManualScan` swallows errors with only a console log
violations.content: In `triggerManualScan`, the catch block calls `console.error` but provides no user feedback. The function also has no handling for the non-OK branch (when `response.ok` is false). The user clicks 'Scan Now', the spinner stops, and they have no indication the scan failed. The catch is also too broad — any kind of failure produces the same console message.
violations.fixPrompt: Add a `showBanner` call inside both the non-OK branch and catch block of `triggerManualScan` so the user knows when a scan fails. Differentiate between network errors (catch) and HTTP errors (non-OK) by reading `response.status` and `response.statusText` in the non-OK branch.

violations.title: `.catch(() => {})` silently swallows auto-scan toggle errors
violations.content: The auto-scan toggle handler at line 291 chains `.catch(() => {})`, which completely discards any error from the fetch or `.then` block. If the `/network/auto-scan` request fails, the user sees no feedback and the UI state (`homeStatus.auto_scan_active`) is not updated to match server reality. The error binding is intentionally omitted, so even diagnostic logging is impossible.
violations.fixPrompt: Replace `.catch(() => {})` with `.catch(err => { console.error('Failed to toggle auto-scan:', err); showBanner('Failed to toggle auto-scan', 'error'); })` so failures are at least logged and surfaced to the user.

violations.title: `dismissAlert` logs failure but UI continues as if dismissal succeeded
violations.content: In `dismissAlert`, the catch block logs the error but provides no user feedback. The alert remains visible (because `fetchAlerts` is never reached on the error path), but the user has no indication that their dismissal action failed. The catch is also too broad — it merges thrown HTTP-status errors (from line 101) with arbitrary network failures with no discrimination.
violations.fixPrompt: Add a user-visible error indicator (toast, banner, or inline error state) when `dismissAlert` fails. Also consider preserving the error type by reading the server response body and including it in the thrown Error's message and `cause` field.

violations.title: `fetchEvents` catch resets state without surfacing failure to user
violations.content: In `fetchEvents`, the catch block logs the error and resets `events` to `[]` and `totalEvents` to `0`. The user sees an empty event list with the existing 'No events found' empty state — indistinguishable from a successful response with zero events. There is no user-facing error indicator, so transient API failures masquerade as 'no data'. This is a misleading transformation of an error into a successful-looking empty result.
violations.fixPrompt: Add a `fetchError` state in `EventLog`, set it inside the catch block with `err.message`, and render an error banner above the event list when set. Distinguish 'no events match filters' from 'failed to load events' in the empty-state rendering.

violations.title: `fetchAlerts` catch hides failures behind empty state
violations.content: Same pattern as `fetchEvents`: the catch resets `alerts` to `[]` and `totalAlerts` to `0` on failure, which the UI renders as 'No active alerts'. A user looking at this screen cannot distinguish 'the alerts endpoint failed' from 'there really are no alerts' — a critical distinction for a network monitoring app where unseen alerts could indicate real problems.
violations.fixPrompt: Add a dedicated `alertsError` state, set it in the catch block, and render an error banner so the user knows the alerts list is stale rather than empty. Keep the previously fetched `alerts` array intact on failure so users do not lose visibility into recently known alerts.

violations.title: `runSpeedTest` catch always blames Chester connectivity
violations.content: The catch block in `runSpeedTest` always displays `'Speed test failed. Check Chester connectivity.'` regardless of the actual error cause. The failure could come from a network timeout, JSON parsing error, CORS issue, or backend crash — none of which are necessarily related to Chester connectivity. Users following this misleading guidance will troubleshoot the wrong subsystem.
violations.fixPrompt: In `runSpeedTest` at lines 75-78 in `frontend/src/hooks/useDevicePolling.js`, differentiate the banner message based on the actual error type. For example, distinguish between network/fetch failures (`TypeError: Failed to fetch`) and JSON parse errors, and include `error.message` in the banner so users see the underlying cause rather than always being directed to check Chester.

violations.title: `checkStatus` catch discards original error completely
violations.content: The catch block in `checkStatus` calls `setError('Failed to check Alexa status')` without including `err.message`, `err.stack`, or any reference to the original error. The original error is never logged either (no `console.error`), so the underlying cause (network failure, parsing error, etc.) is completely lost and unrecoverable for debugging.
violations.fixPrompt: In `checkStatus` at lines 36-39 in `frontend/src/pages/AlexaDevicesPage.jsx`, include the original error in the user-facing message (e.g. `` `Failed to check Alexa status: ${err.message}` ``) and add a `console.error('Alexa status check failed:', err)` call so the stack trace is preserved for debugging.

violations.title: `fetchNodes` maps HTTP status to assumed causes
violations.content: The `fetchNodes` function throws errors with hardcoded explanatory messages based purely on HTTP status code: a 401 is reported as `'Not authenticated with Deco API. Please configure credentials.'` and a 404 as `'Deco API endpoint not available.'`. A 401 can mean expired session, revoked token, or other auth issues unrelated to missing configuration; a 404 could indicate a routing bug rather than a missing endpoint. These messages prescribe a specific remediation that may not match the real cause.
violations.fixPrompt: In `fetchNodes` at lines 36-44 in `frontend/src/pages/DecoNodesPage.jsx`, include the server's response body in the error message when available (read `response.json()` or `response.text()`), and soften the prescriptive language. For example, for 401 say `'Authentication failed (401). Check Deco credentials or session.'` and include any `detail` field from the response.

violations.title: `fetchDevices` catch retains only `err.message`
violations.content: The catch block in `fetchDevices` stores only `err.message` via `setError(err.message)` and discards the rest of the error (stack trace, error name, any nested cause). There is also no `console.error` to preserve the original error in the dev console. Similar patterns appear in `handleLogin` (line 84-85), `handleOtpSubmit` (line 109-110), and `handleSaveCreds` (line 130-131).
violations.fixPrompt: In `fetchDevices`, `handleLogin`, `handleOtpSubmit`, and `handleSaveCreds` in `frontend/src/pages/AlarmComPage.jsx`, add `console.error('<context>:', err)` calls in each catch block so the original error (with stack trace) is logged before the message is extracted for the UI.

violations.title: Multiple silent-fail catch blocks swallow all errors
violations.content: Several fetch helpers in the main `useEffect` (`getActiveAlerts`, `getAnomalyInsights`, `getDailyDigest`, `getHealthScore`) use `catch (error) { /* silent */ }` to swallow every error without logging or surfacing them. This catches too broadly — programming errors (e.g. a typo in state setter, a `TypeError` from `response.json()` returning unexpected shape) will be silently dropped along with the expected network failures, making issues invisible during development.
violations.fixPrompt: In the silent catch blocks at lines 219, 230, 238, 246 in `frontend/src/hooks/useDevicePolling.js`, replace `/* silent */` with `console.debug(...)` calls so errors are still discoverable in dev tools, and consider narrowing the catch to only network/HTTP errors rather than all exceptions.

violations.title: `linkAndRename` swallows errors silently — user has no feedback on failure
violations.content: The `linkAndRename` function catches any error from the two `fetch` calls but only logs to `console.error` and continues execution. The user sees the spinner disappear but receives no indication that linking or renaming failed. Additionally, the code does not check `response.ok` on either fetch, so HTTP error responses (4xx/5xx) won't even be caught — only network-level failures will reach the catch block. The function then calls `await fetchSuggestions()` only on the success path, so on failure the UI silently keeps stale state.
violations.fixPrompt: Update `linkAndRename` in `DeviceNamingPage.jsx` to check `response.ok` after each fetch and throw if not ok. In the catch block, surface the error to the user via `setError` (similar to `fetchSuggestions`) instead of only calling `console.error`.

violations.title: `applyCustomName` swallows errors silently — user has no feedback on failure
violations.content: The `applyCustomName` function catches errors and only logs to `console.error` without surfacing the failure to the user. The `fetch` call also does not check `response.ok`, so server-side errors (e.g. 500, validation failures) pass through as if they succeeded — the catch block won't fire and the code will optimistically call `fetchSuggestions()` and clear the custom name input as if the rename worked. This is logging-and-continuing-as-if-nothing-happened combined with a misleading success path.
violations.fixPrompt: Update `applyCustomName` to check `response.ok` and throw if not, and to call `setError` in the catch block so the user sees rename failures instead of only logging them to the console.

violations.title: `fetchDevices` returns misleading empty result on error
violations.content: The `fetchDevices` catch block logs the error then calls `setDevices([])`, which causes the UI to render as if there are genuinely zero devices. The user cannot distinguish between “backend returned no devices” and “fetch failed.” There is no error state surfaced anywhere in the component, so the rendered `EventLog devices={[]}` is a misleading success-shaped result after a real failure. The fetch also never checks `response.ok`, so HTTP error responses won't reach the catch block at all.
violations.fixPrompt: Add an error state to `EventLogPage`, set it in the catch block, render an error banner when set, and check `response.ok` before calling `response.json()`. Avoid clearing `devices` silently to `[]` on failure — let the caller distinguish empty-vs-error.

violations.title: `fetchDecoStatus` swallows errors without user feedback
violations.content: `fetchDecoStatus` catches any error from the `fetch` and only writes to the console. The status banner that depends on `decoStatus` will simply stay null forever on failure with no indication to the user that the status check failed. The same broad catch-and-log pattern is repeated in `fetchAlexaStatus`, `fetchChesterStatus`, and `fetchHiboostStatus` in this file (lines 99-115, 117-130, 307-318). This is a class of error-and-continue handling that leaves the UI in an indeterminate state.
violations.fixPrompt: Either show a status-banner-level error indicator in `SettingsPage` when status fetches fail, or surface a toast via `pushToast`. At minimum, set a state variable (e.g. `decoStatusError`) the UI can render so users aren't left wondering why no status appears.

violations.title: `startAlexaOAuth` swallows errors and ignores non-OK HTTP responses
violations.content: `startAlexaOAuth` only opens the popup window when `response.ok` is true but does nothing in the else branch — failed OAuth init returns silently. The catch block then only `console.error`s the failure. The user clicks “Connect Alexa Account”, sees the spinner end, and is left with no indication of why nothing happened. Unlike the sibling save/test handlers in this file, this one does not call `pushToast` or set any result state.
violations.fixPrompt: Add an `else` branch in `startAlexaOAuth` to handle non-OK responses by calling `pushToast` with an error message, and update the catch block to `pushToast` the failure instead of only logging it. Mirror the pattern used by `saveAlexaCookies`.

violations.title: `fetchData` catch discards stack trace and error type via `err.message`
violations.content: The catch block in `fetchData` calls `setError(err.message)`, which keeps only the `message` string and discards the stack trace and original error. The function's `throw new Error('HiBoost not connected')` and `throw new Error(`Failed to fetch RF params: ${resp.status}`)` paths, plus any network/JSON parsing error, all collapse into a single string with no way to distinguish them or get the stack. The same lossy pattern is repeated in `handleMgcSave` (line 95) and `handleRfSwitch` (line 113) in this file.
violations.fixPrompt: Store the full `Error` object on a separate state slot (or log it) and keep `setError(err.message)` only for UI display. Alternatively, log the full error via `console.error(err)` in the catch so the stack survives for debugging.

violations.title: `fetchAll` swallows errors from five parallel fetches and continues as if loaded
violations.content: The `catch` block in `fetchAll` (lines 70-74) catches errors from all five parallel `fetch` calls (`/speedtest/latest`, `/speedtest/history`, `/speedtest/hourly-averages`, `/speedtest/insights`, `/speedtest/scheduler/status`), logs only via `console.error`, and then unconditionally calls `setLoading(false)` in the `finally` block. No error state is set, so the UI proceeds to render the empty-data path as if nothing went wrong — users get a silent failure rather than a retry affordance. This is the canonical 'log and continue' anti-pattern.
violations.fixPrompt: In `fetchAll` in `SpeedInsightsPage.jsx`, add an `error` state via `useState` and call `setError(err)` inside the catch block. Render a visible error banner with a Retry button when `error` is set, similar to how `SmartHomePage.jsx` handles fetch failures at lines 170-177. Optionally narrow the catch to only network/parse failures by inspecting `err.name` or `err instanceof TypeError`.

violations.title: `fetchChester` uses an empty catch block that swallows all errors
violations.content: The `catch (e) { /* Chester may not be reachable */ }` block in `fetchChester` (lines 80-82) catches every possible error — not just network failures, but also JSON parse errors, programming bugs (e.g., `setChesterInfo` throwing), and runtime exceptions — and silently discards them. The comment narrows the intent to network failures, but the implementation matches everything. There is no logging, so genuine bugs will be invisible in production.
violations.fixPrompt: In `fetchChester` in `SpeedInsightsPage.jsx`, narrow the catch to network errors (e.g., `if (!(err instanceof TypeError)) throw err;` or check `err.name === 'AbortError'`). At minimum, add a `console.debug` log so non-network failures are observable during development.

violations.title: `fetchHiboostHistory` uses an empty catch block that swallows all errors
violations.content: The `catch (e) { /* HiBoost may not be configured */ }` block in `fetchHiboostHistory` (lines 93-94) silently swallows every error, including JSON parse failures and unexpected programming errors. With no `console.warn`/`console.debug`, runtime issues in the HiBoost integration become invisible. This is overly broad error handling.
violations.fixPrompt: In `fetchHiboostHistory` in `SpeedInsightsPage.jsx`, log unexpected errors via `console.debug` and narrow the swallow-and-continue behavior to only the known 'not configured' case (e.g., a specific HTTP status or `TypeError` from `fetch`).
violations.snippet:
} catch (e) { /* HiBoost may not be configured */ }
    finally { setHiboostLoading(false); }

violations.title: `runTest` shows hardcoded 'Check Chester connectivity' message for any error
violations.content: In `runTest` (lines 120-121), the catch block always shows the banner `'Speed test failed. Check Chester connectivity.'` regardless of the actual cause. The error could be a JSON parse failure on the response (`result = await res.json()` on line 112), a network error, an AbortError, or a downstream `fetchAll` failure (line 118). The user is misdirected to investigate Chester even when the issue is elsewhere (e.g., the local API server).
violations.fixPrompt: In `runTest` in `SpeedInsightsPage.jsx`, include `err.message` (or a categorized reason from `err`) in the banner rather than a hardcoded Chester-specific string. For example: `showBanner(\`Speed test failed: ${err.message}\`, 'error')`.
violations.snippet:
} catch (err) {
      showBanner('Speed test failed. Check Chester connectivity.', 'error');

violations.title: Empty `catch (e) {}` in `carrierHistoryData` silently swallows JSON parse errors
violations.content: The `catch (e) {}` on line 237 inside `carrierHistoryData`'s `chartData.forEach` is completely silent — no comment, no log, no marker. Unlike the sibling at line 197 which at least has a `/* skip bad data */` comment, this version provides no signal that bad data is being skipped. Programming errors inside the loop body (e.g., a `TypeError` from accessing `b.role` on a malformed entry) would be silently swallowed alongside the intended `JSON.parse` failures.
violations.fixPrompt: In `carrierHistoryData` in `SpeedInsightsPage.jsx` (line 237), either narrow the catch to `SyntaxError` from `JSON.parse` (move the `JSON.parse` into its own `try`), or at minimum add a `console.debug('skipping malformed ca_bands', e)` log and an explanatory comment.

violations.title: `fetchCandidates` catches all errors with only a `console.warn`
violations.content: The catch block in `fetchCandidates` (lines 67-69) catches every error, calls `console.warn`, and continues execution. No user-visible feedback is given, no error state is set, and the empty `candidates` map is left in place. Users who rely on the MAC-candidates feature get no indication that it is unavailable, and the broad catch hides programming bugs (e.g., `setCandidates` throwing).
violations.fixPrompt: In `fetchCandidates` in `SmartHomePage.jsx`, either propagate the error to a dedicated candidates-error state for surfacing in the UI, or narrow the catch to network failures only (e.g., `if (!(err instanceof TypeError)) throw err;`) so unexpected errors are not silently logged-and-ignored.

violations.title: `fetchDevices` catch sets only `err.message`, discarding the original Error and stack trace
violations.content: In `fetchDevices` (lines 42-44), the catch handler stores only `err.message` via `setError(err.message)`. The original `Error` object (and its stack trace) is discarded — there is no log, no `cause` chain, and no way for downstream debugging to recover what type of failure occurred (network vs. server vs. parse). Across the file the same pattern is repeated in `sendCommand` (line 86), `identifyStart` (line 108), `identifyComplete` (line 129), and `associateDevice` (line 152).
violations.fixPrompt: In `SmartHomePage.jsx`, log the full error via `console.error('fetchDevices failed', err)` before extracting `err.message`. Consider storing the entire error object in state (or its `name`/`stack`) so debugging info survives, and use `Error` `cause` chaining when rethrowing: `throw new Error(message, { cause: err })`.

violations.title: Check-then-act race in `submit_otp` credential update
violations.content: `submit_otp` performs a read-modify-write on the encrypted `alarm_com_credentials` setting across two separate `db.get_connection()` blocks with an awaitable boundary. It calls `load_encrypted_setting` in the first connection, checks the result, then re-opens a new connection to call `store_encrypted_setting`. If another concurrent request (e.g., `save_alarm_com_credentials` on line 127, or a parallel OTP submission) writes to the same setting between the load and the store, that update is silently overwritten with stale data — effectively losing the username/password change. This is a classic check-then-act / read-modify-write race on shared persistent state.
violations.fixPrompt: Refactor `submit_otp` in `backend/routes/alarm_com.py` so the load and the conditional update to `alarm_com_credentials` happen inside a single `db.get_connection()` block, ideally wrapped in a database transaction (e.g., `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` for SQLite) so that the two_factor_cookie merge is atomic with respect to concurrent writers.
violations.snippet:
if result.get("two_factor_cookie"):
            with db.get_connection() as conn:
                existing = load_encrypted_setting(conn, "alarm_com_credentials")
            if existing:
                existing["two_factor_cookie"] = result["two_factor_cookie"]
                with db.get_connection() as conn:
                    store_encrypted_setting(conn, "alarm_com_credentials", existing)

violations.title: Unsynchronized write to `poller.auto_scan_paused`
violations.content: `toggle_auto_scan` mutates the shared `poller.auto_scan_paused` attribute on the singleton poller without any synchronization. The background polling task (in `PollingServiceManager`) reads this flag on its own schedule, and concurrent HTTP requests can also call this endpoint. Because the write is a plain attribute assignment with no lock, async event, or atomic primitive, there is no happens-before relationship guaranteeing the polling loop observes the new value, and overlapping toggles can interleave with reads in unintended ways.
violations.fixPrompt: Introduce an `asyncio.Lock` or `asyncio.Event` on the poller for the `auto_scan_paused` flag in `backend/main.py` (and `services/polling_service.py`). Acquire it in both `toggle_auto_scan` and the background polling loop's read path so the toggle is synchronized across coroutines.
violations.snippet:
async def toggle_auto_scan(enabled: bool):
    """Toggle auto-scan on/off. When off, background scans are paused."""
    poller = polling_manager.get_poller()
    if poller is None:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=500, detail="Polling service not initialized")
    poller.auto_scan_paused = not enabled
    return {"auto_scan_paused": poller.auto_scan_paused, "enabled": enabled}

violations.title: `get_home_status` crashes if `polling_manager` is uninitialized
violations.content: `get_home_status` directly calls `polling_manager.get_status()` without checking whether `polling_manager` is `None`. If startup partially failed (the polling block on lines 340–352 logs and continues on errors), or if this endpoint is hit before startup completes, the call raises `AttributeError` and returns a 500 to the client instead of degrading gracefully. Other endpoints in this file (e.g., `get_devices`, `get_polling_config`) explicitly guard against `None` services — this one does not.
violations.fixPrompt: Add a `None` guard at the top of `get_home_status` in `backend/main.py` that returns a degraded response (e.g., `{"is_home": status["is_home"], "auto_scan_paused": True, "auto_scan_active": False}`) when `polling_manager` is `None`, instead of letting the request fail with a 500.
violations.snippet:
async def get_home_status():
    """Check if server is on the home network and return auto-scan state."""
    from services.polling_service import check_home_network
    status = check_home_network()
    poller_status = polling_manager.get_status()
    return {
        **status,
        "auto_scan_paused": poller_status.get("auto_scan_paused", False),
        "auto_scan_active": status["is_home"] and not poller_status.get("auto_scan_paused", False),
    }

violations.title: Critical startup steps have no retry or recovery
violations.content: Database, OUI, device, search, group, and event services are constructed on lines 178–204 with no `try/except` and no retry mechanism. If any of these fail (e.g., `Database()` migration error, transient disk issue), the entire app fails to start — even though all later integrations (Deco, Chester, Alexa, HiBoost, etc.) are wrapped in `try/except` that lets the app come up degraded. The most critical initialization paths have the weakest recovery story.
violations.fixPrompt: Wrap each critical service initialization on lines 178–204 of `backend/main.py` in a `try/except` with a bounded retry (e.g., 3 attempts with backoff) for transient errors, and fail fast with a clear log message only after retries are exhausted. Consider returning the app in a degraded state (health endpoint reports `database: failed`) rather than crashing the process when non-essential services fail.
violations.snippet:
# Initialize database
    db = Database()
    db.run_migrations()
    logger.info("Database initialized and migrations applied")

    # Initialize OUI service
    oui_service = OUIService()
    logger.info(f"OUI service initialized with {oui_service.get_database_size()} entries")

    # Initialize device service
    device_service = NetworkDeviceService(db)
    logger.info("Device service initialized")

    # Initialize search service
    search_service = DeviceSearchService(db)
    logger.info("Search service initialized")

    # Initialize group repositories
    group_repo = DeviceGroupRepository(db)
    member_repo = DeviceGroupMemberRepository(db)
    logger.info("Device group repositories initialized")

    # Initialize event service and repositories
    event_service = EventService(db)
    event_repo = DeviceEventRepository(db)
    alert_repo = DeviceAlertRepository(db)
    logger.info("Event service and repositories initialized")

violations.title: Check-then-act race on `_topology_json_cache` allows duplicate expensive work
violations.content: `get_topology` reads module-level `_topology_json_cache` and `_topology_json_cache_time` at line 807 to decide if the cache is fresh, then awaits expensive operations (`deco_service.get_nodes_with_details()`, `correlation_service.get_merged_clients()`, `client.get_topology_local()`), and finally writes back to those globals at lines 1016-1017. Multiple concurrent requests arriving during a cache miss will all see a stale cache, all perform the expensive Deco API calls, and all overwrite the cache — defeating the purpose of caching and causing thundering-herd load on the upstream Deco API. There is no lock or future-deduplication mechanism around the check-then-act sequence.
violations.fixPrompt: Wrap the cache check-then-act in `get_topology` with an `asyncio.Lock` or use a singleflight pattern (e.g. store an in-progress `asyncio.Future` keyed by the cache so concurrent callers await the same computation). Acquire the lock before the freshness check and hold it through the write at lines 1016-1017.

        else:

        else:
            # Fallback: build devices directly from Deco local API client data
            logger.info(f"No merged devices, building from {len(deco_clients)} Deco clients")
            for mac, dc in deco_clients.items():
                dc_name = dc.get("name", "")
                try:
                    dc_name = base64.b64decode(dc_name).decode("utf-8")
                except Exception as e:
                    logger.debug(f"Base64 nickname decode failed: {e}")
                devices.append({
                    "device_id": mac,
                    "mac_address": mac,
                    "device_name": dc_name or "Unknown",
                    "status": "online" if dc.get("online") else "offline",
                    "friendly_name": dc_name,
                    "vendor_name": "",
                    "current_ip": dc.get("ip", ""),
                    "connection_type": client_to_node.get(mac, {}).get("connection_type", ""),
                    "preferred_deco_node": None,
                })

        # Build relationships from per-node client mapping
        relationships = []

        all_device_macs = {d["mac_address"].lower() for d in devices}

        for mac in client_to_node:
            if mac not in all_device_macs:
                dc = deco_clients.get(mac, {})
                dc_name = dc.get("name", "")
                try:
                    dc_name = base64.b64decode(dc_name).decode("utf-8")
                except Exception as e:
                    logger.debug(f"Base64 nickname decode failed: {e}")
                devices.append({
                    "device_id": mac,
                    "mac_address": mac,

                    "friendly_name": dc_name,

                        "connection_type": node_info["connection_type"],

violations.title: Check-then-act race on `_topology_svg_cache` triggers redundant matplotlib renders
violations.content: `get_topology_graph` reads module-level `_topology_svg_cache` and `_topology_svg_cache_time` at line 1038, then performs many heavy synchronous and async operations (matplotlib rendering, NetworkX graph building, Chester/Deco API fetches) before assigning the new SVG to those globals at lines 1443-1444. Concurrent requests during a cache miss will all see stale state, all run the expensive matplotlib pipeline, and the last writer wins. Matplotlib is also not thread-safe; concurrent `plt.subplots`/`plt.close` calls from different requests can corrupt the global figure registry.
violations.fixPrompt: Serialize the cache miss path in `get_topology_graph` with an `asyncio.Lock` so only one request renders at a time. Re-check the cache freshness after acquiring the lock to avoid redundant renders when concurrent callers were queued.
violations.snippet:
# 2026-03-13: Return cached SVG if fresh

    now = time.time()
    if _topology_svg_cache and (now - _topology_svg_cache_time) < TOPOLOGY_ROUTE_CACHE_TTL:
        logger.debug("Returning cached topology SVG")
        return Response(content=_topology_svg_cache, media_type="image/svg+xml")

    import json as _json

    try:
        import networkx as nx
        import matplotlib
        matplotlib.use("Agg")  # Non-interactive backend
        import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
        import matplotlib.patches as mpatches
    except ImportError as e:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=500, detail=f"Missing dependency: {e}")

        raise HTTPException(status_code=500, detail="Deco service not initialized")

    try:
        client = deco_service.deco_client

        # 2026-03-11: Use get_topology_local() for a clean local session

        local_nodes = local_data.get("nodes", []) if local_data else []
        node_clients = local_data.get("node_clients", {}) if local_data else {}

        node_mac_to_name = {}
        if local_nodes:

                try:

                db_name = _get_node_friendly_name(node_mac)
                node_mac_to_name[node_mac] = db_name or nickname or node.get("device_model", node_mac)
        else:
            cloud_nodes = deco_service.get_nodes_with_details()
            for nd in cloud_nodes:
                cloud_mac_raw = nd.get("raw_data", {}).get("deviceMac", "")
                if not cloud_mac_raw:
                    continue
                mac_clean = cloud_mac_raw.lower().replace("-", "").replace(":", "")
                if len(mac_clean) == 12:
                    node_mac = "-".join(mac_clean[i:i+2].upper() for i in range(0, 12, 2))
                else:
                    node_mac = cloud_mac_raw
                node_mac_to_name[node_mac] = nd.get("node_name", nd.get("raw_data", {}).get("alias", node_mac))

        # 2026-03-11: Fetch Chester 5G signal data for tower/band info
        chester_info = {}
        try:
            from routes.chester import chester_service as _chester_svc
            if _chester_svc:
                chester_info = _chester_svc.get_system_info()
        except Exception as e:
            logger.warning(f"Chester info fetch failed for topology: {e}")

        # Build NetworkX graph
        G = nx.Graph()

        # 2026-03-11: Physical topology chain:
        # T-Mobile Tower → Waveform MIMO → Chester 5G → Deco Office → other Decos → devices
        #
        # Build tower label with cell info from Chester
        tower_label = "T-Mobile\nCell Tower"
        cell_id = chester_info.get("cell_id", "")
        if cell_id:
            tower_label += f"\nCellID: {cell_id}"

        # 2026-03-11: Build clean band labels for the tower-to-waveform link
        import re as _re
        ca_bands = chester_info.get("ca_band", [])
        conn_type_str = chester_info.get("connection_type", "NR5G-SA")
        band_str = chester_info.get("band", "")
        tower_bands = []
        for cab in ca_bands:
            # Extract just the band name (e.g. "NR5G BAND 41") from raw AT output
            band_matches = _re.findall(r'((?:NR5G|LTE)\s+BAND\s+\d+)', str(cab), _re.IGNORECASE)
            if band_matches:
                for bm in band_matches:
                    clean = bm.strip()
                    if clean not in tower_bands:
                        tower_bands.append(clean)
            else:
                # Fallback: use as-is but truncate
                clean = str(cab).strip().strip('"')[:30]
                if clean:
                    tower_bands.append(clean)
        if not tower_bands and band_str:
            tower_bands.append(f"Band {band_str}")

        # Build Chester label
        chester_label = "5G Chester AX3000 - SDX75"
        chester_ip = chester_info.get("ipv4_addr", "")
        if chester_ip:

        sinr = chester_info.get("sinr", "")

        if sinr:

        G.add_node("tower", label=tower_label, node_type="tower")
        G.add_node("waveform", label="Waveform\nQualcomm MIMO", node_type="waveform")
        G.add_node("chester", label=chester_label, node_type="chester")

        # Tower ↔ Waveform (wireless 5G bands)
        band_edge_label = conn_type_str
        if tower_bands:
            band_edge_label = "\n".join(tower_bands)
        G.add_edge("tower", "waveform", connection_type="5g_tower",
                   label=band_edge_label)
        # Waveform ↔ Chester (coax/cable)
        G.add_edge("waveform", "chester", connection_type="wired",
                   label="Coax" if not signal_label else signal_label)
        # Chester ↔ Deco Office (wired ethernet)
        # Add Deco nodes
        deco_macs = list(node_mac_to_name.keys())

        # Find the master Deco node (wired to Chester)
        master_mac = None
        for node in local_nodes:
            if node.get("role") == "master":
                master_mac = node.get("mac", "")
                break
        if not master_mac and deco_macs:
            master_mac = deco_macs[0]
        for node_mac, node_name in node_mac_to_name.items():
            G.add_node(node_mac, label=node_name, node_type="deco")

        # Chester → master Deco (wired)
        if master_mac:
            G.add_edge("chester", master_mac, connection_type="wired",
                       label="Ethernet")

        # 2026-03-11: Connect non-master Decos — check if wired or mesh backhaul
        # Build lookup of node connection info from local API data
        node_conn_types = {}
        for node in local_nodes:
            nmac = node.get("mac", "")
            # connection_type can be a list like ["band2_4","band5"] or include "wired"
            ct = node.get("connection_type", [])
            if isinstance(ct, str):
                ct = [ct]
            node_conn_types[nmac] = ct

        for node_mac in deco_macs:
            if node_mac != master_mac:
                ct_list = node_conn_types.get(node_mac, [])
                node_name_lower = node_mac_to_name.get(node_mac, "").lower()
                # Check if wired: API says "wired", or no wifi bands listed,
                # or known hardwired node (Dining Room is hardwired to Office)
                is_wired = (
                    "wired" in ct_list
                    or (ct_list and all(c not in ("band2_4", "band5", "band6") for c in ct_list))
                    or "dining" in node_name_lower
                )
                if is_wired:
                    G.add_edge(master_mac, node_mac, connection_type="wired",
                               label="Ethernet")
                else:

            "wired": "#C62828",
            "5g_tower": "#9C27B0",
            "mesh_backhaul": "#FF9800",
        }
        for node_mac, clients in node_clients.items():
            for c in clients:
                raw_mac = c.get("mac", "")
                mac_clean = raw_mac.lower().replace("-", "").replace(":", "").replace(" ", "")
                if len(mac_clean) != 12:
                    continue
                normalized = ":".join(mac_clean[i:i+2] for i in range(0, 12, 2))

                dc_name = c.get("name", "")
                try:
                    dc_name = base64.b64decode(dc_name).decode("utf-8")
                except Exception as e:
                    logger.debug(f"Base64 nickname decode failed: {e}")
                # 2026-03-11: Prefer DB friendly_name for device labels too
                db_dev_name = _get_node_friendly_name(raw_mac)

                conn_type = c.get("connection_type", "")
                is_online = c.get("online", False)
                ip_addr = c.get("ip", "")

                if not ip_addr:

                label_parts.append(normalized)

                G.add_node(normalized,
                           label="\n".join(label_parts),
                           node_type="device",
                           online=is_online,
                           connection_type=conn_type)

        pos["waveform"] = (3.5, 0)
        pos["chester"] = (7.0, 0)

            pos[deco_macs[0]] = (deco_x, 0)
        else:

                y_offset = (i - (n_decos - 1) / 2) * 2.5

        chester_nodes = [n for n, d in G.nodes(data=True) if d.get("node_type") == "chester"]
        deco_nodes = [n for n, d in G.nodes(data=True) if d.get("node_type") == "deco"]
        online_devices = [n for n, d in G.nodes(data=True) if d.get("node_type") == "device" and d.get("online")]
        offline_devices = [n for n, d in G.nodes(data=True) if d.get("node_type") == "device" and not d.get("online")]

        # Draw edges with connection type colors

                              edgecolor="#CE93D8"))

                               node_color="#9C27B0", node_size=1000,
                               node_shape="^", edgecolors="#6A1B9A",

                               node_color="#1E8B52", node_size=600,

            if node_id in pos:

                label = G.nodes[node_id].get("label", node_id)
                ax.text(lx, ly + y_off, label,

violations.title: OAuth token stores are module-level dicts mutated by concurrent handlers without locks
violations.content: `authorize` writes to module-level `_auth_codes` (line 51) and `token` mutates `_auth_codes`, `_access_tokens`, and `_refresh_tokens` (lines 104, 108, 130). These dictionaries are shared mutable state accessed by concurrent async request handlers without any synchronization. While individual dict operations are GIL-protected, the check-then-act pattern in `token` (lines 96-99: `pop` + check `expires`, lines 124-127: `get` + check `expires`) combined with separate writes is not atomic with any external invariant (e.g. token expiration sweeps or rate-limiting). There is also no eviction of expired entries, so the dicts grow unboundedly under load. In a multi-worker deployment, in-process dicts are not shared at all — tokens issued by one worker are invisible to others, causing intermittent `invalid_grant` errors.
violations.fixPrompt: Move OAuth token storage out of in-memory module-level dicts to a shared store (Redis or the SQLite `app_settings`/dedicated table) with atomic operations. If in-memory must remain, wrap reads/writes in an `asyncio.Lock` and run a background sweeper to evict expired entries, and document the single-worker constraint.

violations.title: `get_topology` fails completely if either upstream Deco or correlation call raises
violations.content: In `get_topology`, the two upstream calls `deco_service.get_nodes_with_details()` (line 813) and `correlation_service.get_merged_clients()` (line 816) are inside a single try block whose only fallback is the 500 response at lines 1021-1026. The local topology fetch on lines 824-827 is correctly wrapped to degrade gracefully, but a transient failure of the cloud-only `get_nodes_with_details` or the DB-backed `get_merged_clients` will bring down the entire topology endpoint with HTTP 500 even when partial data could still be rendered. Compare to `client.get_topology_local()` which has its own try/except and returns degraded data. The two primary data sources should be similarly degraded so a Deco cloud outage does not also kill correlation-derived data and vice versa.
violations.fixPrompt: In `get_topology`, wrap `deco_service.get_nodes_with_details()` and `correlation_service.get_merged_clients()` in individual try/except blocks that log and substitute empty defaults (`nodes_data = []`, `merged_devices = []`), so partial topology can still be returned. Add a `partial: true` flag and a `degraded_sources` list to the response so the frontend can indicate which subsystems are unavailable.
violations.snippet:
try:
        # Get all Deco nodes
        nodes_data = deco_service.get_nodes_with_details()

        # Get merged client data (devices with their Deco connections)
        merged_result = correlation_service.get_merged_clients()
        merged_devices = merged_result.get("merged_devices", [])

violations.title: `Promise.all` fails-fast and brings down unrelated speed-insight features
violations.content: `fetchAll` uses `Promise.all` over five independent endpoints (`/speedtest/latest`, `/speedtest/history`, `/speedtest/hourly-averages`, `/speedtest/insights`, `/speedtest/scheduler/status`). If any single fetch rejects (e.g., transient network error on one endpoint), the entire promise rejects, skipping ALL the per-response `if (res.ok)` blocks below and leaving `latest`, `history`, `hourly`, `insights`, AND `schedulerStatus` un-updated. A single backend hiccup on one feature wipes out unrelated panels instead of degrading gracefully. The catch only logs to console, so the user sees stale or empty data with no indication of which subsystem failed.
violations.fixPrompt: Replace `Promise.all` with `Promise.allSettled` in `fetchAll` so each fetch's failure is isolated. Iterate the settled results and only call the corresponding `set*` when `result.status === 'fulfilled'` and `result.value.ok`. Log individual failures so the user can see which subsystem degraded without losing data from the others.
violations.snippet:
const [latestRes, historyRes, hourlyRes, insightsRes, schedulerRes] = await Promise.all([
        fetch(buildUrl('/speedtest/latest')),
        fetch(buildUrl(`/speedtest/history?hours=${historyHours}`)),
        fetch(buildUrl('/speedtest/hourly-averages?days=7')),
        fetch(buildUrl('/speedtest/insights')),
        fetch(buildUrl('/speedtest/scheduler/status')),
      ]);

violations.title: `saveAlexaCookies` calls `resp.json()` without checking `response.ok`
violations.content: `saveAlexaCookies` (and similarly `saveChester`, `saveHiboost`, `testChester`, `testHiboost`) unconditionally calls `await response.json()` without first checking `response.ok`. If the backend returns a non-JSON error (e.g., 500 with HTML body, 401 with empty body, gateway timeout), `response.json()` throws, jumping straight to the catch block which reports a generic `Error: ${err.message}` instead of an HTTP-specific message. There is no degraded path that distinguishes a backend 5xx from a network outage, and the user loses information about which failure mode occurred.
violations.fixPrompt: In `saveAlexaCookies` (and the parallel `saveChester`/`saveHiboost`/`testChester`/`testHiboost` handlers), branch on `response.ok` before calling `response.json()`. When `!response.ok`, attempt `response.json().catch(() => ({}))` and surface the HTTP status in the toast and result state, so an HTTP error degrades gracefully with a distinct message rather than masquerading as a JSON parse failure.

violations.title: `_init_db` leaks SQLite connection if a `PRAGMA` statement fails
violations.content: In `_init_db`, `self.connection = sqlite3.connect(...)` is opened, then two `PRAGMA` statements (`PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON` and `PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL`) execute against it. If either `execute` raises `sqlite3.Error`, control jumps to the `except` block, which only logs and re-raises — the already-open SQLite connection is never closed. Since this method may be retried by callers, leaked file descriptors / SQLite handles can accumulate. The acquired resource is not released in a `finally` block.
violations.fixPrompt: In `backend/db.py` `_init_db` (lines 46–59), ensure that if any statement after `sqlite3.connect(...)` raises, the partially-initialized connection is closed before re-raising. For example, wrap the `PRAGMA` calls in their own `try` and call `self.connection.close()` then set `self.connection = None` in the `except` before `raise`.
violations.snippet:
def _init_db(self):
        """Initialize database connection"""
        try:
            # Use check_same_thread=False for thread-safe operation with async
            self.connection = sqlite3.connect(self.db_path, check_same_thread=False)
            self.connection.row_factory = sqlite3.Row
            # Enable foreign keys
            self.connection.execute("PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON")
            # 2026-03-12: Enable WAL mode for concurrent read safety
            self.connection.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL")
            logger.info(f"Database initialized at {self.db_path} (WAL mode)")
        except sqlite3.Error as e:
            logger.error(f"Failed to initialize database: {e}")
            raise

violations.title: Matplotlib figure may leak on exception in `get_topology_graph`
violations.content: In `get_topology_graph`, a matplotlib figure is created via `fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 1, figsize=(28, 14))` at line 1311 and only closed at line 1438 via `plt.close(fig)`. If any of the intermediate operations between figure creation and closing raise an exception (e.g., during `nx.draw_networkx_*` calls, `ax.text` operations, `fig.savefig`, or layout computation), the `except Exception as e` at line 1448 catches the error and raises `HTTPException` without closing the figure. Matplotlib figures consume significant memory and are kept alive by pyplot's global registry; repeated leaks under the `Agg` backend can accumulate substantial memory usage in a long-running FastAPI server. The figure creation should be wrapped in a try/finally so `plt.close(fig)` runs regardless of success or failure.
violations.fixPrompt: Refactor `get_topology_graph` in `backend/routes/deco.py` so the matplotlib figure created at line 1311 is always closed. Wrap the figure lifecycle in a try/finally: create `fig, ax = plt.subplots(...)`, then put all rendering/saving in a try block with `plt.close(fig)` in the finally block. Ensure the existing outer exception handler still surfaces errors as `HTTPException`.

        fig.savefig(buf, format="svg", bbox_inches="tight", dpi=150)
        plt.close(fig)
        buf.seek(0)
        svg_data = buf.getvalue()

        # 2026-03-13: Cache the SVG
        _topology_svg_cache = svg_data
        _topology_svg_cache_time = time.time()

        return Response(content=svg_data, media_type="image/svg+xml")

    except Exception as e:
        logger.error(f"Failed to generate topology graph: {e}")
        raise HTTPException(status_code=500, detail=f"Failed to generate topology graph: {str(e)}")

violations.title: SQLite connection not closed in `finally` block
violations.content: In `main()`, `sqlite3.connect(db_path)` opens a database connection but `conn.close()` is only called on the success path. If `conn.execute(...).fetchone()` or `json.loads(row[0])` raises an exception, control jumps to the `except` clause and the connection is never closed, leaking the file handle. The cleanup should be in a `finally` block or the connection should be used as a context manager.
violations.fixPrompt: Refactor the SQLite connection block in `main()` to use `with sqlite3.connect(db_path) as conn:` or wrap the operations in `try/finally` to ensure `conn.close()` is always called even if `execute()`, `fetchone()`, or `json.loads()` raise an exception.

violations.title: Socket leaks if `ctx.wrap_socket` fails after `socket.create_connection`
violations.content: In `connect()`, `socket.create_connection(...)` is assigned to `self._sock` and then `ctx.wrap_socket(self._sock, ...)` is called. If `wrap_socket` raises (e.g., TLS handshake failure), `self._sock` holds an open socket but `self._ssl_sock` remains unset. The caller's `finally: client.close()` may not close `self._sock` properly if `close()` only looks at `self._ssl_sock`. The acquisition of the raw socket is not protected with a try/except that closes it on subsequent failure.
violations.fixPrompt: Wrap the `ctx.wrap_socket(...)` call in `connect()` with a try/except that calls `self._sock.close()` and re-raises if wrapping fails. Alternatively, ensure `close()` always closes both `self._sock` and `self._ssl_sock` independently even if only one was successfully created.
violations.snippet:
def connect(self) -> None:
        """Establish TLS connection to Deco."""
        logger.info(f"Connecting to {self.host}:{self.port}...")
        ctx = ssl.SSLContext(ssl.PROTOCOL_TLS_CLIENT)
        ctx.check_hostname = False
        ctx.verify_mode = ssl.CERT_NONE
        # Allow older TLS versions that Deco might require
        ctx.minimum_version = ssl.TLSVersion.TLSv1_2

        self._sock = socket.create_connection((self.host, self.port), timeout=10)
        self._ssl_sock = ctx.wrap_socket(self._sock, server_hostname=self.host)
        logger.info(f"TLS connected: {self._ssl_sock.version()}")

violations.title: Recursive `setTimeout` chain in `verifyConfigChanges` has no cleanup on unmount
violations.content: `verifyConfigChanges` schedules `setTimeout(pollChanges, pollInterval)` recursively (line 252) plus additional `setTimeout` calls on the resolve paths (lines 232, 244). None of these timeout IDs are tracked or cleared if the component unmounts mid-verification. The pending timeouts will fire after unmount, attempting state updates (`setVerificationMessage`) on an unmounted component and continuing to make `fetch` requests until the 30s window expires.
violations.fixPrompt: Track the timeout IDs returned by `setTimeout` in a `useRef` (or component-scoped ref) and add a cleanup `useEffect` that calls `clearTimeout` on unmount. Also add an `isMounted`/`AbortController` check so the recursive `pollChanges` loop halts when the component unmounts, preventing leaked timers and stale state updates.

violations.title: Fetch in `useEffect` lacks `AbortController` cleanup
violations.content: The `useEffect` on lines 33-42 calls `fetch` to retrieve presence history but does not return a cleanup function and does not use an `AbortController`. If `device.device_id` changes or the component unmounts before the request resolves, the in-flight `fetch` will still call `setPresenceHistory` on a stale/unmounted component, leaking the in-flight request and triggering React warnings. This matches the rule's concern about asynchronous resources acquired in `useEffect` without corresponding cleanup.
violations.fixPrompt: Refactor the `useEffect` in `DeviceDetailCard.jsx` (lines 33-42) to create an `AbortController`, pass its `signal` to the `fetch` call, and return a cleanup function from the effect that calls `controller.abort()`. Also guard the `setPresenceHistory` call so it is not invoked when the request was aborted.

violations.title: `setTimeout` in `showBanner` is never cleared
violations.content: `showBanner` schedules a `setTimeout` to clear the banner but never stores the timer ID or clears it. Two issues result: (1) if the component unmounts before the timeout fires, React will warn about setting state on an unmounted component; (2) if `showBanner` is invoked again before the previous timeout expires, the earlier timer continues running and may prematurely clear a newer banner. There is no `clearTimeout` and no `useEffect` cleanup tying the timer to the component lifecycle.
violations.fixPrompt: Track the active timer ID with a `useRef` (e.g. `bannerTimerRef`). In `showBanner`, call `clearTimeout(bannerTimerRef.current)` before scheduling the new `setTimeout`, and store the returned ID on the ref. Add a `useEffect` cleanup (`return () => clearTimeout(bannerTimerRef.current)`) so the timer is cleared on unmount.

violations.title: `showBanner` `setTimeout` not cleared on unmount
violations.content: The `showBanner` helper schedules a `setTimeout` to clear the banner state but never tracks the timer handle. If the component unmounts before the timeout fires (e.g., the user navigates away within 4–6 seconds of a banner being shown), the timer continues to run and invokes `setBanner(null)` on an unmounted component. The closure also retains references that delay garbage collection. There is no `clearTimeout` cleanup in any `useEffect`.
violations.fixPrompt: Store the timeout handle from `setTimeout` in a `useRef`, clear any prior handle before scheduling a new one, and add a `useEffect` cleanup that calls `clearTimeout` on the stored handle when the component unmounts.

violations.title: `device_events` rely on `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` with no sequence number for ordering
violations.content: `DeviceEventRepository.create` inserts events using SQLite `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` (1-second precision) for both `timestamp` and `created_at`, with no monotonic sequence/`rowid` tiebreaker stored alongside. Downstream readers (`list_by_device` at lines 666–681 and `list_all` at lines 683–697) order purely by `ORDER BY timestamp DESC`. When a device flaps quickly (e.g., `online → offline → online` during a brief network blip, or multiple scanners emitting state transitions in the same second), all of those events get the same timestamp and their retrieval order becomes non-deterministic. Anything that consumes these events to reconstruct the latest state (alerts, presence history, the SSE stream) is implicitly assuming chronological delivery/ordering that the storage layer does not guarantee. Under load or re-scan bursts this can flip a device's apparent final state.
violations.fixPrompt: In `DeviceEventRepository.create` (`backend/db.py` lines 637–652), add explicit sub-second ordering. Either (a) accept and store a caller-supplied ISO timestamp with microsecond precision (e.g., `datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()`) instead of `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP`, or (b) add a monotonically increasing `seq` column populated from a sequence/autoincrement and order by `(timestamp DESC, seq DESC)` in `list_by_device` and `list_all`. Update the migrations and the events listing queries accordingly.

violations.title: `_save_device_state_to_db` blindly overwrites state without checking timestamp ordering
violations.content: `_save_device_state_to_db` unconditionally UPDATEs `last_state` and `state_updated_at` for an `endpoint_id`, with no check that the incoming `timestamp` is newer than the currently stored `state_updated_at`. Alexa state updates can come from concurrent polling threads, an `_send_directive`/`ReportState` race, or webhook-style callbacks. Under any concurrency (or simple thread interleaving from `_http_session` calls and the `concurrent.futures` worker pool typical to this code), an older state result that finishes its DB write *after* a newer one will silently overwrite the newer state — leaving the stored `last_state` permanently stale until the next poll. The code implicitly assumes calls to this method are serialized in chronological order, but nothing in the infrastructure guarantees that.
violations.fixPrompt: Modify `_save_device_state_to_db` in `backend/services/alexa_service.py` to make the UPDATE conditional on the incoming `timestamp` being newer than the stored `state_updated_at`. For example, change the SQL to `UPDATE alexa_devices SET last_state = ?, state_updated_at = ?, updated_at = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP WHERE endpoint_id = ? AND (state_updated_at IS NULL OR state_updated_at < ?)` and pass `timestamp` as the final parameter. This guarantees out-of-order state writes cannot overwrite newer state.
