        # Load RSA public key
        pub_key_bytes = base64.b64decode(RSA_PUBLIC_KEY_B64)
        self._rsa_key = load_der_public_key(pub_key_bytes)

violations.title: Auto-refresh polling lacks circuit breaker
violations.content: The `useEffect` in `DecoTopologyView` schedules `fetchTopology` and `fetchGraph` on a fixed `setInterval` of `autoRefreshInterval` (default 30s) with no failure-rate tracking. If the `/deco/topology` or `/deco/topology-graph` endpoints are persistently failing (e.g., Deco router unreachable, backend down, auth lost returning 401), the interval keeps firing requests indefinitely. `fetchTopology` swallows errors into local state and `fetchGraph` only logs warnings — neither stops or backs off the interval. This means one failing dependency causes the UI to hammer the backend every 30s forever, exhausting backend connection pools to the Deco API and cascading failures.
violations.fixPrompt: Add a consecutive-failure counter to `fetchTopology` and `fetchGraph`. When failures exceed a threshold (e.g., 5 consecutive failures), open a circuit by clearing the interval (or skipping calls) and entering a cooldown period (e.g., 5 minutes) before retrying. Reset the counter on success. Show the user a circuit-open state with a manual retry button instead of silently looping.

violations.title: QoS polling continues regardless of failures
violations.content: The `useEffect` in `DecoWiFiQoSView` sequentially calls `/deco/wifi-config` and `/deco/qos` every `refreshInterval` (default 10s) with no failure tracking. When the Deco backend is failing, the interval keeps firing both fetches every 10 seconds indefinitely — there is no maximum-failure threshold after which calls stop or back off. With a 10-second cadence this is especially aggressive: two upstream Deco API calls every tick from every mounted instance. This can exhaust connection pools on the backend and the upstream Deco router during outages.
violations.fixPrompt: Track consecutive failures in a ref. After N consecutive failures (e.g., 3-5), stop the `setInterval` or switch to an exponential-backoff schedule until a successful call resets the breaker. Surface the open-circuit state in the UI with a manual retry button rather than silently continuing the loop.

violations.title: `verifyConfigChanges` retries on failure with no breaker
violations.content: `verifyConfigChanges` polls `/deco/wifi-config` every 5 seconds for up to `maxWaitMs` (30s). The `catch` block in `pollChanges` resolves silently on error and stops, which is fine — but on success paths that return non-OK responses, the code throws and falls into the catch. More importantly, there's no tracking of intermittent failures across retries: if the backend is degraded and returning 5xx, the poller keeps retrying every 5s until timeout with no failure-rate threshold to short-circuit early. While `maxWaitMs` bounds the loop, the function lacks a circuit-breaker pattern that would stop after a small number of consecutive failures rather than continuing to hammer a failing endpoint.
violations.fixPrompt: Add a consecutive-failure counter inside `pollChanges`. After 2-3 consecutive non-OK or thrown responses, stop polling early, set `verificationMessage` to an error state, and resolve. This avoids continuing to call a clearly-failing endpoint up to the full 30-second budget.

violations.title: Polling intervals lack circuit breaker on repeated failures
violations.content: `fastIntervalRef` (15s), `slowIntervalRef` (30s), and `speedIntervalRef` (60s) in `useDevicePolling` continue firing indefinitely regardless of failure rates. Each interval triggers multiple `fetch` calls (`/health`, `/devices`, `/config/polling`, `/device-groups`, `/network/home-status`, `/events/alerts`, `/deco/client-node-map`, `/chester/system-info`, `/network/health-score`, `/speedtest/latest`, `/speedtest/insights`) whose individual catch blocks silently swallow errors and immediately schedule another round. There is no consecutive-failure threshold, no exponential backoff, and no open/half-open state. If the backend (or the downstream Deco/Chester/Alexa/Alarm.com services it proxies) is degraded, the browser keeps hammering it at fixed intervals, potentially exhausting connection pools and amplifying cascading failures rather than failing fast.
violations.fixPrompt: Introduce a circuit-breaker wrapper around the polling callbacks in `useDevicePolling`. Track consecutive failure counts per endpoint group (`fastPoll`, `slowPoll`, `speedPoll`); after N (e.g. 5) consecutive failures, open the circuit by skipping calls and lengthening the interval (exponential backoff). After a cool-down, allow a single probe call (half-open); on success, reset the counter and resume normal cadence. Surface the open state via `apiStatus` so the UI can indicate degraded mode.

violations.title: `pollUnseen` polls every 10s with no failure threshold
violations.content: The `pollUnseen` callback in the notifications `useEffect` hits `/events/alerts/unseen` and `/events/alerts/mark-seen` every 10 seconds via `setInterval(pollUnseen, 10000)`. The catch block is a silent `/* silent */`, so repeated failures are invisible and the polling loop keeps issuing requests at full cadence. There is no failure counter, no backoff, and no circuit-open state. If the backend is overloaded or unreachable, this loop will continue to consume browser sockets and add load to a struggling server rather than failing fast.
violations.fixPrompt: Wrap `pollUnseen` with a circuit-breaker: count consecutive failures, open the circuit after a threshold, apply exponential backoff (e.g. 10s → 30s → 2m), and re-probe periodically. Reset on success. Log/surface the breaker state so the user knows notifications are paused.

violations.title: `DecoNodesPage` auto-refresh has no failure threshold
violations.content: The auto-refresh `useEffect` schedules `fetchNodes` via `setInterval(..., refreshInterval)` (default 60s) and never stops on failures. `fetchNodes` calls `/deco/nodes`, which proxies to the TP-Link Deco cloud — an external service that is known to throttle and to require re-authentication. When `fetchNodes` throws (401/404/network error), the error is set in state but the interval keeps firing on the same cadence, continuously hammering the Deco cloud through the backend. There is no consecutive-failure counter, no backoff, and no open-circuit short-circuit.
violations.fixPrompt: Track consecutive `fetchNodes` failures in a ref. After ~3 failures, pause the `setInterval` (or skip its body via an `if (breakerOpen) return;` guard) and start an exponentially backed-off probe timer. On a successful probe, reset the counter and restore the normal interval. Consider surfacing the breaker state in the UI banner so the user understands why auto-refresh has paused.

violations.title: `_call_backend` lacks circuit breaker for backend HTTP calls
violations.content: The `_call_backend` helper makes HTTP requests to the HomeSentinel backend (potentially through `ngrok`) with a 25-second timeout, but has no circuit breaker. Each Lambda invocation independently attempts the call and logs failures, with no shared failure-rate tracking, no fast-fail state, and no cooldown. If the backend is down or slow, every Alexa Smart Home directive triggers a fresh 25s wait, exhausting Lambda execution time and the upstream connection budget. A circuit breaker that tracks consecutive failures and short-circuits to `None` for a cooldown window would fail fast and protect both Lambda and the backend.
violations.fixPrompt: Add a circuit breaker around `_call_backend` in `lambda/lambda_function.py`. Track consecutive failure count and a `cooldown_until` timestamp in module-level state (or DynamoDB for cross-invocation persistence). When failures exceed a threshold (e.g. 5 in a row), open the circuit and short-circuit subsequent calls to return `None` immediately until the cooldown elapses. Reset the counter on success. Consider using a library like `pybreaker` or `circuitbreaker`.

violations.title: Polling intervals in `SpeedInsightsPage` keep hammering failing endpoints
violations.content: The `useEffect` sets three `setInterval` loops that call `fetchAll` (60s), `fetchChester` (30s), and `fetchHiboostHistory` (300s) indefinitely. The fetch helpers swallow errors but do not track failure rates, do not back off, and do not stop polling after consecutive failures. If `/chester/system-info` or `/hiboost/history` are persistently unreachable, the page continues to fire requests at the same cadence, wasting browser sockets and backend resources. A simple failure-threshold check that pauses or exponentially backs off polling after N consecutive errors would prevent cascading load against failing dependencies.
violations.fixPrompt: In `frontend/src/pages/SpeedInsightsPage.jsx`, add per-endpoint failure counters that pause the corresponding `setInterval` (or switch to exponential backoff) after several consecutive failures. Reset the counter and resume normal cadence after the next successful response. Surface the paused state via the existing `banner` so the user knows polling stopped.

violations.title: `fetchChester` and `fetchHiboostHistory` silently retry on every interval
violations.content: `fetchChester` and `fetchHiboostHistory` catch all errors silently (comments say "Chester may not be reachable" / "HiBoost may not be configured"), but the surrounding `setInterval` keeps calling them at fixed cadence regardless. There is no consecutive-failure threshold after which polling stops, no exponential backoff, and no awareness of whether the dependency is healthy. For optional integrations that may be unconfigured, this generates continuous noise traffic against backend routes that will never succeed. A circuit-breaker style guard (track failure count, open after threshold, attempt half-open probe at backoff intervals) would eliminate the steady-state failed-request load.
violations.fixPrompt: Wrap `fetchChester` and `fetchHiboostHistory` in a small client-side circuit-breaker helper that tracks consecutive failure count, returns early once a threshold (e.g. 5) is reached, and only retries a single probe call on a backoff schedule (e.g. doubling delay). On a successful probe, close the breaker and resume normal polling.

violations.title: `Promise.all` on independent fetches aborts entire batch on single failure
violations.content: `fetchAll` uses `Promise.all` to fetch five independent endpoints (`/speedtest/latest`, `/speedtest/history`, `/speedtest/hourly-averages`, `/speedtest/insights`, `/speedtest/scheduler/status`). These populate independent state slots (`setLatest`, `setHistory`, `setHourlyAvgs`, `setInsights`, `setSchedulerStatus`) and have no dependencies between them. If any single fetch rejects (e.g., network error on one endpoint, or one endpoint is temporarily unavailable), `Promise.all` short-circuits and rejects, sending control directly to the `catch` block on line 70. None of the response handlers (lines 49–69) run, so even endpoints that successfully responded have their data discarded and corresponding UI state is never updated. The user sees a fully empty page even when 4 of 5 endpoints worked. The downstream `if (res.ok)` checks indicate the code already expects partial failures at the HTTP layer — the same expectation should apply at the Promise layer.
violations.fixPrompt: Replace `Promise.all` with `Promise.allSettled` in `fetchAll` so each fetch settles independently. For each result, check `status === 'fulfilled'` before accessing `.value`, then run the existing `res.ok` / `await res.json()` logic. This preserves partial-success behavior: endpoints that succeed populate their state slots, and only the failing endpoint's data is missing.
violations.snippet:
const [latestRes, historyRes, hourlyRes, insightsRes, schedulerRes] = await Promise.all([
        fetch(buildUrl('/speedtest/latest')),
        fetch(buildUrl(`/speedtest/history?hours=${historyHours}`)),
        fetch(buildUrl('/speedtest/hourly-averages?days=7')),
        fetch(buildUrl('/speedtest/insights')),
        fetch(buildUrl('/speedtest/scheduler/status')),
      ]);

violations.title: Background poller `pollUnseen` silently swallows all errors
violations.content: The `pollUnseen` function is a background polling worker that fetches unseen alerts and triggers browser notifications. The entire body is wrapped in `try { ... } catch (error) { /* silent */ }` with no logging, no failure-state tracking, and no consecutive-failure counter. If the alerts endpoint, the mark-seen call, or notification creation fails repeatedly, users will never see new-device or device-offline notifications and nobody will know the poller is broken.
violations.fixPrompt: Update `pollUnseen` in `frontend/src/hooks/useDevicePolling.js` to at minimum `console.error` the caught error (matching the convention used elsewhere in this hook) and track consecutive failures in state so the UI can surface a 'notifications poller is failing' indicator after N successive errors. Do not leave the catch block as `/* silent */`.

violations.title: Background fetch `getClientNodeMap` silently fails with no logging
violations.content: `getClientNodeMap` is invoked as part of the periodic polling pipeline. The catch block only contains the comment `// Silently fail — Deco may not be configured` and does not log, increment a failure counter, or surface state to the UI. A misconfigured Deco integration will look identical to a transient network error or a real bug — operators have no signal that the background data refresh is broken.
violations.fixPrompt: In `getClientNodeMap`, log the caught error via `console.warn` (so true 'not configured' cases are still visible) and consider tracking consecutive failures so persistent errors can be distinguished from a one-time misconfiguration.

violations.title: Background fetch `getSpeedTestLatest` silently fails
violations.content: `getSpeedTestLatest` runs as part of the polling hook and its catch block is `// Silently fail — speed test may not have run yet`. There is no log, no failure tracking, and no UI signal. If the `/speedtest/latest` endpoint starts returning errors indefinitely, the UI will continue to show stale (or empty) speed data with no indication that the background fetch loop is broken.
violations.fixPrompt: Add `console.error` logging to the catch block in `getSpeedTestLatest` and consider exposing a polling-health flag so the UI can show a 'speed data unavailable' state instead of silently displaying nothing.

violations.title: Background fetch `getChesterInfo` silently fails
violations.content: `getChesterInfo` is part of the background polling pipeline and only contains `// Silently fail — Chester may not be reachable` in its catch block. There is no logging or failure-state tracking, so persistent Chester connectivity issues will be indistinguishable from intentional 'not configured' scenarios.
violations.fixPrompt: In `getChesterInfo`, log the caught error and surface a Chester-reachability flag in state so the UI (and operators) can tell the difference between 'unconfigured' and 'configured but failing'.

violations.title: Background fetch `getHomeStatus` silently fails
violations.content: `getHomeStatus` is a background polling fetch whose catch block is only `// Silently fail`. No logging, no failure state. The home-status UI will simply show stale data forever if this endpoint breaks.
violations.fixPrompt: Add `console.error` to the catch block in `getHomeStatus` and consider tracking a failure count so the dashboard can flag a degraded state.

violations.title: Background fetch `getActiveAlerts` silently swallows errors
violations.content: `getActiveAlerts` polls the alerts endpoint and its catch block is `catch (error) { /* silent */ }`. Active alerts are user-safety-critical data; silently failing means users may believe their network is healthy while the alerts fetch has actually been broken for hours.
violations.fixPrompt: Replace the `/* silent */` catch with `console.error('Failed to fetch active alerts:', error)` and track consecutive failures in state so the UI can surface a clear 'alerts unavailable' indicator after repeated failures.

violations.title: Background fetch `getAnomalyInsights` silently swallows errors
violations.content: `getAnomalyInsights` is a background polling fetch with a `catch (error) { /* silent */ }` block. Anomaly detection failures will never be surfaced — users may assume their network is anomaly-free when the underlying fetch has been failing.
violations.fixPrompt: Replace `/* silent */` with `console.error` logging and add failure tracking so persistent anomaly-feed failures can be distinguished from 'no anomalies detected'.

violations.title: Background fetch `getDailyDigest` silently swallows errors
violations.content: `getDailyDigest` runs as part of background polling and its catch block is `catch (error) { /* silent */ }`. No logging or failure tracking — the daily digest will simply be empty if the endpoint fails, with no operator-visible signal.
violations.fixPrompt: Replace the silent catch with `console.error('Failed to fetch daily digest:', error)` to match the convention used elsewhere in this hook.

violations.title: Background fetch `getHealthScore` silently swallows errors
violations.content: `getHealthScore` is a background polling fetch with a `catch (error) { /* silent */ }` block. The network health score is a primary dashboard indicator — silent failures here mean the score may stop updating without anyone noticing, defeating the purpose of a health indicator.
violations.fixPrompt: Replace the silent catch in `getHealthScore` with `console.error` logging and consider invalidating the displayed score (or marking it stale) after repeated failures so the dashboard does not show a misleading 'healthy' state from an outdated value.

violations.title: Unbounded `ip_history` list grows on every IP change
violations.content: In `NetworkDeviceRepository.create_or_update`, the `ip_history` list is loaded from the database, appended to whenever a device's IP changes, and re-serialized to JSON — with no size cap, ring-buffer, or eviction policy. A device that frequently churns IPs (DHCP renewals, network instability, an attacker spoofing DHCP leases, or a misbehaving client) will cause this list to grow without bound. Each call also loads, parses, mutates, and re-writes the full JSON blob, so memory and disk usage scale linearly with history length. Under sustained churn this can balloon the `network_devices` row, slow down every `create_or_update` call, and eventually pressure memory when many devices have long histories.
violations.fixPrompt: In `backend/db.py` `NetworkDeviceRepository.create_or_update` (around lines 189–203), cap `ip_history` to a maximum number of entries (e.g. 50) using a trailing slice such as `ip_history = ip_history[-49:]` before appending the new entry, or trim by retention window (e.g. drop entries older than 30 days). Make the cap configurable via an env var like `IP_HISTORY_MAX_ENTRIES` and document the limit.

violations.title: `_identify_snapshots` dict grows unbounded across `identify_start` calls
violations.content: The module-level `_identify_snapshots: Dict[str, Dict]` cache at line 960 stores a full Deco client-list snapshot (every online MAC + name + IP) per `entity_id` whenever `POST /smart-home/{entity_id}/identify/start` is called (line 990). Entries are only removed in two places: when `identify_complete` runs successfully (line 1064), and when `identify_complete` detects a stale snapshot (line 1019). There is no background sweep, no `__len__` cap, no LRU eviction, and the staleness check only fires when `identify_complete` is invoked. A client that repeatedly calls `/identify/start` with different `entity_id` values (or the same one without ever calling `/identify/complete`) will accumulate per-entity snapshots indefinitely. Each snapshot scales with the number of online network clients (potentially hundreds), so under abuse or buggy clients the dict can grow without bound and exhaust memory.
violations.fixPrompt: Add a bound on `_identify_snapshots` in `backend/routes/alexa.py`. Options: (1) enforce a maximum size (e.g. `MAX_IDENTIFY_SNAPSHOTS = 32`) and evict the oldest entry by `ts` before inserting in `identify_start`; (2) proactively prune entries older than 300s on every `identify_start` call rather than only inside `identify_complete`; (3) replace the raw dict with a TTL-bounded structure such as `cachetools.TTLCache(maxsize=N, ttl=300)`. Whichever approach you choose, ensure both stale-time AND maximum-cardinality limits are enforced regardless of which endpoint is called.

violations.title: Unbounded in-memory OAuth token stores
violations.content: The module-level dicts `_auth_codes`, `_access_tokens`, and `_refresh_tokens` accumulate entries indefinitely with no size limit or eviction policy. `_auth_codes` is popped on successful redemption but unredeemed codes remain forever; `_access_tokens` and `_refresh_tokens` are never cleaned up at all — every call to `/oauth/token` adds new entries (e.g., refresh-token grants in lines 129-133 add a new access token without removing the old one). Under sustained load — for example, an Alexa skill or attacker repeatedly hitting `/oauth/authorize` and `/oauth/token` — these dicts will grow without bound, eventually causing OOM. Expired entries are detected only when explicitly looked up, never proactively reaped.
violations.fixPrompt: In `backend/routes/oauth.py`, add a periodic cleanup task (e.g., a background asyncio task started at app startup) that walks `_auth_codes`, `_access_tokens`, and `_refresh_tokens` and removes entries whose `expires` timestamp is in the past. Alternatively, replace the raw dicts with a TTL-aware structure (e.g., `cachetools.TTLCache`) sized to a reasonable maximum to bound memory even under abuse. When issuing a refresh-token grant, also evict any prior access token associated with the same refresh token.

violations.title: Unbounded `OUIService.cache` dictionary
violations.content: `OUIService.cache` is initialized as an empty `Dict[str, str]` (line 28) and populated by `lookup_vendor` (line 80) on every successful lookup, but there is no maximum size, TTL, or eviction policy. The cache key is a normalized MAC address, so over the lifetime of the process every distinct MAC ever queried — including transient devices, randomized Wi-Fi MACs (which are 46-bit randomized per network on iOS/Android), and scan probes — adds a permanent entry. On a long-running deployment with frequent ARP scans against many subnets, this will steadily grow and can lead to memory exhaustion. The only way to free entries is the manual `clear_cache` method, which is not called on a schedule.
violations.fixPrompt: Bound `OUIService.cache` with an explicit size cap and eviction policy. Replace the plain `Dict[str, str]` with an `OrderedDict` and implement LRU eviction in `lookup_vendor` (e.g., on insert, `popitem(last=False)` once `len(self.cache) > MAX_CACHE_SIZE`), or use `functools.lru_cache` on a helper method. Choose a `MAX_CACHE_SIZE` appropriate for the expected device population (e.g., 10000).
violations.snippet:
self.cache: Dict[str, str] = {}
        self._load_database()

    def _load_database(self) -> None:
        """Load OUI database from CSV file"""
        try:
            if not os.path.exists(self.oui_csv_path):
                logger.warning(f"OUI database file not found: {self.oui_csv_path}")
                return

            with open(self.oui_csv_path, 'r', encoding='utf-8') as f:
                reader = csv.DictReader(f)
                for row in reader:
                    if row and 'OUI' in row and 'COMPANY' in row:
                        # Normalize OUI to uppercase without colons
                        oui = row['OUI'].strip().upper().replace(':', '').replace('-', '')
                        company = row['COMPANY'].strip()
                        # Only add if not already present (keep first occurrence)
                        if oui not in self.oui_database:
                            self.oui_database[oui] = company

            logger.info(f"OUI database loaded successfully: {len(self.oui_database)} entries")

        except Exception as e:
            logger.error(f"Failed to load OUI database: {e}")

    def lookup_vendor(self, mac_address: str) -> str:
        """
        Lookup vendor name by MAC address

        Args:
            mac_address: MAC address in format "AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF" or "AABBCCDDEE:FF"

        Returns:
            Vendor name or "Unknown Vendor" if not found
        """
        # Normalize MAC address
        normalized_mac = self._normalize_mac(mac_address)
        if not normalized_mac:
            return "Unknown Vendor"

        # Check cache first
        if normalized_mac in self.cache:

        # Look up in database

violations.title: `HiBoostService` cache has TTL but no size limit or expired-entry eviction
violations.content: `HiBoostService._cache` and `_cache_ts` (lines 64-65) accumulate entries via `_set_cache` (lines 70-72) keyed by `dashboard` and per-device `detail:{device_id}` strings. `_is_cached` only checks freshness on read; expired entries are never removed from the dictionaries. There is also no maximum size. While the number of HiBoost devices is typically small, if `device_id` values ever vary (e.g., transient IDs, retries with mutated identifiers, or future expansion to many devices), both dicts grow without bound and never shrink except via the manual `clear_cache`.
violations.fixPrompt: In `HiBoostService._set_cache`, also evict any keys whose `_cache_ts` value is older than `CACHE_TTL` so stale entries do not accumulate. Additionally, enforce a hard cap (e.g., 1000 entries) and drop the oldest by timestamp once exceeded. Alternatively, switch to a `cachetools.TTLCache` with an explicit `maxsize` and `ttl=CACHE_TTL`.

violations.title: `_recv_tslp` reads attacker-controlled `payload_len` into an unbounded buffer
violations.content: In `_recv_tslp`, after reading the 24-byte header, `payload_len` is parsed as a 4-byte big-endian unsigned integer from untrusted network data and then used as the size of the in-memory `payload` buffer that is grown via repeated `recv` calls. There is no upper bound check on `payload_len` before allocating/growing this buffer. A malicious or malfunctioning peer can advertise a `payload_len` near 2^32 (4 GiB) per frame and cause the Python process to allocate memory without bound, leading to OOM and a crash. The TSLP framing here mirrors the `_recv_tmp` path for `TMPPacket.decode`, so the same unbounded-buffer concern applies to any frame received over this socket.
violations.fixPrompt: In `_recv_tslp` (around lines 559-578 of `backend/tmp_client.py`), define a sane maximum frame size constant (e.g., `MAX_TSLP_PAYLOAD = 1 << 20` for 1 MiB, sized to legitimate Deco/TMP traffic) and after unpacking `payload_len` from the header raise a `ValueError` / close the socket if `payload_len` exceeds that limit, before entering the `while len(payload) < payload_len` read loop. Consider reading into a preallocated `bytearray` of bounded size and using `recv_into` for efficiency.

violations.title: `useToasts` toast list has no size cap or eviction policy
violations.content: The `useToasts` hook stores notifications in an in-memory `toasts` array that is appended to on every `push` call (`setToasts((prev) => [...prev, { id, message, type, duration }])`). There is no maximum size, no FIFO eviction, and no rate-limiting. Auto-dismissal relies on each `ToastItem` running a `setTimeout` — but `ToastItem` explicitly skips the timeout when `toast.duration === 0` (line 22), meaning sticky toasts never get cleared automatically. If `push` is invoked rapidly (e.g. a burst of errors from polling/SSE failures in `useDevicePolling.js`) or repeatedly with `duration: 0`, the array — and the DOM nodes it renders — grow without bound, leading to memory/UI bloat and eventual unresponsiveness.
violations.fixPrompt: In `useToasts` (`frontend/src/components/Toast.jsx`), cap the toast list. In the `push` callback, after computing the new array, truncate it to a maximum (e.g. 5 most recent) by slicing: `setToasts((prev) => [...prev, newToast].slice(-MAX_TOASTS))`. Also enforce a minimum auto-dismiss duration for sticky toasts or guarantee callers manually dismiss `duration: 0` toasts, so the queue cannot grow without bound under burst conditions.

violations.title: Module-level discovery/state caches define `CACHE_TTL` but never enforce it
violations.content: The module declares in-memory caches `_discovery_cache`/`_state_cache` along with `_discovery_cache_time`/`_state_cache_time` timestamps and a `CACHE_TTL = 300` constant, but `CACHE_TTL` is never referenced anywhere else in the file. `_refresh_state_cache` (lines 1551-1609) writes to `_state_cache` and updates `_state_cache_time`, yet no reader compares `time.time() - _state_cache_time` against `CACHE_TTL` to expire entries, and there is no invalidation when underlying Deco/Chester state changes (e.g., when a node is added/removed, when WiFi is toggled via the API, or when credentials are updated). If the Lambda endpoints at lines 1539-1548 and 1675-1678 are ever re-enabled, callers would receive indefinitely stale endpoint and state data.
violations.fixPrompt: In `backend/routes/alexa.py`, either remove the unused `_discovery_cache`, `_state_cache`, `_discovery_cache_time`, `_state_cache_time`, and `CACHE_TTL` symbols (lines 30-35) if the disabled Lambda routes are not coming back, or wire up real invalidation: (1) add a helper `_cache_is_fresh(ts)` that returns `time.time() - ts < CACHE_TTL` and have any reader (including a re-enabled `lambda_discover`/`lambda_get_state`) call `_refresh_state_cache` / discovery rebuild when the cache is stale or empty; (2) call an invalidation function that clears `_state_cache`/`_discovery_cache` whenever Deco WiFi, node, or Chester state is mutated via the existing routes (`/api/deco/...`, `/api/chester/...`, settings updates) so source-of-truth changes do not leave clients reading 5+ minute old data.

violations.title: Topology route cache lacks event-based invalidation on mutations
violations.content: The module-level caches `_topology_json_cache` and `_topology_svg_cache` use only a 60-second TTL (`TOPOLOGY_ROUTE_CACHE_TTL`) for invalidation. Several mutation endpoints in this same file change data that appears in the topology response — `rename_deco_client` (writes new device/node names), `update_wifi_config` (changes SSID/band settings), `optimize_network` (re-evaluates mesh associations), and `refresh_deco_nodes` (explicitly intended to bypass cache). None of these call any invalidation routine on `_topology_json_cache` / `_topology_svg_cache`, so `GET /topology` and `GET /topology-graph` can serve stale data for up to 60 seconds after a user-initiated change. Even `/nodes/refresh`, whose entire purpose is to bypass the cache, only clears `deco_service.clear_cache()` while leaving the route-level topology cache stale. Users who rename a client or run "Optimize Network" will see no immediate effect in the topology view.

violations.content: The `_deco_node_macs_cache` set in `NetworkDeviceService.__init__` stores Deco node MAC addresses without any TTL or expiration. violations.title: `devices` fetched on mount with no invalidation
violations.content: The `useEffect` in `EventLogPage` calls `fetchDevices` exactly once on mount (empty deps array on line 39) and stores the result in the `devices` state. There is no polling interval, no SSE subscription, no manual refresh button, and no other invalidation path. Combined with the codebase's documented lazy-mount pattern (pages stay in the DOM via `display: none` after first visit per project `CLAUDE.md`), this state acts as an in-memory cache that is never cleared when the source data changes. Users returning to the Events & Alerts tab will see device lists captured at the moment of first navigation, even if devices appear/disappear or change status afterward.
violations.fixPrompt: Add an invalidation strategy to `devices` in `EventLogPage.jsx`: either subscribe to the existing `/api/sse/events` stream to refetch on `device_update` events, add a `setInterval` polling refresh similar to `useDevicePolling.js`, or expose a refresh trigger and re-run `fetchDevices` when the page becomes visible (visibilitychange / when the user navigates to the Events & Alerts tab).

violations.title: Alexa `devices`/`echoDevices`/`status` cached with no automatic invalidation
violations.content: `AlexaDevicesPage` calls `checkStatus` once on mount (line 19-21), which loads `status`, `devices`, and `echoDevices` into React state. There is no polling, no SSE subscription, and no visibility-based refresh — the only way to invalidate this state is the manual `Refresh` button or the post-action `setTimeout(() => fetchDevices(), 2000)` after a single device command. Under the project's lazy-mount pattern (pages stay mounted via `display: none`), users returning to the Alexa tab can see stale `is_online` flags, missing newly-discovered devices, and outdated Echo lists indefinitely. The `status.authenticated` flag in particular is loaded once and never re-checked, so a session expiry on the backend will not be reflected until reload.
violations.fixPrompt: Add automatic invalidation to `AlexaDevicesPage.jsx`: introduce a polling interval (e.g., 30–60s) for `fetchDevices`/`fetchEchoDevices`, subscribe to relevant SSE events if available, and re-run `checkStatus` on `document.visibilitychange` so authentication state and device lists are refreshed when the user returns to the tab.

violations.title: Alarm.com `status`/`devices` cached without automatic invalidation
violations.content: The `init` effect runs once on mount and never re-runs (deps are stable callbacks). `status` (including `logged_in`/`configured`) and `devices` (partitions, sensors, locks, etc.) are stored in component state with no polling, no SSE subscription, and no visibility-based refresh. Under the project's lazy-mount pattern, a partition that is armed/disarmed elsewhere, a sensor that trips, or a session that expires on the backend will not appear in this view until the user clicks `Refresh` or sends a command. For a security-system integration where state freshness matters (e.g., a sensor showing OPEN vs CLOSED), this stale-cache risk is meaningful.
violations.fixPrompt: In `AlarmComPage.jsx`, add an automatic invalidation mechanism: poll `/alarm-com/status` and `/alarm-com/devices` on an interval (e.g., 15–30s) while the page is mounted/visible, pause when `document.hidden`, and re-run `fetchStatus`/`fetchDevices` on `visibilitychange` so partition/sensor/lock states reflect backend changes without manual refresh.

violations.title: `suggestions`/`unlinkedAlexa` fetched once with no automatic invalidation
violations.content: `DeviceNamingPage` calls `fetchSuggestions` once on mount (empty deps array) and stores `suggestions`, `unlinkedAlexa`, and `stats` in component state. The only invalidation paths are explicit user actions (`Refresh`, `Import Deco Names`, `Auto-Name Deco Nodes`, link/rename completion). With the lazy-mount pattern, when a new device joins the network or an Alexa device is added, this view will not reflect the change until the user remembers to click `Refresh`. The `stats` (totalNetwork / totalAlexa / totalLinked) will likewise drift from the dashboard's polled counts.
violations.fixPrompt: Add a polling refresh (e.g., 60s) for `fetchSuggestions` in `DeviceNamingPage.jsx`, or trigger a refetch on `document.visibilitychange` when the page becomes visible, so suggestions and stats stay in sync with backend state without manual user action.

                cursor = conn.cursor()
                cursor.execute("""
                    INSERT INTO device_groups (group_id, name, color, created_at, updated_at)
                    VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)
                """, (group_id, name, color, datetime.now(timezone.utc), datetime.now(timezone.utc)))
                conn.commit()
                return self.get_by_id(group_id)
        except sqlite3.Error as e:
            logger.error(f"Failed to create group: {e}")
            raise

    def get_by_id(self, group_id: str) -> Optional[dict]:
        """Get group by ID"""
        try:
            with self.db.get_connection() as conn:
                cursor = conn.cursor()
                cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM device_groups WHERE group_id = ?", (group_id,))
                row = cursor.fetchone()
                return dict(row) if row else None
        except sqlite3.Error as e:
            logger.error(f"Failed to get group: {e}")
            raise

    def get_by_name(self, name: str) -> Optional[dict]:
        """Get group by name"""
        try:
            with self.db.get_connection() as conn:
                cursor = conn.cursor()
                cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM device_groups WHERE name = ?", (name,))
                row = cursor.fetchone()
                return dict(row) if row else None
        except sqlite3.Error as e:

        """List all groups"""
        try:
            with self.db.get_connection() as conn:

                rows = cursor.fetchall()
                return [dict(row) for row in rows]
        except sqlite3.Error as e:
            logger.error(f"Failed to list groups: {e}")
            raise

    def update_group(self, group_id: str, name: Optional[str] = None,
                     color: Optional[str] = None) -> Optional[dict]:
        """Update group metadata"""
        try:
            with self.db.get_connection() as conn:
                cursor = conn.cursor()
                updates = []
                params = []

                if name is not None:
                    updates.append("name = ?")
                    params.append(name)
                if color is not None:
                    updates.append("color = ?")
                    params.append(color)

                if not updates:
                    return self.get_by_id(group_id)

                updates.append("updated_at = ?")
                params.append(datetime.now(timezone.utc))
                params.append(group_id)

                cursor.execute(f"""
                    UPDATE device_groups
                    SET {', '.join(updates)}
                    WHERE group_id = ?
                """, params)
                conn.commit()
                return self.get_by_id(group_id)
        except sqlite3.Error as e:
            logger.error(f"Failed to update group: {e}")
            raise

        """Delete a group"""
        try:

violations.content: `logger.info(f"MAC import: source={source}, total_devices={total_devices}, with_mac={len(endpoint_macs)}")` embeds multiple variables via f-string interpolation.     def get_all_device_macs(self) -> List[Dict[str, str]]:
        """Get MAC addresses for all Echo/Fire hardware devices.

        Calls devices-v2 to get the device list, then device-wifi-details
        for each device to get MAC addresses. Skips groups and non-hardware.
        Returns list of dicts with: serialNumber, accountName, deviceFamily,
        deviceType, macAddress (normalized aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff), essid
        """
        devices = self.get_echo_devices_web()
        if not devices:
            return []

        results = []
        for d in devices:
            if not isinstance(d, dict):
                continue
            serial = d.get("serialNumber", "")
            dtype = d.get("deviceType", "")
            name = d.get("accountName", "")
            family = d.get("deviceFamily", "")
            if not serial or not dtype:
                continue

            wifi = self.get_device_wifi_details(serial, dtype)
            if not wifi:
                continue
            mac_raw = wifi.get("macAddress", "")
            if not mac_raw or len(mac_raw) != 12:
                continue

            # Normalize: "ACCCFC637684" -> "ac:cc:fc:63:76:84"
            mac_normalized = ":".join(mac_raw[i:i+2].lower() for i in range(0, 12, 2))
            results.append({
                "serialNumber": serial,
                "accountName": name,
                "deviceFamily": family,
                "deviceType": dtype,
                "macAddress": mac_normalized,
                "essid": wifi.get("essid"),
            })

        logger.info(f"Got MAC addresses for {len(results)} of {len(devices)} Echo/Fire devices")
        return results

    def get_routines(self) -> List[Dict[str, Any]]:
        """Get Alexa routines via the web API."""
        if not self._cookies:
            return []
        headers = self._get_alexa_web_headers()
        cookies = self._get_cookie_jar()
        try:
            response = self._http_session.get(
                f"{self.ALEXA_API_BASE}/api/behaviors/automations",
                headers=headers, cookies=cookies, timeout=15,
            )
            if response.status_code == 200:
                data = response.json()
                return data if isinstance(data, list) else data.get("automations", [])
            return []
        except Exception as e:
            logger.warning(f"Routines API failed: {e}")

    def _save_device_to_db(self, device: Dict):
        """Persist Alexa device to database"""
        if not self.db:
            return
        try:
            with self.db.get_connection() as conn:
                cursor = conn.cursor()
                cursor.execute("""
                    INSERT OR REPLACE INTO alexa_devices
                    (endpoint_id, friendly_name, description, manufacturer, model,
                     device_type, capabilities, is_echo_device, updated_at)
                    VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP)
                """, (
                    device["endpoint_id"],
                    device["friendly_name"],
                    device["description"],
                    device["manufacturer"],
                    device["model"],
                    device["device_type"],
                    json.dumps(device["capabilities"]),
                    1 if device["is_echo_device"] else 0,
                ))
                conn.commit()
        except Exception as e:
            logger.error(f"Failed to save Alexa device to DB: {e}")

    def _save_device_state_to_db(self, endpoint_id: str, state: Dict, timestamp: datetime):
        """Persist device state to database"""
        if not self.db:
            return
        try:
            with self.db.get_connection() as conn:
                cursor = conn.cursor()
                cursor.execute("""
                    UPDATE alexa_devices
                    SET last_state = ?, state_updated_at = ?, updated_at = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
                    WHERE endpoint_id = ?
                """, (json.dumps(state), timestamp, endpoint_id))
                conn.commit()
        except Exception as e:
            logger.error(f"Failed to save Alexa device state: {e}")

    def get_topology_local(self) -> Dict[str, Any]:
        """Get node list and per-node client mappings via local Deco API.

        with _local_api_lock:

            if _topology_cache and _topology_cache_time and (now - _topology_cache_time) < TOPOLOGY_CACHE_TTL:

    def scan_subnet_with_nmap(self, subnet: str) -> List[DeviceInfo]:
        """Scan subnet using nmap, then resolve MACs from ARP table"""
        devices = []
        try:
            # Use nmap -sn for ping scan (triggers ARP resolution)
            cmd = ['nmap', '-sn', subnet, '-oG', '-']
            result = subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, timeout=120, text=True)

            if result.returncode != 0 and result.returncode != 1:
                logger.warning(f"nmap scan had issues: {result.stderr}")

            # Collect discovered IPs and hostnames
            discovered = []
            for line in result.stdout.split('\n'):
                if line.startswith('Host:'):
                    match = re.search(r'Host:\s+([\d.]+)', line)
                    if match:
                        ip = match.group(1)
                        hostname_match = re.search(r'\((.*?)\)', line)
                        hostname = hostname_match.group(1) if hostname_match else None
                        discovered.append((ip, hostname))

            # Now read the ARP table to get real MAC addresses
            arp_map = self._read_arp_table()

            for ip, hostname in discovered:
                mac = arp_map.get(ip)
                if not mac:
                    logger.debug(f"No MAC in ARP table for {ip}, skipping")
                    continue

                vendor = self._get_vendor(mac)
                device = DeviceInfo(
                    mac_address=mac,
                    ip_address=ip,
                    hostname=hostname,
                    vendor=vendor
                )
                devices.append(device)
                logger.debug(f"Discovered device: {ip} ({mac})")

        except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
            logger.error("nmap scan timed out")
        except Exception as e:
            logger.error(f"Error scanning with nmap: {e}")

    def _find_dhcp_file(self) -> Optional[str]:
        """Find DHCP lease file by trying standard paths"""
        for path in self.DHCP_PATHS:
            if os.path.exists(path):
                try:
                    # Verify file is readable
                    with open(path, 'r') as f:
                        f.read(1)
                    return path
                except (PermissionError, IOError):
                    logger.debug(f"DHCP file found but not readable: {path}")
                    continue
        return None

    @staticmethod
    def normalize_mac(mac_address: str) -> str:
        """Normalize MAC address to AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF format

        Handles various formats:
        - aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff (standard)
        - aa-bb-cc-dd-ee-ff (hyphen separated)
        - aabbccddeeff (no separator)
        """
        if not mac_address:
            return ""

        # Remove common separators
        mac_clean = mac_address.lower().replace("-", "").replace(":", "").replace(" ", "")

        # Validate length (should be 12 hex characters)
        if len(mac_clean) != 12 or not all(c in "0123456789abcdef" for c in mac_clean):
            logger.debug(f"Invalid MAC address format: {mac_address}")
            return ""

        # Format as AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF
        return ":".join(mac_clean[i:i+2] for i in range(0, 12, 2))

    def parse_dhcp_leases(self) -> List[Dict]:
        """Parse DHCP lease file and extract device information

        Returns a list of dicts with keys: mac, ip, hostname
        Each dict represents a device discovered via DHCP leases.

        Returns empty list if:
        - No lease file found
        - File cannot be read
        - No valid leases parsed
        """
        leases = []

        if not self.dhcp_path or not os.path.exists(self.dhcp_path):
            logger.debug("DHCP lease file not accessible")
            return leases

        try:
            with open(self.dhcp_path, 'r') as f:
                content = f.read()

            # Parse lease entries
            # ISC DHCP format: lease 192.168.1.100 { hardware ethernet aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff; ... }
            lease_pattern = r'lease\s+([\d.]+)\s*\{([^}]*)\}'

            for match in re.finditer(lease_pattern, content):
                ip = match.group(1)
                lease_block = match.group(2)

                # Extract MAC address (required)
                # Matches: aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff, aa-bb-cc-dd-ee-ff, aabbccddeeff
                mac_match = re.search(r'hardware\s+ethernet\s+([\da-f:\-]+)', lease_block, re.IGNORECASE)
                mac_raw = mac_match.group(1) if mac_match else None

                if not mac_raw:
                    logger.debug(f"Lease {ip} has no MAC address, skipping")
                    continue

                # Normalize MAC
                mac = self.normalize_mac(mac_raw)
                if not mac:
                    logger.debug(f"Failed to normalize MAC {mac_raw} for lease {ip}")
                    continue

                # Extract hostname if present (optional)
                hostname_match = re.search(r'client-hostname\s+"([^"]+)"', lease_block, re.IGNORECASE)
                hostname = hostname_match.group(1) if hostname_match else None

                lease_dict = {
                    'mac': mac,
                    'ip': ip,
                    'hostname': hostname
                }
                leases.append(lease_dict)
                logger.debug(f"Parsed DHCP lease: {ip} ({mac})" + (f" hostname={hostname}" if hostname else ""))

        except PermissionError:
            logger.warning(f"Permission denied reading DHCP file: {self.dhcp_path}")
        except Exception as e:
            logger.error(f"Error parsing DHCP leases: {e}")

violations.title: `send_partition_command` arms/disarms alarm without authorization check or step-up confirmation
violations.content: `send_partition_command` accepts an arbitrary `partition_id` and an `arm_away`/`arm_stay`/`disarm` command from any caller that passes the global API key. There is no per-user authorization, no role check, no PIN/MFA, and no verification that the requester is allowed to control this specific partition. Disarming an alarm system is a high-impact physical-security operation and should require step-up auth comparable to the Alexa `unlock` flow (which mandates a PIN in `send_device_command`). Anyone with the shared key — or a CSRF/SSRF foothold — can disarm the home alarm.
violations.fixPrompt: Add an authorization check to `send_partition_command` in `backend/routes/alarm_com.py`: require a user-bound session (not just the shared API key), verify the user is permitted to control the partition, and require a confirmation PIN/MFA for `disarm` (mirroring the `unlock` PIN requirement in `send_device_command` in `backend/routes/alexa.py`).

violations.title: `send_lock_command` unlocks physical doors with no PIN or authorization check
violations.content: `send_lock_command` accepts a `lock_id` path parameter plus a `lock`/`unlock` action and calls the Alarm.com client directly with no PIN, no per-user authorization, and no ownership verification. Compare with `send_device_command` in `backend/routes/alexa.py` (lines 471–491), which explicitly requires `cmd.pin` for `unlock`. Anyone who can reach this endpoint with the shared `HOMESENTINEL_API_KEY` can remotely unlock any lock — a high-impact physical-security failure.
violations.fixPrompt: In `send_lock_command` in `backend/routes/alarm_com.py`, require a PIN/MFA confirmation for `unlock` (matching the existing `send_device_command` pattern in `backend/routes/alexa.py`), and add a per-user authorization check rather than relying solely on the global API key.

violations.title: `submit_otp` has no attempt limit or lockout on OTP verification
violations.content: `submit_otp` forwards `body.code` to `alarm_com_client.submit_otp` and returns either success (with a persisted 2FA cookie) or a 400 on failure. There is no per-account attempt counter, no exponential backoff, and no lockout after repeated invalid codes. An attacker who can reach the endpoint can brute-force the (typically 6-digit) OTP at line speed, defeating the second factor.
violations.fixPrompt: Add rate limiting and attempt counting to `submit_otp` in `backend/routes/alarm_com.py`: track failed `code` submissions per account/IP, lock out after N (e.g. 5) failures within a window, and clear the counter on success. Consider using `slowapi` or a Redis-backed counter.

async def submit_otp(body: OtpSubmit) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    """Submit OTP code. Returns 2FA cookie on success (save for future logins)."""
    if alarm_com_client is None:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=500, detail="Alarm.com client not initialized")
    try:
        result = await alarm_com_client.submit_otp(body.code, body.method)
        # Persist the 2FA cookie so future restarts don't need OTP again
        # 2026-03-12: Use encrypted storage
        if result.get("two_factor_cookie"):
            with db.get_connection() as conn:
                existing = load_encrypted_setting(conn, "alarm_com_credentials")
            if existing:
                existing["two_factor_cookie"] = result["two_factor_cookie"]
                with db.get_connection() as conn:
                    store_encrypted_setting(conn, "alarm_com_credentials", existing)
        return result
    except Exception as e:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail=str(e))

violations.title: `login_alarm_com` has no rate limiting on login attempts
violations.content: `login_alarm_com` calls `alarm_com_client.login()` and converts any exception into an HTTP 401, but never tracks failed attempts. With no lockout or backoff, an attacker can repeatedly call this endpoint to brute-force the stored Alarm.com username/password (or trigger upstream lockouts at Alarm.com itself, causing DoS of the alarm integration).
violations.fixPrompt: Add rate limiting and account lockout to `login_alarm_com` in `backend/routes/alarm_com.py`: count consecutive failed logins, reject further attempts after a threshold within a window, and surface a clear 429 response.

violations.title: `request_otp` has no rate limit on OTP delivery
violations.content: `request_otp` calls `alarm_com_client.request_otp(body.method)` with no per-account or per-IP rate limiting. An attacker can spam OTP requests via SMS/email, both as a nuisance/DoS for the legitimate account holder and as a way to enumerate which delivery methods are configured.
violations.fixPrompt: Add a short-window rate limiter (e.g. max 3 requests per 10 minutes per account) to `request_otp` in `backend/routes/alarm_com.py` before invoking `alarm_com_client.request_otp`.

violations.title: `delete_device` removes any device by ID with no ownership/permission check
violations.content: `delete_device` accepts a user-supplied `device_id` and calls `device_service.device_repo.delete(device_id)` after only checking the record exists. There is no verification that the caller is allowed to delete this device. In any multi-user deployment, this is a textbook IDOR — enumerating `device_id` values lets any authenticated caller permanently delete records belonging to others. Similar issues apply to `update_device` (lines 661–690), `delete_device_group` (lines 790–804), and `dismiss_alert` (lines 915–930).
violations.fixPrompt: Introduce an ownership/permission model and check it in `delete_device`, `update_device`, `delete_device_group`, and `dismiss_alert` in `backend/main.py` before mutating the resource. At minimum, scope mutations to the authenticated user/tenant or require an explicit admin role.

violations.title: `identify_associate` rewrites `network_devices` rows from caller-supplied MAC with no ownership check
violations.content: `identify_associate` takes `entity_id` from the path and `body.mac_address` / `body.alexa_name` from the request body and unconditionally updates `network_devices.alexa_name` and `network_devices.alexa_entity_id` for any row matching that MAC. There is no check that the caller is permitted to modify the targeted network device, and the `alexa_name` is taken directly from the body without sanitization. An attacker who reaches this endpoint can rewrite arbitrary device labels and Alexa associations.
violations.fixPrompt: In `identify_associate` in `backend/routes/alexa.py`, verify the caller is authorized to modify the targeted `network_devices` row before issuing the `UPDATE`, and validate/limit `alexa_name` length and character set.
violations.snippet:
async def identify_associate(entity_id: str, body: AssociateRequest) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    """Step 3: Link a dropped MAC to this Alexa entity in the DB.
    Sets alexa_name and alexa_device_type on the network_devices row.
    """
    if db is None:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=500, detail="Database not initialized")

    mac_norm = body.mac_address.lower().replace("-", ":")

    with db.get_connection() as conn:
        cursor = conn.cursor()
        # Check device exists
        cursor.execute("SELECT device_id FROM network_devices WHERE mac_address = ?", (mac_norm,))
        row = cursor.fetchone()
        if not row:
            raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail=f"No network device with MAC {mac_norm}")

        # Look up the Alexa entity name if not provided
        alexa_name = body.alexa_name
        if not alexa_name and alexa_client and alexa_client.has_cookies():
            try:
                entities = alexa_client.get_smart_home_devices()
                for e in entities:
                    if e.get("id") == entity_id:
                        alexa_name = e.get("displayName", "")
                        break
            except Exception:
                pass

        # Update the network device with Alexa association
        cursor.execute(
            "UPDATE network_devices SET alexa_name = ?, alexa_entity_id = ?, updated_at = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP WHERE mac_address = ?",
            (alexa_name or "", entity_id, mac_norm),
        )
        conn.commit()

        logger.info(f"Associated MAC {mac_norm} with Alexa entity {entity_id} ({alexa_name})")

    return {
        "success": True,
        "mac_address": mac_norm,
        "entity_id": entity_id,
        "alexa_name": alexa_name,
    }

There is no verification that the caller is allowed to control this specific entity. Combined with the `link_alexa_to_network` / `unlink_alexa_from_network` endpoints (lines 512–546) which also accept raw IDs without authorization, an attacker with the shared API key can toggle any linked plug/light or rewrite link tables.

violations.title: OAuth `authorize` endpoint auto-approves consent without authenticating the user
violations.content: The `authorize` handler (lines 36-64) acts as an OAuth 2.0 authorization endpoint but performs no user authentication or consent check before issuing an auth code. The comment on line 59 explicitly states "Auto-approve (personal skill — no login needed)". Any party who learns or guesses the `client_id` (a public value by OAuth design) and can supply a `redirect_uri` can obtain a valid `code` and exchange it for tokens. There is no verification that the requester is the legitimate account owner, no logged-in user check, and no `redirect_uri` allowlist validation against a registered URI for `CLIENT_ID`. This effectively bypasses the entire authorization step of OAuth and allows token issuance to any caller who reaches the endpoint.
violations.fixPrompt: In `backend/routes/oauth.py` `authorize`, require an authenticated session before issuing an auth code (e.g., redirect to a login page if no session exists, then show a consent screen). Additionally, validate `redirect_uri` against an allowlist of pre-registered URIs for the given `client_id` to prevent open-redirect / code-theft attacks. Do not auto-approve.
violations.snippet:
async def authorize(
    client_id: str,
    response_type: str,
    redirect_uri: str,
    state: str = "",
    scope: str = "",
):
    """OAuth authorization endpoint — shows consent page and redirects with auth code."""
    if client_id != CLIENT_ID:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail="Invalid client_id")
    if response_type != "code":
        raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail="Only 'code' response_type supported")

    # Generate auth code
    code = secrets.token_urlsafe(32)
    _auth_codes[code] = {
        "redirect_uri": redirect_uri,
        "expires": time.time() + 300,  # 5 min
        "client_id": client_id,
    }

    logger.info("OAuth authorize: issuing code for redirect to %s", redirect_uri)

    # Auto-approve (personal skill — no login needed)
    # Build redirect with code and state
    separator = "&" if "?" in redirect_uri else "?"
    redirect_url = f"{redirect_uri}{separator}{urlencode({'code': code, 'state': state})}"

    return RedirectResponse(url=redirect_url)

violations.title: OAuth `token` endpoint lacks rate limiting / lockout on credential and auth-code attempts
violations.content: The `token` handler validates `client_id`/`client_secret` (line 90) and consumes `code`/`refresh_token` values (lines 95-99, 122-127) but has no rate limiting, attempt counting, or lockout mechanism. An attacker can brute-force `CLIENT_SECRET`, guess outstanding auth codes, or guess refresh tokens at unlimited rate. The only response on failure is a 401/400 with no backoff. Even though `secrets.token_urlsafe(32)` produces high-entropy values, the lack of rate limiting still permits credential-stuffing and token-guessing patterns and prevents detection of abuse. Add per-IP and per-`client_id` rate limiting, exponential backoff on repeated failures, and structured logging/alerting on bursts of `invalid_client` / `invalid_grant` responses.
violations.fixPrompt: Add rate limiting to `backend/routes/oauth.py` `token` (e.g., via `slowapi` or a Redis-backed counter) keyed by client IP and `client_id`. Track consecutive `invalid_client` and `invalid_grant` failures, apply exponential backoff, and emit an alert when thresholds are exceeded so brute-force attempts on `CLIENT_SECRET` and refresh tokens are detected and throttled.

violations.title: Unescaped exception text rendered as HTML in OAuth callback
violations.content:
The `alexa_auth_callback` error handler builds an HTML response with an f-string that interpolates the raw exception `e` (`

The `code` query parameter is attacker-controlled, and exception messages from `alexa_client.exchange_code(code, redirect_uri)` (or upstream HTTP errors) commonly echo back attacker-supplied values or URL fragments. Because the response is returned via `HTMLResponse` with `Content-Type: text/html`, any HTML/JS characters present in the exception string will be rendered/executed by the browser. This is user-controlled data injected into an HTML context without encoding — a reflected XSS vector reachable via `GET /api/alexa/auth/callback?code=`.

violations.content: The `ChesterCredentials` Pydantic model defines `verify_ssl: bool = False` as the default. When a client posts credentials without explicitly setting `verify_ssl`, TLS certificate verification will be silently disabled — even when `use_https` is enabled. Insecure-by-default TLS handling is a security anti-pattern: a misconfigured deployment will accept any TLS certificate (including attacker-controlled ones) without warning, enabling man-in-the-middle attacks on the Chester router credentials.

violations.title: `/oauth/authorize` performs unvalidated open redirect on user-supplied `redirect_uri`
violations.content: The `authorize` handler accepts `redirect_uri` directly from the query string and concatenates it into a `RedirectResponse` without validating it against an allow-list of registered redirect URIs. An attacker can call `/oauth/authorize?client_id=homesentinel&response_type=code&redirect_uri=https://evil.example.com` and the server will issue a valid auth code redirected to the attacker's domain. Although the `code` and `state` query parameters are url-encoded, the `redirect_uri` itself is treated as a trusted URL string. OAuth requires the authorization server to validate `redirect_uri` against a pre-registered value for the client.
violations.fixPrompt: In `backend/routes/oauth.py`, validate `redirect_uri` against a configured allow-list (e.g., the Alexa-registered redirect URIs) before generating the auth code on line 50 and building the redirect on line 62. Reject with HTTP 400 if the URI is not in the allow-list.

@router.get("/authorize")
async def authorize(
    client_id: str,
    response_type: str,
    redirect_uri: str,
    state: str = "",
    scope: str = "",
):
    """OAuth authorization endpoint — shows consent page and redirects with auth code."""
    if client_id != CLIENT_ID:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail="Invalid client_id")
    if response_type != "code":
        raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail="Only 'code' response_type supported")

    # Generate auth code
    code = secrets.token_urlsafe(32)
    _auth_codes[code] = {
        "redirect_uri": redirect_uri,
        "expires": time.time() + 300,  # 5 min
        "client_id": client_id,
    }

    logger.info("OAuth authorize: issuing code for redirect to %s", redirect_uri)

    # Auto-approve (personal skill — no login needed)
    # Build redirect with code and state
    separator = "&" if "?" in redirect_uri else "?"
    redirect_url = f"{redirect_uri}{separator}{urlencode({'code': code, 'state': state})}"

    return RedirectResponse(url=redirect_url)

violations.content: `/oauth/token` compares the supplied `client_secret` to the configured `CLIENT_SECRET` using Python's `==` operator, which short-circuits on the first differing byte. This makes the comparison vulnerable to timing attacks that can leak the secret one byte at a time over many requests. Use `secrets.compare_digest()` for constant-time comparison of secrets/tokens. (The `secrets` module is already imported at line 9.)

The same insecure default is also propagated through `set_credentials` on line 74. Defaulting TLS verification off is a security anti-pattern; verification should default to on, and disabling it should be an explicit opt-in for known self-signed local devices.

violations.title: SSH host key verification disabled in `run_speedtest`
violations.content: The `ssh_cmd` built in `run_speedtest` passes `StrictHostKeyChecking=no` and `UserKnownHostsFile=/dev/null`, which disables SSH host key verification analogous to setting `rejectUnauthorized: false` for TLS. Combined with `sshpass -p <password>`, this opens the SSH session (with the Chester admin password) to a trivial man-in-the-middle on the LAN: any host that ARP-spoofs or otherwise impersonates `creds["host"]` will silently receive the password instead of being rejected on host-key mismatch. The inline comment justifies the choice as 'local network device,' but local networks are exactly where ARP/DHCP spoofing attacks live. A pinned `known_hosts` file (recorded on first use) would preserve usability while restoring authentication of the remote endpoint.
violations.fixPrompt: In `backend/services/speedtest_service.py` `run_speedtest`, replace the `-o StrictHostKeyChecking=no` and `-o UserKnownHostsFile=/dev/null` flags with a persisted known_hosts file (for example `~/.homesentinel/chester_known_hosts`) and use `StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new` so the host key is pinned on first connection and any subsequent change causes the connection to fail. Also stop passing the password on the command line via `sshpass -p`; use `sshpass -e` with `SSHPASS` in the environment or, preferably, key-based authentication so the credential is not exposed in the process argv.

violations.title: TLS certificate verification disabled in `TMPClient.connect`
violations.content: `TMPClient.connect` builds an `ssl.SSLContext` with `ctx.check_hostname = False` and `ctx.verify_mode = ssl.CERT_NONE`, then wraps the socket without validating the peer's certificate. This is a classic disabled-TLS-verification anti-pattern: any attacker able to intercept traffic between this client and the Deco router (ARP spoof on the LAN, rogue Wi-Fi, etc.) can present a self-signed certificate and complete the TLS handshake. Because the same channel carries SPAKE2+ authentication material and AES-128-CCM-encrypted business data, MITM could enable password-recovery via offline cracking of the PAKE confirmation values and downgrade the security guarantees the protocol is meant to provide. If the Deco genuinely uses a self-signed cert, the correct fix is certificate pinning (verify against a stored fingerprint or pinned cert) rather than blanket `CERT_NONE`.
violations.fixPrompt: In `backend/tmp_client.py` `TMPClient.connect` (around lines 540-547), replace the `ssl.CERT_NONE` / `check_hostname = False` configuration with certificate pinning: load the Deco's expected certificate or SHA-256 fingerprint from configuration and, after `wrap_socket`, call `getpeercert(binary_form=True)`, hash it with `hashlib.sha256`, and compare to the pinned value, raising on mismatch. If a CA-signed cert is available, instead use `ctx = ssl.create_default_context()` and set `check_hostname = True`.

violations.title: `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` renders backend-supplied SVG containing device-controlled strings
violations.content: The `networkx-svg-wrapper` div uses `dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: graphSvg }}` to inject the response body of `GET /deco/topology-graph` directly into the DOM. That SVG is generated server-side from network inventory data — device `friendly_name`, `vendor_name`, `device_name`, hostnames, SSIDs, MAC vendor lookups — which originate from untrusted sources on the LAN (DHCP-supplied hostnames, OUI lookups, Deco controller responses, user-editable friendly names). SVG supports executable content via `<script>`, `<foreignObject>` with HTML, and `on*` event handlers, so any unescaped string interpolated by the backend SVG generator becomes a stored XSS vector. Even if the backend currently escapes correctly, this client-side pattern silently inherits whatever the server emits, with no defense-in-depth.

violations.title: Unsanitized `endpoint_id` interpolated into backend URL path
violations.content: In `handle_report_state`, `endpoint_id` is read from the incoming Alexa directive (`endpoint.get("endpointId", "")` on line 524) and then interpolated directly into the backend URL via an f-string: `f"/api/alexa/lambda/state/{endpoint_id}"`. violations.title: `get_daily_digest` recomputes immutable past digests on every request
violations.content: `get_daily_digest` calls `digest_service.compute_daily_digest(date=date)` on every request with no caching. A daily digest for a past date is immutable — the events for yesterday will never change once the day is over. Computing it on every call wastes DB queries and computation. Even today's digest changes slowly enough that a short TTL (e.g., 5 minutes) would be appropriate, while past dates can be cached effectively forever.

The frontend's `useDevicePolling` hook polls this kind of data every 15-60s, so without caching this expensive aggregation runs on every poll. A short TTL (e.g., 30 seconds) would dramatically reduce load without affecting UX.

Unlike `get_topology` and `get_topology_graph` (which share a `TOPOLOGY_ROUTE_CACHE_TTL` cache), this endpoint has no caching despite calling the same expensive local topology API and being a likely high-frequency frontend poll target. The data changes infrequently (mesh associations are stable for minutes at a time).
violations.fixPrompt: Add module-level cache variables `_client_node_map_cache` and `_client_node_map_cache_time` in `backend/routes/deco.py`, reusing the existing `TOPOLOGY_ROUTE_CACHE_TTL` constant. At the top of `get_client_node_map`, return the cached dict if `time.time() - _client_node_map_cache_time < TOPOLOGY_ROUTE_CACHE_TTL`; otherwise build the mapping and store it before returning.
violations.snippet:
async def get_client_node_map() -> Dict[str, Any]:
    """Return a mapping of client MAC addresses to their connected Deco node names."""
    if deco_service is None:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=500, detail="Deco service not initialized")

    try:
        import base64
        client = deco_service.deco_client

        # 2026-03-11: Use get_topology_local() which creates its own local session.
        # This avoids 'NoneType aes_encrypt' errors from using the cloud client for local API.
        local_data = None
        try:
            local_data = client.get_topology_local()
        except Exception as e:
            logger.warning(f"Local topology fetch failed for client-node-map: {e}")

        node_names = {}
        # 2026-03-11: Rich node info with backhaul type for signal icons
        node_details = {}
        mapping = {}

        if local_data and local_data.get("nodes"):
            for node in local_data["nodes"]:
                node_mac = node.get("mac", "")
                nickname = node.get("nickname", "")
                try:
                    nickname = base64.b64decode(nickname).decode("utf-8")
                except Exception as e:
                    logger.debug(f"Base64 nickname decode failed: {e}")
                # 2026-03-11: Prefer HomeSentinel friendly_name over Deco nickname
                # (Deco nickname can get corrupted with client device names)
                db_name = _get_node_friendly_name(node_mac)
                display_name = db_name or nickname or node.get("device_model", node_mac)
                node_names[node_mac] = display_name
                # connection_type for nodes = backhaul type (list or string)
                ct = node.get("connection_type", [])
                if isinstance(ct, str):
                    ct = [ct]
                raw_role = node.get("role", "slave")
                role = _remap_role(raw_role)
                # Determine if wired backhaul
                node_name_lower = display_name.lower()
                is_wired_backhaul = (
                    raw_role == "master"
                    or "wired" in ct
                    or (ct and all(c not in ("band2_4", "band5", "band6") for c in ct))
                    or "dining" in node_name_lower
                )
                node_details[node_mac] = {
                    "name": display_name,
                    "role": role,
                    "backhaul": "wired" if is_wired_backhaul else "wireless",
                    "backhaul_bands": ct,
                }

            for node_mac, clients in local_data.get("node_clients", {}).items():
                node_name = node_names.get(node_mac, node_mac)
                for c in clients:
                    raw_mac = c.get("mac", "")
                    mac_clean = raw_mac.lower().replace("-", "").replace(":", "").replace(" ", "")
                    if len(mac_clean) == 12:
                        normalized = ":".join(mac_clean[i:i+2] for i in range(0, 12, 2))
                        mapping[normalized] = {
                            "node_name": node_name,
                            "node_mac": node_mac,
                            "connection_type": c.get("connection_type", ""),
                            "client_mesh": c.get("client_mesh", False),
                            # 2026-03-11: Pass wire_type and speed for signal indicator
                            "wire_type": c.get("wire_type", ""),
                            "down_speed": c.get("down_speed", 0),
                            "up_speed": c.get("up_speed", 0),
                        }

        return {
            "client_node_map": mapping,
            "nodes": node_names,
            "node_details": node_details,
            "total_mapped": len(mapping),
        }
    except Exception as e:
        logger.error(f"Failed to build client-node map: {e}")
        raise HTTPException(status_code=500, detail=f"Failed to build client-node map: {str(e)}")

violations.title: `get_hiboost_history` re-queries and re-groups history on every request
violations.content: `get_hiboost_history` runs a full SQL query over `hiboost_history` for the given hours window and then performs Python-side grouping/formatting on every request. Since historical RF data points are appended at the polling interval (`HIBOOST_POLL_INTERVAL`, default 300s), the response is effectively unchanged between polls. The chart endpoint is a common dashboard data source — caching the formatted result per `hours` value for ~60 seconds would eliminate redundant DB scans and Python loops.
violations.fixPrompt: Add a module-level dict `_hiboost_history_cache: dict[int, tuple[float, dict]]` keyed by the `hours` parameter in `backend/routes/hiboost.py`. Define a TTL constant (e.g., 60 seconds). In `get_hiboost_history`, return the cached payload if the entry exists and is fresh; otherwise execute the query, build the response, store `(time.time(), response)` in the cache, and return it.
violations.snippet:
async def get_hiboost_history(hours: int = Query(default=24, ge=1)) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    """Get historical RF data for charting. Returns time-series per band."""
    if _db is None:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=500, detail="Database not initialized")

    cutoff = (datetime.now(timezone.utc) - timedelta(hours=hours)).isoformat()

    with _db.get_connection() as conn:
        cursor = conn.cursor()
        cursor.execute(
            """SELECT band, output_power_dl, gain_dl, gain_ul, mgc_dl, mgc_ul,
                      temperature, timestamp
               FROM hiboost_history
               WHERE timestamp >= ?
               ORDER BY timestamp ASC""",
            (cutoff,),
        )
        rows = cursor.fetchall()
        cols = [d[0] for d in cursor.description]

    # Group by timestamp for charting
    by_time: Dict[str, Dict] = {}
    for row in rows:
        r = dict(zip(cols, row))
        ts = r["timestamp"]
        if ts not in by_time:
            by_time[ts] = {"timestamp": ts, "temperature": r.get("temperature")}
        band = r["band"]
        by_time[ts][f"{band}_power"] = r["output_power_dl"]
        by_time[ts][f"{band}_gain"] = r["gain_dl"]

    data = list(by_time.values())

    # Format timestamps for display
    for d in data:
        try:
            dt = datetime.fromisoformat(d["timestamp"].replace("Z", "+00:00"))
            d["time"] = dt.strftime("%-m/%-d %H:%M")
            d["dateTime"] = dt.strftime("%b %d, %Y %I:%M %p")
        except Exception:
            d["time"] = d["timestamp"]
            d["dateTime"] = d["timestamp"]

    return {
        "data": data,
        "total": len(data),
        "hours": hours,
        "bands": ["LTE700", "CELL800", "PCS1900", "AWS2100"],
    }
