violations.title: `_create_session` configures retries without a circuit breaker
violations.content: `_create_session` builds a `requests.Session` with a `Retry` strategy (`total=3`, `backoff_factor=1`) for the Deco API but has no circuit breaker. Every call to a failing Deco endpoint will go through the full retry cycle, holding connections and threads. If the Deco router is consistently unreachable, the system will keep hammering it instead of failing fast, which can exhaust connection pools and cascade slowness to the entire backend (device polling, topology refreshes, schedulers).
violations.fixPrompt: Wrap the `requests.Session` returned by `_create_session` (or the call sites in `_local_encrypted_request` / `_cloud_request`) with a circuit breaker (e.g. `pybreaker.CircuitBreaker`) that opens after N consecutive failures, returns fast for a cooldown window, then half-opens to probe recovery. Track failure counts at the host/endpoint level so a failing Deco device doesn't block unrelated calls.
violations.snippet:
def _create_session(self) -> requests.Session:
        session = requests.Session()
        retry_strategy = Retry(
            total=3,
            status_forcelist=[429, 500, 502, 503, 504],
            allowed_methods=["HEAD", "GET", "POST", "PUT", "DELETE"],
            backoff_factor=1,
        )
        adapter = HTTPAdapter(max_retries=retry_strategy)
        session.mount("http://", adapter)
        session.mount("https://", adapter)
        return session

violations.title: `_local_encrypted_request` re-authenticates and recurses without a failure threshold
violations.content: `_local_encrypted_request` makes HTTP calls to the local Deco API and, on 403 / empty-data / AES-decrypt failure, calls `self.authenticate()` then recursively retries. There is no circuit breaker tracking how often the Deco API is failing across calls — if the router is down or rejecting sessions persistently, every caller (`get_device_list`, `get_client_list`, `get_topology_local`, `optimize_network`, scheduler polls) will keep re-authenticating and re-trying, on top of the underlying `Retry(total=3)` adapter. There is no fail-fast path and no global failure-rate gate, which means one failing dependency can stall the polling scheduler and cascade slowness.
violations.fixPrompt: Introduce a circuit breaker around `_local_encrypted_request` (e.g. `pybreaker` or a small counter of consecutive failures with timestamped open/half-open state). Once N consecutive failures occur within a window, raise `APIConnectionError` immediately without performing the HTTP call, authentication, or retry recursion. Reset on a successful call after the cooldown.

violations.title: `get_client_list` iterates devices calling cloud API without a failure threshold
violations.content: The cloud branch of `get_client_list` loops over every device returned by `get_device_list` and issues a `_cloud_request("passthrough", ...)` for each. Failures are caught per-device with `logger.warning` and the loop continues, but there is no shared failure counter or circuit breaker — if the regional cloud endpoint is degraded, every device call will hit the timeout/retry path, multiplied by the device count, on every poll cycle. A circuit breaker would let the method fail fast and skip the remaining devices once a failure rate threshold is exceeded.
violations.fixPrompt: Track consecutive `_cloud_request` failures within the loop (or via a shared breaker on `_cloud_request`). After M consecutive failures inside one invocation, break out of the loop early and return what has been collected so far. Additionally, gate `_cloud_request` itself with a circuit breaker so subsequent polls fail fast while the cloud is unhealthy.

violations.title: `get_topology_local` loops over nodes calling Deco API without a failure threshold
violations.content: `get_topology_local` iterates over each Deco node and issues an `admin/client?form=client_list` request per node via `_local_encrypted_request`. Per-node failures are swallowed with `logger.warning`, but there is no failure-rate tracking — if the local API is unresponsive, every node call will go through its own retry/auth cycle on every topology refresh, blocking the request thread for an extended period. There is no fast-fail path once the dependency is clearly unhealthy.
violations.fixPrompt: Add a per-call failure counter inside the loop: if K consecutive node requests fail, abort the remaining iterations and return partial results (or raise). Better, share a circuit breaker with `_local_encrypted_request` so once it opens, subsequent node calls return immediately without I/O.

    # 2026-03-11: Get per-node client lists and node list via local API.
    # Creates a temp local session to avoid conflicts with the main cloud client.
    def get_topology_local(self) -> Dict[str, Any]:
        """Get node list and per-node client mappings via local Deco API.

        Returns:
            Dict with 'nodes' (list of node dicts) and 'node_clients' (node_mac -> list of clients)
        """
        if not HAS_CRYPTO:
            raise APIConnectionError("pycryptodome required for local API")

        # Return cached data if fresh enough
        global _topology_cache, _topology_cache_time
        import time
        now = time.time()
        if _topology_cache and _topology_cache_time and (now - _topology_cache_time) < TOPOLOGY_CACHE_TTL:
            logger.debug("Returning cached topology data")
            return _topology_cache

        with _local_api_lock:
            # Double-check cache after acquiring lock (another thread may have filled it)
            now = time.time()
            if _topology_cache and _topology_cache_time and (now - _topology_cache_time) < TOPOLOGY_CACHE_TTL:
                return _topology_cache

            logger.info("Creating temporary local DecoClient for topology fetch")
            local_client = DecoClient(
                local_endpoint=self.local_endpoint,
                use_cloud=False,
                verify_ssl=False,
            )
            local_client.username = "admin"
            local_client.password = self.password

            try:
                local_client.authenticate()

                # Get all nodes
                node_result = local_client._local_encrypted_request(
                    "admin/device?form=device_list",
                    json.dumps({"operation": "read"})
                )
                nodes = node_result.get("device_list", [])
                logger.info(f"Local API returned {len(nodes)} nodes")

                # Get per-node clients
                node_clients = {}
                for node in nodes:
                    node_mac = node.get("mac", "")
                    try:
                        result = local_client._local_encrypted_request(
                            "admin/client?form=client_list",
                            json.dumps({"operation": "read", "params": {"device_mac": node_mac}})
                        )
                        clients = result.get("client_list", [])
                        node_clients[node_mac] = clients
                        logger.debug(f"Node {node_mac}: {len(clients)} clients")
                    except Exception as e:
                        logger.warning(f"Failed to get clients for node {node_mac}: {e}")
                        node_clients[node_mac] = []

                result = {"nodes": nodes, "node_clients": node_clients}
                _topology_cache = result
                _topology_cache_time = time.time()
                return result
            except Exception as e:
                logger.error(f"get_topology_local failed: {e}")

    def _save_device_to_db(self, device: Dict):
        """Persist Alexa device to database"""
        if not self.db:
            return
        try:
            with self.db.get_connection() as conn:
                cursor = conn.cursor()
                cursor.execute("""
                    INSERT OR REPLACE INTO alexa_devices
                    (endpoint_id, friendly_name, description, manufacturer, model,
                     device_type, capabilities, is_echo_device, updated_at)
                    VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP)
                """, (
                    device["endpoint_id"],
                    device["friendly_name"],
                    device["description"],
                    device["manufacturer"],
                    device["model"],
                    device["device_type"],
                    json.dumps(device["capabilities"]),
                    1 if device["is_echo_device"] else 0,
                ))
                conn.commit()
        except Exception as e:
            logger.error(f"Failed to save Alexa device to DB: {e}")

    def _save_device_state_to_db(self, endpoint_id: str, state: Dict, timestamp: datetime):
        """Persist device state to database"""
        if not self.db:
            return
        try:
            with self.db.get_connection() as conn:
                cursor = conn.cursor()
                cursor.execute("""
                    UPDATE alexa_devices
                    SET last_state = ?, state_updated_at = ?, updated_at = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
                    WHERE endpoint_id = ?
                """, (json.dumps(state), timestamp, endpoint_id))
                conn.commit()
        except Exception as e:
            logger.error(f"Failed to save Alexa device state: {e}")

    def scan_subnet_with_nmap(self, subnet: str) -> List[DeviceInfo]:
        """Scan subnet using nmap, then resolve MACs from ARP table"""
        devices = []
        try:
            # Use nmap -sn for ping scan (triggers ARP resolution)
            cmd = ['nmap', '-sn', subnet, '-oG', '-']
            result = subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, timeout=120, text=True)

            if result.returncode != 0 and result.returncode != 1:
                logger.warning(f"nmap scan had issues: {result.stderr}")

            # Collect discovered IPs and hostnames
            discovered = []
            for line in result.stdout.split('\n'):
                if line.startswith('Host:'):
                    match = re.search(r'Host:\s+([\d.]+)', line)
                    if match:
                        ip = match.group(1)
                        hostname_match = re.search(r'\((.*?)\)', line)
                        hostname = hostname_match.group(1) if hostname_match else None
                        discovered.append((ip, hostname))

            # Now read the ARP table to get real MAC addresses
            arp_map = self._read_arp_table()

            for ip, hostname in discovered:
                mac = arp_map.get(ip)
                if not mac:
                    logger.debug(f"No MAC in ARP table for {ip}, skipping")
                    continue

                vendor = self._get_vendor(mac)
                device = DeviceInfo(
                    mac_address=mac,
                    ip_address=ip,
                    hostname=hostname,
                    vendor=vendor
                )
                devices.append(device)
                logger.debug(f"Discovered device: {ip} ({mac})")

        except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
            logger.error("nmap scan timed out")
        except Exception as e:
            logger.error(f"Error scanning with nmap: {e}")

    def _find_dhcp_file(self) -> Optional[str]:
        """Find DHCP lease file by trying standard paths"""
        for path in self.DHCP_PATHS:
            if os.path.exists(path):
                try:
                    # Verify file is readable
                    with open(path, 'r') as f:
                        f.read(1)
                    return path
                except (PermissionError, IOError):
                    logger.debug(f"DHCP file found but not readable: {path}")
                    continue
        return None

    @staticmethod
    def normalize_mac(mac_address: str) -> str:
        """Normalize MAC address to AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF format

        Handles various formats:
        - aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff (standard)
        - aa-bb-cc-dd-ee-ff (hyphen separated)
        - aabbccddeeff (no separator)
        """
        if not mac_address:
            return ""

        # Remove common separators
        mac_clean = mac_address.lower().replace("-", "").replace(":", "").replace(" ", "")

        # Validate length (should be 12 hex characters)
        if len(mac_clean) != 12 or not all(c in "0123456789abcdef" for c in mac_clean):
            logger.debug(f"Invalid MAC address format: {mac_address}")
            return ""

        # Format as AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF
        return ":".join(mac_clean[i:i+2] for i in range(0, 12, 2))

    def parse_dhcp_leases(self) -> List[Dict]:
        """Parse DHCP lease file and extract device information

        Returns a list of dicts with keys: mac, ip, hostname
        Each dict represents a device discovered via DHCP leases.

        Returns empty list if:
        - No lease file found
        - File cannot be read
        - No valid leases parsed
        """
        leases = []

        if not self.dhcp_path or not os.path.exists(self.dhcp_path):
            logger.debug("DHCP lease file not accessible")
            return leases

        try:
            with open(self.dhcp_path, 'r') as f:
                content = f.read()

            # Parse lease entries
            # ISC DHCP format: lease 192.168.1.100 { hardware ethernet aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff; ... }
            lease_pattern = r'lease\s+([\d.]+)\s*\{([^}]*)\}'

            for match in re.finditer(lease_pattern, content):
                ip = match.group(1)
                lease_block = match.group(2)

                # Extract MAC address (required)
                # Matches: aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff, aa-bb-cc-dd-ee-ff, aabbccddeeff
                mac_match = re.search(r'hardware\s+ethernet\s+([\da-f:\-]+)', lease_block, re.IGNORECASE)
                mac_raw = mac_match.group(1) if mac_match else None

                if not mac_raw:
                    logger.debug(f"Lease {ip} has no MAC address, skipping")
                    continue

                # Normalize MAC
                mac = self.normalize_mac(mac_raw)
                if not mac:
                    logger.debug(f"Failed to normalize MAC {mac_raw} for lease {ip}")
                    continue

                # Extract hostname if present (optional)
                hostname_match = re.search(r'client-hostname\s+"([^"]+)"', lease_block, re.IGNORECASE)
                hostname = hostname_match.group(1) if hostname_match else None

                lease_dict = {
                    'mac': mac,
                    'ip': ip,
                    'hostname': hostname
                }
                leases.append(lease_dict)
                logger.debug(f"Parsed DHCP lease: {ip} ({mac})" + (f" hostname={hostname}" if hostname else ""))

        except PermissionError:
            logger.warning(f"Permission denied reading DHCP file: {self.dhcp_path}")
        except Exception as e:
            logger.error(f"Error parsing DHCP leases: {e}")

violations.content: The `HiBoostClient.__init__` creates a bare `requests.Session()` at line 102 without mounting a `Retry`/`HTTPAdapter` strategy. Subsequent HTTP calls to the external HiBoost API (auth, RF parameter polling, etc.) over this session will fail permanently on the first transient network error (timeouts, 5xx, connection resets). Contrast with `DecoClient._create_session` (lines 175-186) which mounts a `Retry(total=3, status_forcelist=[429, 500, 502, 503, 504], backoff_factor=1)` adapter for the same kind of external integration. Given the HiBoost API is a remote third-party service and the client runs on a periodic poller, transient failures are likely and should be retried with exponential backoff.

Use `total=3`, `status_forcelist=[429, 500, 502, 503, 504]`, `allowed_methods=["HEAD", "GET", "POST", "PUT", "DELETE"]`, and `backoff_factor=1`, mirroring `DecoClient._create_session`. Mount the adapter on both `http://` and `https://`.

violations.title: `HiBoostClient.__init__` creates a `requests.Session` with no circuit breaker for the HiBoost API
violations.content: `HiBoostClient` initializes a bare `requests.Session` with a 15s timeout for calls to the HiBoost cloud API but never configures a circuit breaker (and does not even configure retry/backoff). The HiBoost scheduler polls this external service every `HIBOOST_POLL_INTERVAL` seconds; if the upstream API degrades or hangs near the timeout, every poll will pay the full timeout cost, tying up worker threads. Without a circuit breaker the service has no way to back off and fail fast when HiBoost is unhealthy.
violations.fixPrompt: Wrap HiBoost HTTP request methods with a circuit breaker (e.g. `pybreaker.CircuitBreaker(fail_max=5, reset_timeout=60)`). When the breaker is open, raise immediately so the scheduler skips the poll cycle instead of waiting on timeouts. Optionally pair it with a `urllib3.util.Retry` adapter for short-lived transient errors, but ensure the breaker — not retries — governs sustained outages.

violations.fixPrompt: Replace the multi-line f-string `logger.info(...)` at lines 149-152 with structured logging that passes the metrics as keyword fields, e.g. `logger.info("Chester speedtest complete", extra={"download_mbps": download_mbps, "upload_mbps": upload_mbps, "ping_ms": ping_ms, "jitter_ms": jitter_ms, "server_name": server.get("name", "unknown")})`.

violations.title: Cellular snapshot warning uses f-string for exception
violations.content: `logger.warning(f"Failed to capture cellular snapshot: {e}")` interpolates the exception into the message. Structured logging would pass the exception via `exc_info=True` and/or `extra` fields for better aggregation and stack-trace handling.
violations.fixPrompt: Replace `logger.warning(f"Failed to capture cellular snapshot: {e}")` with `logger.warning("Failed to capture cellular snapshot", exc_info=True)` or pass the exception as a structured field via `extra={"error": str(e)}`.

violations.title: Error result log embeds error string in f-string
violations.content: `logger.error(f"Speed test error stored: {error}")` embeds the error string. The `error` field should be emitted as structured data so downstream tooling can group failures by reason.
violations.fixPrompt: Replace `logger.error(f"Speed test error stored: {error}")` with `logger.error("Speed test error stored", extra={"error": error})`.

violations.title: `_recv_tslp` reads attacker-controlled `payload_len` into an unbounded buffer
violations.content: In `_recv_tslp`, after reading the 24-byte header, `payload_len` is parsed as a 4-byte big-endian unsigned integer from untrusted network data and then used as the size of the in-memory `payload` buffer that is grown via repeated `recv` calls. There is no upper bound check on `payload_len` before allocating/growing this buffer. A malicious or malfunctioning peer can advertise a `payload_len` near 2^32 (4 GiB) per frame and cause the Python process to allocate memory without bound, leading to OOM and a crash. The TSLP framing here mirrors the `_recv_tmp` path for `TMPPacket.decode`, so the same unbounded-buffer concern applies to any frame received over this socket.
violations.fixPrompt: In `_recv_tslp` (around lines 559-578 of `backend/tmp_client.py`), define a sane maximum frame size constant (e.g., `MAX_TSLP_PAYLOAD = 1 << 20` for 1 MiB, sized to legitimate Deco/TMP traffic) and after unpacking `payload_len` from the header raise a `ValueError` / close the socket if `payload_len` exceeds that limit, before entering the `while len(payload) < payload_len` read loop. Consider reading into a preallocated `bytearray` of bounded size and using `recv_into` for efficiency.

violations.title: SPAKE2+ success log embeds truncated `stok` via f-string
violations.content: `logger.info(f"SPAKE2+ authentication successful! stok={self.stok[:20]}...")` interpolates a session token prefix into the message. The token (or its prefix) should be a structured field so it can be redacted/filtered consistently in pipelines.
violations.fixPrompt: Change `logger.info(f"SPAKE2+ authentication successful! stok={self.stok[:20]}...")` to `logger.info("SPAKE2+ authentication successful", extra={"stok_prefix": self.stok[:20]})` so the token prefix is a parseable field.

These connection-context fields should be structured so they can be correlated across log lines.

violations.title: WiFi config `PUT` in `confirmAndSubmit` has no retry on transient failure
violations.content: The critical state-changing `PUT /deco/wifi-config` call inside `confirmAndSubmit` fails permanently on the first transient error — there is no retry with backoff. Because this request reconfigures the Deco mesh (SSID/password/band steering) and the user is already shown a verification flow, a transient network blip will surface as a hard failure even though the operation could succeed on retry. Apply exponential backoff retry (e.g., 2–3 attempts) for transient/5xx/network errors before surfacing the error to the user.
violations.fixPrompt: Wrap the `fetch(buildUrl('/deco/wifi-config'), { method: 'PUT', ... })` call in `confirmAndSubmit` with a retry helper that retries on network errors and 5xx responses with exponential backoff (e.g., 3 attempts, 500ms→1s→2s). Do not retry on 4xx client errors. Surface the final error only after retries are exhausted.

violations.title: `verifyConfigChanges` retries on failure with no breaker
violations.content: `verifyConfigChanges` polls `/deco/wifi-config` every 5 seconds for up to `maxWaitMs` (30s). The `catch` block in `pollChanges` resolves silently on error and stops, which is fine — but on success paths that return non-OK responses, the code throws and falls into the catch. More importantly, there's no tracking of intermittent failures across retries: if the backend is degraded and returning 5xx, the poller keeps retrying every 5s until timeout with no failure-rate threshold to short-circuit early. While `maxWaitMs` bounds the loop, the function lacks a circuit-breaker pattern that would stop after a small number of consecutive failures rather than continuing to hammer a failing endpoint.
violations.fixPrompt: Add a consecutive-failure counter inside `pollChanges`. After 2-3 consecutive non-OK or thrown responses, stop polling early, set `verificationMessage` to an error state, and resolve. This avoids continuing to call a clearly-failing endpoint up to the full 30-second budget.

violations.title: Alexa `devices`/`echoDevices`/`status` cached with no automatic invalidation
violations.content: `AlexaDevicesPage` calls `checkStatus` once on mount (line 19-21), which loads `status`, `devices`, and `echoDevices` into React state. There is no polling, no SSE subscription, and no visibility-based refresh — the only way to invalidate this state is the manual `Refresh` button or the post-action `setTimeout(() => fetchDevices(), 2000)` after a single device command. Under the project's lazy-mount pattern (pages stay mounted via `display: none`), users returning to the Alexa tab can see stale `is_online` flags, missing newly-discovered devices, and outdated Echo lists indefinitely. The `status.authenticated` flag in particular is loaded once and never re-checked, so a session expiry on the backend will not be reflected until reload.
violations.fixPrompt: Add automatic invalidation to `AlexaDevicesPage.jsx`: introduce a polling interval (e.g., 30–60s) for `fetchDevices`/`fetchEchoDevices`, subscribe to relevant SSE events if available, and re-run `checkStatus` on `document.visibilitychange` so authentication state and device lists are refreshed when the user returns to the tab.

violations.title: Polling intervals in `SpeedInsightsPage` keep hammering failing endpoints
violations.content: The `useEffect` sets three `setInterval` loops that call `fetchAll` (60s), `fetchChester` (30s), and `fetchHiboostHistory` (300s) indefinitely. The fetch helpers swallow errors but do not track failure rates, do not back off, and do not stop polling after consecutive failures. If `/chester/system-info` or `/hiboost/history` are persistently unreachable, the page continues to fire requests at the same cadence, wasting browser sockets and backend resources. A simple failure-threshold check that pauses or exponentially backs off polling after N consecutive errors would prevent cascading load against failing dependencies.
violations.fixPrompt: In `frontend/src/pages/SpeedInsightsPage.jsx`, add per-endpoint failure counters that pause the corresponding `setInterval` (or switch to exponential backoff) after several consecutive failures. Reset the counter and resume normal cadence after the next successful response. Surface the paused state via the existing `banner` so the user knows polling stopped.

violations.title: `fetchChester` and `fetchHiboostHistory` silently retry on every interval
violations.content: `fetchChester` and `fetchHiboostHistory` catch all errors silently (comments say "Chester may not be reachable" / "HiBoost may not be configured"), but the surrounding `setInterval` keeps calling them at fixed cadence regardless. There is no consecutive-failure threshold after which polling stops, no exponential backoff, and no awareness of whether the dependency is healthy. For optional integrations that may be unconfigured, this generates continuous noise traffic against backend routes that will never succeed. A circuit-breaker style guard (track failure count, open after threshold, attempt half-open probe at backoff intervals) would eliminate the steady-state failed-request load.
violations.fixPrompt: Wrap `fetchChester` and `fetchHiboostHistory` in a small client-side circuit-breaker helper that tracks consecutive failure count, returns early once a threshold (e.g. 5) is reached, and only retries a single probe call on a backoff schedule (e.g. doubling delay). On a successful probe, close the breaker and resume normal polling.

violations.title: `Promise.all` on independent fetches aborts entire batch on single failure
violations.content: `fetchAll` uses `Promise.all` to fetch five independent endpoints (`/speedtest/latest`, `/speedtest/history`, `/speedtest/hourly-averages`, `/speedtest/insights`, `/speedtest/scheduler/status`). These populate independent state slots (`setLatest`, `setHistory`, `setHourlyAvgs`, `setInsights`, `setSchedulerStatus`) and have no dependencies between them. If any single fetch rejects (e.g., network error on one endpoint, or one endpoint is temporarily unavailable), `Promise.all` short-circuits and rejects, sending control directly to the `catch` block on line 70. None of the response handlers (lines 49–69) run, so even endpoints that successfully responded have their data discarded and corresponding UI state is never updated. The user sees a fully empty page even when 4 of 5 endpoints worked. The downstream `if (res.ok)` checks indicate the code already expects partial failures at the HTTP layer — the same expectation should apply at the Promise layer.
violations.fixPrompt: Replace `Promise.all` with `Promise.allSettled` in `fetchAll` so each fetch settles independently. For each result, check `status === 'fulfilled'` before accessing `.value`, then run the existing `res.ok` / `await res.json()` logic. This preserves partial-success behavior: endpoints that succeed populate their state slots, and only the failing endpoint's data is missing.
violations.snippet:
const [latestRes, historyRes, hourlyRes, insightsRes, schedulerRes] = await Promise.all([
        fetch(buildUrl('/speedtest/latest')),
        fetch(buildUrl(`/speedtest/history?hours=${historyHours}`)),
        fetch(buildUrl('/speedtest/hourly-averages?days=7')),
        fetch(buildUrl('/speedtest/insights')),
        fetch(buildUrl('/speedtest/scheduler/status')),
      ]);

violations.title: `console.error` concatenates message and error in `fetchAll`
violations.content: `console.error('Failed to fetch speed data:', err)` passes the message and the `err` object as separate positional arguments. While not template-literal interpolation, this pattern produces inconsistent log output (object stringification varies by environment) and is not parseable by frontend log shippers. Prefer a structured object: `console.error({ event: 'fetch_speed_data_failed', error: err.message, stack: err.stack })`.
violations.fixPrompt: Replace `console.error('Failed to fetch speed data:', err)` with a structured log entry: `console.error({ event: 'fetch_speed_data_failed', error: err?.message, stack: err?.stack })` so log aggregators can index on `event`.
violations.snippet: console.error('Failed to fetch speed data:', err);

violations.title: Frontend uses raw `console.*` calls with no logging library
violations.content: The frontend codebase relies exclusively on `console.error`, `console.warn`, and `console.log` for operational logging across many files (`ErrorBoundary.jsx`, `DeviceTable.jsx`, `useDevicePolling.js`, `AlexaDeviceCard.jsx`, `DecoTopologyView.jsx`, `SettingsPage.jsx`, `SpeedInsightsPage.jsx`, `SmartHomePage.jsx`, `EventLog.jsx`, `DeviceSearch.jsx`, etc.). There is no abstraction over logging — no `winston`, `pino`, or even a custom logger module. Meanwhile the Python backend uses the `logging` module consistently with `logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)`. This split means frontend errors cannot be centrally controlled (log levels, redaction, remote shipping) and `console.log` calls leak into production builds. The `ErrorBoundary` component, which is the last line of defense for React render errors, only invokes `console.error` — there is no path to forward those errors to a monitoring backend.
violations.fixPrompt: Introduce a small frontend logger module (e.g. `frontend/src/utils/logger.js`) that wraps `console` with named log levels (`debug`, `info`, `warn`, `error`) and a build-time switch to suppress `debug`/`info` in production. Replace direct `console.*` calls in components, pages, and `hooks/useDevicePolling.js` with the new logger. In `ErrorBoundary.jsx`, route `componentDidCatch` errors through the logger so they can later be forwarded to an error-monitoring service.

violations.title: React `ErrorBoundary` does not report to any monitoring service
violations.content: `frontend/src/components/ErrorBoundary.jsx` only imports `react` and calls `console.error`, `window.location.reload`, and `this.state.error.toString`. There is no integration with Sentry, Bugsnag, Datadog RUM, or any browser error reporter. Combined with the absence of a global `window.addEventListener('error', ...)` / `'unhandledrejection'` reporter (none observed in `App.jsx` or `index.jsx`), production React render errors and unhandled promise rejections from `fetch` calls (in `DeviceTable.jsx`, `useDevicePolling.js`, `SpeedInsightsPage.jsx`, etc.) are silently lost.
violations.fixPrompt: Add `@sentry/react` (or equivalent) to `frontend/package.json`. Initialize it in `frontend/src/index.jsx` with `Sentry.init({ dsn: import.meta.env.VITE_SENTRY_DSN, integrations: [Sentry.browserTracingIntegration()] })`. In `ErrorBoundary.jsx`, call `Sentry.captureException(error, { extra: errorInfo })` inside `componentDidCatch`. Optionally wrap the root `App` in `Sentry.ErrorBoundary` and add global handlers for `unhandledrejection`.

violations.title: `publish_event` does not attach correlation/trace ID to SSE messages
violations.content: `publish_event(event_type: str, data: dict)` in `backend/routes/sse.py` publishes events to subscribers without accepting or attaching the originating request's correlation/trace ID. Downstream consumers receiving these events cannot correlate them to the HTTP request, background scan, or scheduler tick that produced them. This violates the rule that event/message publishing must carry the originating request ID for cross-boundary tracing. The `_event_generator` and `sse_events` handler likewise lack request-context identifiers in their stream payloads.
violations.fixPrompt: Update `publish_event` in `backend/routes/sse.py` to accept an optional `correlation_id: Optional[str] = None` parameter and inject it into the event payload (e.g., `{"correlation_id": cid, "type": event_type, "data": data}`). At each call site (device scanner, polling service, deco service, alexa service, etc.), propagate the correlation ID from the originating request context (use `contextvars.ContextVar` populated by a FastAPI middleware that reads `X-Request-Id`/`X-Correlation-Id` headers or generates a UUID). Ensure the SSE generator emits the `correlation_id` field so frontend listeners can tie events back to triggering requests.

violations.title: `authorize` and `token` OAuth handlers do not extract or log a correlation ID
violations.content: `authorize` and `token` in `backend/routes/oauth.py` handle externally-initiated authentication flows (Alexa account linking) but show no correlation/trace ID handling. `token` accepts a `Request` but, given imports (`os`, `secrets`, `time`, `logging`, `urllib.parse`, `base64`), there is no `correlation_service` import nor a header-extraction pattern. OAuth flows that span Alexa → backend → Lambda especially benefit from a propagated trace ID for debugging linking failures; without it, log statements during token exchange cannot be tied to a specific authorization attempt.
violations.fixPrompt: In `backend/routes/oauth.py`, extract `X-Request-Id` (or generate a new UUID) at the top of `authorize` and `token` from the incoming `Request.headers`. Set it on the correlation `ContextVar` used by the logger, include it in every `logger.info`/`logger.error` call within these handlers, and forward it via header on any outbound HTTP call to Alexa/Lambda. Return the ID in the response header `X-Request-Id` so client logs can reference it.

violations.title: `authorize` issues a new auth code on every call with no idempotency
violations.content: The OAuth `authorize` endpoint generates a fresh `code` via `secrets.token_urlsafe(32)` and stores it in `_auth_codes` on every invocation. There is no idempotency key, no deduplication by `(client_id, state)` tuple, and no rate limiting. While OAuth spec permits issuing new codes per request, the combination here — auto-approve with no consent gate and unbounded code issuance — means a retried or replayed authorize request will silently grow `_auth_codes` and produce divergent redirect URLs the client must reconcile. For a personal skill this is low blast radius, but on retry the second code supersedes the first, which can produce confusing auth failures if the first redirect actually completed.
violations.fixPrompt: In `backend/routes/oauth.py`, deduplicate authorization codes within a short window: if an authorize call arrives with the same `(client_id, redirect_uri, state)` as a recent (<60s) request, return the existing code rather than minting a new one. Also add a periodic pruning step or TTL-based cleanup for `_auth_codes` to prevent unbounded growth on retry storms.
violations.snippet:
async def authorize(
    client_id: str,
    response_type: str,
    redirect_uri: str,
    state: str = "",
    scope: str = "",
):
    """OAuth authorization endpoint — shows consent page and redirects with auth code."""
    if client_id != CLIENT_ID:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail="Invalid client_id")
    if response_type != "code":
        raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail="Only 'code' response_type supported")

    # Generate auth code
    code = secrets.token_urlsafe(32)
    _auth_codes[code] = {
        "redirect_uri": redirect_uri,
        "expires": time.time() + 300,  # 5 min
        "client_id": client_id,
    }

    logger.info("OAuth authorize: issuing code for redirect to %s", redirect_uri)

    # Auto-approve (personal skill — no login needed)
    # Build redirect with code and state
    separator = "&" if "?" in redirect_uri else "?"
    redirect_url = f"{redirect_uri}{separator}{urlencode({'code': code, 'state': state})}"

    return RedirectResponse(url=redirect_url)

violations.title: `token` refresh_token grant issues new access token on every retry
violations.content: The `refresh_token` grant branch in `token` mints a brand-new `access_token` on every call (line 129) and stores it in `_access_tokens` without any idempotency check. A retried token-refresh request — common on flaky network connections from Alexa/Lambda — will produce multiple valid access tokens for the same refresh, bloating `_access_tokens` and making session revocation/auditing impossible. There is no idempotency key support and no dedup of in-flight refreshes for the same refresh token.
violations.fixPrompt: In the `refresh_token` branch of `token` in `backend/routes/oauth.py`, track recent refreshes keyed by the refresh token string with a short TTL (e.g. 10 seconds). If the same refresh token is presented within the window, return the previously issued access token instead of minting a new one. Alternatively, accept an `Idempotency-Key` header and cache the response by that key.

violations.title: Unbounded in-memory OAuth token stores
violations.content: The module-level dicts `_auth_codes`, `_access_tokens`, and `_refresh_tokens` accumulate entries indefinitely with no size limit or eviction policy. `_auth_codes` is popped on successful redemption but unredeemed codes remain forever; `_access_tokens` and `_refresh_tokens` are never cleaned up at all — every call to `/oauth/token` adds new entries (e.g., refresh-token grants in lines 129-133 add a new access token without removing the old one). Under sustained load — for example, an Alexa skill or attacker repeatedly hitting `/oauth/authorize` and `/oauth/token` — these dicts will grow without bound, eventually causing OOM. Expired entries are detected only when explicitly looked up, never proactively reaped.
violations.fixPrompt: In `backend/routes/oauth.py`, add a periodic cleanup task (e.g., a background asyncio task started at app startup) that walks `_auth_codes`, `_access_tokens`, and `_refresh_tokens` and removes entries whose `expires` timestamp is in the past. Alternatively, replace the raw dicts with a TTL-aware structure (e.g., `cachetools.TTLCache`) sized to a reasonable maximum to bound memory even under abuse. When issuing a refresh-token grant, also evict any prior access token associated with the same refresh token.

violations.title: `run_speedtest` mutation endpoint lacks idempotency key
violations.content: The `run_speedtest` endpoint triggers a side-effecting operation (SSH into the Chester router and execute a speed test) on every invocation without accepting an idempotency key or checking for an in-flight test. If a client or proxy retries due to a transient network error or timeout, the handler will SSH in and run another full speed test, consuming bandwidth, contending for the router's SSH session, and producing duplicate rows in the speed test history plus duplicate insight generation. There is no deduplication window, no lock against concurrent invocations, and no idempotency-key-based replay of the prior result.
violations.fixPrompt: Add idempotency support to `run_speedtest` in `backend/routes/speedtest.py`. Accept an optional `Idempotency-Key` header; if a recent (e.g., within the last few minutes) test was executed with the same key, return the cached result rather than running a new speed test. Additionally, guard against concurrent invocations with an in-flight flag or asyncio lock so that a retry while a test is in progress returns the in-progress result instead of starting a second SSH speed test.

violations.title: `generate_insights` mutation endpoint is not idempotent
violations.content: The `generate_insights` endpoint manually triggers insight generation from accumulated test data without an idempotency key or deduplication check. Each call invokes `speedtest_service.generate_insights`, which produces and persists insights. Retries (from clients, proxies, or browser refreshes) will run insight generation repeatedly, likely producing duplicate or near-duplicate insight rows for the same underlying data window. The handler returns `generated: len(insights)` but does not dedupe against insights already produced for the same observation window.
violations.fixPrompt: Add idempotency to `generate_insights` in `backend/routes/speedtest.py`. Either accept an `Idempotency-Key` header and cache the response for that key, or have `speedtest_service.generate_insights` deduplicate based on the observation window / content hash so repeated calls within the same period return the existing insights rather than creating new ones. Also consider using a lock to serialize concurrent generations.

async def generate_insights() -> Dict[str, Any]:
    """Manually trigger insight generation from accumulated test data."""
    if speedtest_service is None:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=500, detail="Speed test service not initialized")

    import asyncio
    loop = asyncio.get_event_loop()
    insights = await loop.run_in_executor(None, speedtest_service.generate_insights)
    return {
        "generated": len(insights),
        "insights": insights,
    }

violations.title: `smart_home_control` HTTP PUT to Alexa API lacks retry logic
violations.content: The `smart_home_control` method in `alexa_client.py` performs an `_http_session.put()` call to the external Alexa `phoenix/state` API without any retry on transient failures. Network blips, brief 5xx responses, or temporary connection resets will cause smart home control commands (turn on/off lights, plugs, etc.) to fail permanently on the first try, degrading reliability of user-facing actions. Critical control calls should retry with exponential backoff for transient errors (network errors, 5xx, 429).
violations.fixPrompt: Wrap the `_http_session.put()` call in `smart_home_control` with retry logic (e.g., using `tenacity` or a manual loop) that retries 2-3 times with exponential backoff on `requests.exceptions.ConnectionError`, `requests.exceptions.Timeout`, and 5xx/429 responses. Do not retry on 401 (auth) or 4xx client errors.

violations.title: `smart_home_control` lacks circuit breaker for Alexa API
violations.content: The `smart_home_control` method in `alexa_client.py` issues a `PUT` request to the external Alexa Phoenix State API (`ALEXA_API_BASE/api/phoenix/state`) with only a 10-second timeout. There is no circuit breaker, no failure-rate tracking, and no fail-fast behavior after repeated failures. If Amazon's Alexa API is down or returning errors, callers will continue to hammer the endpoint on every device control request, exhausting the shared `_http_session` connection pool and cascading slowness/failures to the dashboard and Alexa control routes that depend on this client.
violations.fixPrompt: Add a circuit breaker around the `smart_home_control` HTTP call in `backend/services/alexa_client.py`. Use a library like `pybreaker` or implement a simple state machine that tracks consecutive failures and `429`/`5xx`/timeout responses, opens the circuit after a threshold (e.g. 5 failures in 60 seconds), and short-circuits subsequent calls with an `AlexaAPIError` for a cooldown period before transitioning to half-open.

violations.title: `set_tokens` log embeds token expiry in f-string
violations.content: `logger.info(f"Alexa tokens set, expires at {self._token_expiry}")` interpolates the expiry datetime into the message. Treating `expires_at` as a separate structured field would let monitoring tools alert on token lifetimes programmatically.
violations.fixPrompt: In `set_tokens` in `backend/services/alexa_client.py`, replace `logger.info(f"Alexa tokens set, expires at {self._token_expiry}")` with `logger.info("Alexa tokens set", extra={"expires_at": self._token_expiry.isoformat()})`.

violations.title: Discovery/state logs interpolate counts and IDs in f-strings
violations.content: `logger.info(f"Discovered {len(endpoints)} Alexa devices")`, `logger.info(f"Getting state for device {endpoint_id}")`, and `logger.warning(f"Failed to get state for {endpoint_id}: {e}")` embed counts, endpoint IDs, and exceptions directly in messages. Structured fields would allow filtering on `endpoint_id` and aggregating success/failure counts.
violations.fixPrompt: In `discover_devices` and `get_device_state` in `backend/services/alexa_client.py`, replace the f-string log calls with structured forms like `logger.info("Discovered Alexa devices", extra={"count": len(endpoints)})`, `logger.info("Getting device state", extra={"endpoint_id": endpoint_id})`, and `logger.warning("Failed to get device state", extra={"endpoint_id": endpoint_id, "error": str(e)})`.

violations.title: Endpoints/Phoenix/Devices-v2 logs embed HTTP status and counts in f-strings
violations.content: Multiple log calls in `get_endpoints` and `get_smart_home_devices_with_connections` use f-strings like `logger.warning(f"Endpoints API returned {response.status_code}: {response.text[:200]}")`, `logger.info(f"Endpoints API returned {len(endpoints)} endpoints (expand={expand})")`, `logger.info(f"Phoenix API returned data with {len(devices_with_mac)} MAC-bearing devices")`, `logger.warning(f"Phoenix API failed: {e}")`, `logger.info(f"Devices-v2 API: {len(raw_devices)} total, found MAC addresses in some")`, and `logger.warning(f"Devices-v2 API failed for MAC fetch: {e}")`. Status codes, counts, and errors should be structured fields so the API surface can be monitored programmatically.
violations.fixPrompt: In `get_endpoints` and `get_smart_home_devices_with_connections` in `backend/services/alexa_client.py`, replace these f-string log calls with structured equivalents: `logger.warning("Endpoints API failed", extra={"status": response.status_code, "body": response.text[:200]})`, `logger.info("Endpoints API ok", extra={"count": len(endpoints), "expand": expand})`, `logger.info("Phoenix API result", extra={"mac_count": len(devices_with_mac)})`, `logger.warning("Phoenix API failed", extra={"error": str(e)})`, and similarly for Devices-v2.

violations.title: Cookie/web-API logs embed counts, status, and serials in f-strings
violations.content: `logger.info(f"Alexa cookies set ({len(self._cookies)} cookies)")`, `logger.info(f"Behaviors/entities API returned {response.status_code}")`, `logger.info(f"Got {len(data)} smart home entities")`, `logger.warning(f"Behaviors/entities returned {response.status_code}")`, `logger.warning(f"Behaviors/entities API failed: {e}")`, `logger.info(f"Echo devices API returned {response.status_code}")`, and `logger.warning(f"Echo devices API failed: {e}")` all use interpolation rather than structured fields. This prevents grouping by `status` or `endpoint_name` across log streams.
violations.fixPrompt: In `set_cookies`, `get_smart_home_devices`, and `get_echo_devices_web` in `backend/services/alexa_client.py`, replace each f-string log with `logger.info("<message>", extra={...})` form so that `cookie_count`, `status`, `count`, and `error` are structured fields rather than embedded in the message text.

violations.content: `logger.warning(f"device-wifi-details failed for {serial_number}: {e}")`, `logger.info(f"Got MAC addresses for {len(results)} of {len(devices)} Echo/Fire devices")`, and `logger.warning(f"Routines API failed: {e}")` interpolate serial numbers, counts, and exceptions into the message. Structured logging would let operators filter by `serial_number` or aggregate MAC-coverage statistics.
violations.fixPrompt: In `get_device_wifi_details`, `get_all_device_macs`, and `get_routines` in `backend/services/alexa_client.py`, replace the f-string log calls with structured calls passing `serial_number`, `error`, `match_count`, and `total_count` via `extra={...}`.
violations.snippet:
logger.warning(f"device-wifi-details failed for {serial_number}: {e}")
            return None

    def get_all_device_macs(self) -> List[Dict[str, str]]:
        """Get MAC addresses for all Echo/Fire hardware devices.

        Calls devices-v2 to get the device list, then device-wifi-details
        for each device to get MAC addresses. Skips groups and non-hardware.
        Returns list of dicts with: serialNumber, accountName, deviceFamily,
        deviceType, macAddress (normalized aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff), essid
        """
        devices = self.get_echo_devices_web()
        if not devices:
            return []

        results = []
        for d in devices:
            if not isinstance(d, dict):
                continue
            serial = d.get("serialNumber", "")
            dtype = d.get("deviceType", "")
            name = d.get("accountName", "")
            family = d.get("deviceFamily", "")
            if not serial or not dtype:
                continue

            wifi = self.get_device_wifi_details(serial, dtype)
            if not wifi:
                continue
            mac_raw = wifi.get("macAddress", "")
            if not mac_raw or len(mac_raw) != 12:
                continue

            # Normalize: "ACCCFC637684" -> "ac:cc:fc:63:76:84"
            mac_normalized = ":".join(mac_raw[i:i+2].lower() for i in range(0, 12, 2))
            results.append({
                "serialNumber": serial,
                "accountName": name,
                "deviceFamily": family,
                "deviceType": dtype,
                "macAddress": mac_normalized,
                "essid": wifi.get("essid"),
            })

        logger.info(f"Got MAC addresses for {len(results)} of {len(devices)} Echo/Fire devices")
        return results

    def get_routines(self) -> List[Dict[str, Any]]:
        """Get Alexa routines via the web API."""
        if not self._cookies:
            return []
        headers = self._get_alexa_web_headers()
        cookies = self._get_cookie_jar()
        try:
            response = self._http_session.get(
                f"{self.ALEXA_API_BASE}/api/behaviors/automations",
                headers=headers, cookies=cookies, timeout=15,
            )
            if response.status_code == 200:
                data = response.json()
                return data if isinstance(data, list) else data.get("automations", [])
            return []
        except Exception as e:
            logger.warning(f"Routines API failed: {e}")

violations.title: `smart_home_control` and groups fetch logs embed errors in f-strings
violations.content: `logger.warning(f"Smart home control errors: {errors}")` and `logger.warning(f"Smart home groups fetch failed: {e}")` embed the errors list and exception object inside the message. Structured logging would treat `errors` and `error` as separate fields so they can be searched and aggregated.

violations.title: `sendCommand` `fetch` to Alexa command endpoint has no retry on transient failures
violations.content: The `sendCommand` callback in `AlexaDeviceCard` issues a single `fetch` POST to `/alexa/devices/{endpoint_id}/command` (lines 51-58) with no retry on transient network errors (offline blips, 502/503/504 from the backend reverse proxy). On failure the catch block only logs `console.error('Command failed:', err)` and the user sees nothing happen. For idempotent commands (`power_on`, `power_off`, `lock`, `set_brightness`, `set_thermostat`), a small bounded retry with backoff would noticeably improve UX over flaky home networks. Note: `unlock` is intentionally non-idempotent due to the PIN — exclude it from retry.
violations.fixPrompt: Wrap the `fetch` call in `sendCommand` with a bounded retry helper that retries on network errors and on responses with status in `{502, 503, 504}`. Use up to 2 retries with exponential backoff (e.g. 300ms, 900ms). Skip retry for the `unlock` command since it is not idempotent. Surface a user-visible error toast when all retries fail instead of only logging to the console.

violations.title: `fetchTopology` lacks retry logic for transient network failures
violations.content: `fetchTopology` calls `fetch(buildUrl('/deco/topology'))` and treats any non-`ok` response or thrown exception as a terminal error. Topology data drives the primary network visualization and is auto-refreshed; a single transient failure (network blip, backend restart) immediately puts the UI into an error state. Add retry-with-backoff for network errors and 5xx responses before showing the error banner.
violations.fixPrompt: Add a retry wrapper around the `fetch(buildUrl('/deco/topology'))` call inside `fetchTopology`. Retry up to 3 times with exponential backoff (e.g., 500ms, 1s, 2s) on network errors and 5xx responses; do not retry on 4xx (especially 401). Only set `error` after retries are exhausted.

violations.title: Auto-refresh polling lacks circuit breaker
violations.content: The `useEffect` in `DecoTopologyView` schedules `fetchTopology` and `fetchGraph` on a fixed `setInterval` of `autoRefreshInterval` (default 30s) with no failure-rate tracking. If the `/deco/topology` or `/deco/topology-graph` endpoints are persistently failing (e.g., Deco router unreachable, backend down, auth lost returning 401), the interval keeps firing requests indefinitely. `fetchTopology` swallows errors into local state and `fetchGraph` only logs warnings — neither stops or backs off the interval. This means one failing dependency causes the UI to hammer the backend every 30s forever, exhausting backend connection pools to the Deco API and cascading failures.
violations.fixPrompt: Add a consecutive-failure counter to `fetchTopology` and `fetchGraph`. When failures exceed a threshold (e.g., 5 consecutive failures), open a circuit by clearing the interval (or skipping calls) and entering a cooldown period (e.g., 5 minutes) before retrying. Reset the counter on success. Show the user a circuit-open state with a manual retry button instead of silently looping.

violations.title: `handleSaveField` device update has no retry on transient failure
violations.content: `handleSaveField` issues a `PUT /devices/{id}` to persist user edits (friendly name, type, notes). A transient network failure or 5xx response causes immediate user-visible failure ("Failed to save changes. Please try again.") with no automatic retry. For user-initiated writes, retrying transient failures with exponential backoff produces a more reliable experience.
violations.fixPrompt: Wrap the `fetch(buildUrl(`/devices/${device.device_id}`), { method: 'PUT', ... })` call in `handleSaveField` with a retry helper that retries 2–3 times with exponential backoff on network errors and 5xx responses. Do not retry on 4xx. Show the existing error message only after retries are exhausted.

violations.title: `handleDelete` device delete call lacks retry on transient errors
violations.content: `handleDelete` issues a `DELETE /devices/{id}` and on any non-ok response or thrown error sets a generic error. A transient network failure (e.g., during backend restart) will fail this user-initiated destructive operation immediately without retrying. Retry transient/5xx failures with backoff before reporting failure.
violations.fixPrompt: Wrap the `fetch(buildUrl(`/devices/${device.device_id}`), { method: 'DELETE' })` call in `handleDelete` with a retry helper (2–3 attempts, exponential backoff) for network errors and 5xx responses. Do not retry on 4xx. Surface the existing error message only after retries are exhausted.

violations.title: `handleDismiss` alert dismiss call has no retry on transient failure
violations.content: `handleDismiss` posts to `/api/events/alerts/{id}/dismiss` and on any failure resets `isDismissing` without retrying. A transient network failure leaves the alert undismissed with no automatic recovery. Add retry-with-backoff for network errors and 5xx responses so transient failures don't strand the user.
violations.fixPrompt: Wrap the `fetch('/api/events/alerts/${alert.alert_id}/dismiss', { method: 'POST', ... })` call in `handleDismiss` with a retry helper (2–3 attempts, exponential backoff) for network errors and 5xx responses. Do not retry on 4xx. Surface the error only after retries are exhausted.

violations.title: `fetchData` for WiFi/QoS lacks retry on transient errors
violations.content: The polling `fetchData` in `DecoWiFiQoSView` issues two sequential GETs (`/deco/wifi-config`, `/deco/qos`); a single transient failure on either flips the entire view into an error state until the next poll interval (10s default). Retry transient/5xx failures with backoff before setting `error` to avoid spurious error UI from brief blips.
violations.fixPrompt: Add a retry helper around the two `fetch` calls inside `fetchData` (the `/deco/wifi-config` and `/deco/qos` GETs). Retry up to 2–3 times with exponential backoff on network errors and 5xx responses; do not retry on 4xx. Only set `error` after retries are exhausted.

violations.title: QoS polling continues regardless of failures
violations.content: The `useEffect` in `DecoWiFiQoSView` sequentially calls `/deco/wifi-config` and `/deco/qos` every `refreshInterval` (default 10s) with no failure tracking. When the Deco backend is failing, the interval keeps firing both fetches every 10 seconds indefinitely — there is no maximum-failure threshold after which calls stop or back off. With a 10-second cadence this is especially aggressive: two upstream Deco API calls every tick from every mounted instance. This can exhaust connection pools on the backend and the upstream Deco router during outages.
violations.fixPrompt: Track consecutive failures in a ref. After N consecutive failures (e.g., 3-5), stop the `setInterval` or switch to an exponential-backoff schedule until a successful call resets the breaker. Surface the open-circuit state in the UI with a manual retry button rather than silently continuing the loop.

violations.title: `sendPartitionCommand` has no retry on security-critical Alarm.com call
violations.content: `sendPartitionCommand` issues a single `fetch` to `/alarm-com/partitions/{id}/command` (arm/disarm) with no retry on transient network failure. This is a security-critical mutation to an external service (Alarm.com); a transient TLS/network hiccup will silently fail to arm or disarm the partition. The user only sees a banner and would have to manually retry, with no exponential backoff.
violations.fixPrompt: Wrap the `fetch` in `sendPartitionCommand` with a retry helper that retries up to 2-3 times on network errors or 5xx responses, using exponential backoff (e.g. 500ms, 1s, 2s). Do NOT retry on 4xx responses or after the user-confirmed `disarm` succeeds. Surface the final error via `showBanner` only after retries are exhausted.

violations.title: `sendLockCommand` has no retry on physical-lock command
violations.content: `sendLockCommand` posts to `/alarm-com/locks/{id}/command` with a single `fetch` and no retry. Lock/unlock commands traverse the Alarm.com cloud and a physical Z-Wave lock — transient failures along that chain are common. Without retry-with-backoff, a momentary network blip means the lock stays in its previous state with only a toast banner shown to the user.
violations.fixPrompt: Add a retry wrapper around the `fetch` call in `sendLockCommand` that retries 2-3 times with exponential backoff on network errors or 5xx responses. Skip retries on 4xx. After exhausting retries, call `showBanner` with a clear failure message including that retries were attempted.

violations.title: `handleLogin` lacks retry on Alarm.com login POST
violations.content: `handleLogin` posts to `/alarm-com/login` which initiates an upstream login to Alarm.com — a session-creating call against an external service known for rate-limit/CAPTCHA flakiness. A single transient failure surfaces an error to the user with no backoff retry on network or 5xx errors.
violations.fixPrompt: Add a small retry helper for the `fetch(buildUrl('/alarm-com/login'), ...)` call: retry 1-2 times on network errors or 5xx responses with backoff (e.g. 1s, 3s). Never retry once the server returns `otp_required: true`, `success: true`, or any explicit `data.detail` 4xx (e.g. invalid credentials).

violations.title: Alarm.com `status`/`devices` cached without automatic invalidation
violations.content: The `init` effect runs once on mount and never re-runs (deps are stable callbacks). `status` (including `logged_in`/`configured`) and `devices` (partitions, sensors, locks, etc.) are stored in component state with no polling, no SSE subscription, and no visibility-based refresh. Under the project's lazy-mount pattern, a partition that is armed/disarmed elsewhere, a sensor that trips, or a session that expires on the backend will not appear in this view until the user clicks `Refresh` or sends a command. For a security-system integration where state freshness matters (e.g., a sensor showing OPEN vs CLOSED), this stale-cache risk is meaningful.
violations.fixPrompt: In `AlarmComPage.jsx`, add an automatic invalidation mechanism: poll `/alarm-com/status` and `/alarm-com/devices` on an interval (e.g., 15–30s) while the page is mounted/visible, pause when `document.hidden`, and re-run `fetchStatus`/`fetchDevices` on `visibilitychange` so partition/sensor/lock states reflect backend changes without manual refresh.

violations.title: `runSpeedTest` lacks retry on external speed-test trigger
violations.content: `runSpeedTest` issues a single POST to `/speedtest/run` which proxies through to the external Chester 5G router. This call can take a long time and is prone to transient failure (cellular link, router responsiveness). On failure the user is shown `Speed test failed. Check Chester connectivity.` with no automatic retry, forcing them to click again.
violations.fixPrompt: Wrap the `fetch(buildUrl('/speedtest/run'), ...)` call with a retry helper that retries 1-2 times on network errors or 5xx responses with exponential backoff (e.g. 1s, 3s). Only show the failure banner after retries are exhausted. Do not retry on 4xx responses or once `result.error` is set in the response body.

violations.title: Polling intervals lack circuit breaker on repeated failures
violations.content: `fastIntervalRef` (15s), `slowIntervalRef` (30s), and `speedIntervalRef` (60s) in `useDevicePolling` continue firing indefinitely regardless of failure rates. Each interval triggers multiple `fetch` calls (`/health`, `/devices`, `/config/polling`, `/device-groups`, `/network/home-status`, `/events/alerts`, `/deco/client-node-map`, `/chester/system-info`, `/network/health-score`, `/speedtest/latest`, `/speedtest/insights`) whose individual catch blocks silently swallow errors and immediately schedule another round. There is no consecutive-failure threshold, no exponential backoff, and no open/half-open state. If the backend (or the downstream Deco/Chester/Alexa/Alarm.com services it proxies) is degraded, the browser keeps hammering it at fixed intervals, potentially exhausting connection pools and amplifying cascading failures rather than failing fast.
violations.fixPrompt: Introduce a circuit-breaker wrapper around the polling callbacks in `useDevicePolling`. Track consecutive failure counts per endpoint group (`fastPoll`, `slowPoll`, `speedPoll`); after N (e.g. 5) consecutive failures, open the circuit by skipping calls and lengthening the interval (exponential backoff). After a cool-down, allow a single probe call (half-open); on success, reset the counter and resume normal cadence. Surface the open state via `apiStatus` so the UI can indicate degraded mode.

violations.title: `pollUnseen` polls every 10s with no failure threshold
violations.content: The `pollUnseen` callback in the notifications `useEffect` hits `/events/alerts/unseen` and `/events/alerts/mark-seen` every 10 seconds via `setInterval(pollUnseen, 10000)`. The catch block is a silent `/* silent */`, so repeated failures are invisible and the polling loop keeps issuing requests at full cadence. There is no failure counter, no backoff, and no circuit-open state. If the backend is overloaded or unreachable, this loop will continue to consume browser sockets and add load to a struggling server rather than failing fast.
violations.fixPrompt: Wrap `pollUnseen` with a circuit-breaker: count consecutive failures, open the circuit after a threshold, apply exponential backoff (e.g. 10s → 30s → 2m), and re-probe periodically. Reset on success. Log/surface the breaker state so the user knows notifications are paused.

violations.title: Background poller `pollUnseen` silently swallows all errors
violations.content: The `pollUnseen` function is a background polling worker that fetches unseen alerts and triggers browser notifications. The entire body is wrapped in `try { ... } catch (error) { /* silent */ }` with no logging, no failure-state tracking, and no consecutive-failure counter. If the alerts endpoint, the mark-seen call, or notification creation fails repeatedly, users will never see new-device or device-offline notifications and nobody will know the poller is broken.
violations.fixPrompt: Update `pollUnseen` in `frontend/src/hooks/useDevicePolling.js` to at minimum `console.error` the caught error (matching the convention used elsewhere in this hook) and track consecutive failures in state so the UI can surface a 'notifications poller is failing' indicator after N successive errors. Do not leave the catch block as `/* silent */`.

violations.title: Background fetch `getClientNodeMap` silently fails with no logging
violations.content: `getClientNodeMap` is invoked as part of the periodic polling pipeline. The catch block only contains the comment `// Silently fail — Deco may not be configured` and does not log, increment a failure counter, or surface state to the UI. A misconfigured Deco integration will look identical to a transient network error or a real bug — operators have no signal that the background data refresh is broken.
violations.fixPrompt: In `getClientNodeMap`, log the caught error via `console.warn` (so true 'not configured' cases are still visible) and consider tracking consecutive failures so persistent errors can be distinguished from a one-time misconfiguration.

violations.title: Background fetch `getSpeedTestLatest` silently fails
violations.content: `getSpeedTestLatest` runs as part of the polling hook and its catch block is `// Silently fail — speed test may not have run yet`. There is no log, no failure tracking, and no UI signal. If the `/speedtest/latest` endpoint starts returning errors indefinitely, the UI will continue to show stale (or empty) speed data with no indication that the background fetch loop is broken.
violations.fixPrompt: Add `console.error` logging to the catch block in `getSpeedTestLatest` and consider exposing a polling-health flag so the UI can show a 'speed data unavailable' state instead of silently displaying nothing.

violations.title: Background fetch `getChesterInfo` silently fails
violations.content: `getChesterInfo` is part of the background polling pipeline and only contains `// Silently fail — Chester may not be reachable` in its catch block. There is no logging or failure-state tracking, so persistent Chester connectivity issues will be indistinguishable from intentional 'not configured' scenarios.
violations.fixPrompt: In `getChesterInfo`, log the caught error and surface a Chester-reachability flag in state so the UI (and operators) can tell the difference between 'unconfigured' and 'configured but failing'.

violations.title: Background fetch `getHomeStatus` silently fails
violations.content: `getHomeStatus` is a background polling fetch whose catch block is only `// Silently fail`. No logging, no failure state. The home-status UI will simply show stale data forever if this endpoint breaks.
violations.fixPrompt: Add `console.error` to the catch block in `getHomeStatus` and consider tracking a failure count so the dashboard can flag a degraded state.

violations.title: Background fetch `getActiveAlerts` silently swallows errors
violations.content: `getActiveAlerts` polls the alerts endpoint and its catch block is `catch (error) { /* silent */ }`. Active alerts are user-safety-critical data; silently failing means users may believe their network is healthy while the alerts fetch has actually been broken for hours.
violations.fixPrompt: Replace the `/* silent */` catch with `console.error('Failed to fetch active alerts:', error)` and track consecutive failures in state so the UI can surface a clear 'alerts unavailable' indicator after repeated failures.

violations.title: Background fetch `getAnomalyInsights` silently swallows errors
violations.content: `getAnomalyInsights` is a background polling fetch with a `catch (error) { /* silent */ }` block. Anomaly detection failures will never be surfaced — users may assume their network is anomaly-free when the underlying fetch has been failing.
violations.fixPrompt: Replace `/* silent */` with `console.error` logging and add failure tracking so persistent anomaly-feed failures can be distinguished from 'no anomalies detected'.

violations.title: Background fetch `getDailyDigest` silently swallows errors
violations.content: `getDailyDigest` runs as part of background polling and its catch block is `catch (error) { /* silent */ }`. No logging or failure tracking — the daily digest will simply be empty if the endpoint fails, with no operator-visible signal.
violations.fixPrompt: Replace the silent catch with `console.error('Failed to fetch daily digest:', error)` to match the convention used elsewhere in this hook.

violations.title: Background fetch `getHealthScore` silently swallows errors
violations.content: `getHealthScore` is a background polling fetch with a `catch (error) { /* silent */ }` block. The network health score is a primary dashboard indicator — silent failures here mean the score may stop updating without anyone noticing, defeating the purpose of a health indicator.
violations.fixPrompt: Replace the silent catch in `getHealthScore` with `console.error` logging and consider invalidating the displayed score (or marking it stale) after repeated failures so the dashboard does not show a misleading 'healthy' state from an outdated value.

violations.title: `handleManualRefresh` lacks retry on Deco cloud refresh
violations.content: `handleManualRefresh` posts to `/deco/nodes/refresh` which forces a cache-bypassed call to the TP-Link Deco cloud API. The Deco cloud is well-known for transient 5xx errors and timeouts. A single failure leaves the UI in an error state with no automatic retry/backoff.
violations.fixPrompt: Wrap the `fetch(buildUrl('/deco/nodes/refresh'), ...)` call in `handleManualRefresh` with a retry helper that retries 1-2 times on network errors or 5xx responses using exponential backoff. Skip retries on 4xx (e.g. 401 unauthenticated). Surface `setError(err.message)` only after retries are exhausted.

violations.title: `DecoNodesPage` auto-refresh has no failure threshold
violations.content: The auto-refresh `useEffect` schedules `fetchNodes` via `setInterval(..., refreshInterval)` (default 60s) and never stops on failures. `fetchNodes` calls `/deco/nodes`, which proxies to the TP-Link Deco cloud — an external service that is known to throttle and to require re-authentication. When `fetchNodes` throws (401/404/network error), the error is set in state but the interval keeps firing on the same cadence, continuously hammering the Deco cloud through the backend. There is no consecutive-failure counter, no backoff, and no open-circuit short-circuit.
violations.fixPrompt: Track consecutive `fetchNodes` failures in a ref. After ~3 failures, pause the `setInterval` (or skip its body via an `if (breakerOpen) return;` guard) and start an exponentially backed-off probe timer. On a successful probe, reset the counter and restore the normal interval. Consider surfacing the breaker state in the UI banner so the user understands why auto-refresh has paused.

violations.title: Unbounded `ip_history` list grows on every IP change
violations.content: In `NetworkDeviceRepository.create_or_update`, the `ip_history` list is loaded from the database, appended to whenever a device's IP changes, and re-serialized to JSON — with no size cap, ring-buffer, or eviction policy. A device that frequently churns IPs (DHCP renewals, network instability, an attacker spoofing DHCP leases, or a misbehaving client) will cause this list to grow without bound. Each call also loads, parses, mutates, and re-writes the full JSON blob, so memory and disk usage scale linearly with history length. Under sustained churn this can balloon the `network_devices` row, slow down every `create_or_update` call, and eventually pressure memory when many devices have long histories.
violations.fixPrompt: In `backend/db.py` `NetworkDeviceRepository.create_or_update` (around lines 189–203), cap `ip_history` to a maximum number of entries (e.g. 50) using a trailing slice such as `ip_history = ip_history[-49:]` before appending the new entry, or trim by retention window (e.g. drop entries older than 30 days). Make the cap configurable via an env var like `IP_HISTORY_MAX_ENTRIES` and document the limit.

violations.title: F-string interpolation in `_init_db` log messages
violations.content: `logger.info(f"Database initialized at {self.db_path} (WAL mode)")` and `logger.error(f"Failed to initialize database: {e}")` embed values directly into the message string. This prevents programmatic log parsing (e.g. extracting `db_path` or error details as fields) and forces eager formatting even when the log level is disabled. Prefer structured key-value logging via `extra=` or lazy `%s` substitution.
violations.fixPrompt: Refactor `logger.info(f"Database initialized at {self.db_path} (WAL mode)")` and `logger.error(f"Failed to initialize database: {e}")` in `_init_db` to use structured logging: `logger.info("Database initialized", extra={"db_path": self.db_path, "journal_mode": "WAL"})` and `logger.error("Failed to initialize database", extra={"error": str(e)})` so values are parseable fields rather than embedded text.

violations.title: F-string error logs in `get_connection`/`write_connection`
violations.content: `logger.error(f"Database error: {e}")` (line 73) and `logger.error(f"Database write error: {e}")` (line 90) inline the exception via f-string. This loses structured error fields and prevents downstream tools from extracting error type/message. Use `extra={"error": str(e)}` or `logger.exception()` for stack trace plus structured context.
