                    ORDER BY created_at DESC
                    LIMIT ? OFFSET ?
                """, (limit, offset))
                rows = cursor.fetchall()
                return [dict(row) for row in rows]
        except sqlite3.Error as e:
            logger.error(f"Failed to list active alerts: {e}")
            raise

    def dismiss(self, alert_id: str) -> bool:
        """Dismiss an alert"""
        try:
            with self.db.get_connection() as conn:
                cursor = conn.cursor()
                cursor.execute("""
                    UPDATE device_alerts
                    SET dismissed = 1, dismissed_at = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, updated_at = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
                    WHERE alert_id = ?
                """, (alert_id,))
                conn.commit()
                return cursor.rowcount > 0
        except sqlite3.Error as e:
            logger.error(f"Failed to dismiss alert: {e}")
            raise

    def list_by_device(self, device_id: str, limit: int = 50, offset: int = 0) -> List[dict]:
        """List alerts for a device"""
        try:
            with self.db.get_connection() as conn:
                cursor = conn.cursor()
                cursor.execute("""
                    SELECT * FROM device_alerts
                    WHERE device_id = ?
                    ORDER BY created_at DESC
                    LIMIT ? OFFSET ?
                """, (device_id, limit, offset))
                rows = cursor.fetchall()
                return [dict(row) for row in rows]
        except sqlite3.Error as e:
            logger.error(f"Failed to list alerts by device: {e}")

violations.title: `HiBoostService` cache has TTL but no size limit or expired-entry eviction
violations.content: `HiBoostService._cache` and `_cache_ts` (lines 64-65) accumulate entries via `_set_cache` (lines 70-72) keyed by `dashboard` and per-device `detail:{device_id}` strings. `_is_cached` only checks freshness on read; expired entries are never removed from the dictionaries. There is also no maximum size. While the number of HiBoost devices is typically small, if `device_id` values ever vary (e.g., transient IDs, retries with mutated identifiers, or future expansion to many devices), both dicts grow without bound and never shrink except via the manual `clear_cache`.
violations.fixPrompt: In `HiBoostService._set_cache`, also evict any keys whose `_cache_ts` value is older than `CACHE_TTL` so stale entries do not accumulate. Additionally, enforce a hard cap (e.g., 1000 entries) and drop the oldest by timestamp once exceeded. Alternatively, switch to a `cachetools.TTLCache` with an explicit `maxsize` and `ttl=CACHE_TTL`.

violations.title: `useToasts` toast list has no size cap or eviction policy
violations.content: The `useToasts` hook stores notifications in an in-memory `toasts` array that is appended to on every `push` call (`setToasts((prev) => [...prev, { id, message, type, duration }])`). There is no maximum size, no FIFO eviction, and no rate-limiting. Auto-dismissal relies on each `ToastItem` running a `setTimeout` — but `ToastItem` explicitly skips the timeout when `toast.duration === 0` (line 22), meaning sticky toasts never get cleared automatically. If `push` is invoked rapidly (e.g. a burst of errors from polling/SSE failures in `useDevicePolling.js`) or repeatedly with `duration: 0`, the array — and the DOM nodes it renders — grow without bound, leading to memory/UI bloat and eventual unresponsiveness.
violations.fixPrompt: In `useToasts` (`frontend/src/components/Toast.jsx`), cap the toast list. In the `push` callback, after computing the new array, truncate it to a maximum (e.g. 5 most recent) by slicing: `setToasts((prev) => [...prev, newToast].slice(-MAX_TOASTS))`. Also enforce a minimum auto-dismiss duration for sticky toasts or guarantee callers manually dismiss `duration: 0` toasts, so the queue cannot grow without bound under burst conditions.

violations.title: `devices` fetched on mount with no invalidation
violations.content: The `useEffect` in `EventLogPage` calls `fetchDevices` exactly once on mount (empty deps array on line 39) and stores the result in the `devices` state. There is no polling interval, no SSE subscription, no manual refresh button, and no other invalidation path. Combined with the codebase's documented lazy-mount pattern (pages stay in the DOM via `display: none` after first visit per project `CLAUDE.md`), this state acts as an in-memory cache that is never cleared when the source data changes. Users returning to the Events & Alerts tab will see device lists captured at the moment of first navigation, even if devices appear/disappear or change status afterward.
violations.fixPrompt: Add an invalidation strategy to `devices` in `EventLogPage.jsx`: either subscribe to the existing `/api/sse/events` stream to refetch on `device_update` events, add a `setInterval` polling refresh similar to `useDevicePolling.js`, or expose a refresh trigger and re-run `fetchDevices` when the page becomes visible (visibilitychange / when the user navigates to the Events & Alerts tab).

violations.title: `suggestions`/`unlinkedAlexa` fetched once with no automatic invalidation
violations.content: `DeviceNamingPage` calls `fetchSuggestions` once on mount (empty deps array) and stores `suggestions`, `unlinkedAlexa`, and `stats` in component state. The only invalidation paths are explicit user actions (`Refresh`, `Import Deco Names`, `Auto-Name Deco Nodes`, link/rename completion). With the lazy-mount pattern, when a new device joins the network or an Alexa device is added, this view will not reflect the change until the user remembers to click `Refresh`. The `stats` (totalNetwork / totalAlexa / totalLinked) will likewise drift from the dashboard's polled counts.
violations.fixPrompt: Add a polling refresh (e.g., 60s) for `fetchSuggestions` in `DeviceNamingPage.jsx`, or trigger a refetch on `document.visibilitychange` when the page becomes visible, so suggestions and stats stay in sync with backend state without manual user action.

violations.title: `request_otp` sends an OTP notification with no deduplication
violations.content: `request_otp` calls `alarm_com_client.request_otp(body.method)` which causes Alarm.com to deliver a one-time password to the user via app push, email, or SMS. There is no idempotency key, no rate-limiting, and no deduplication of recent OTP requests for the same `(user, method)` pair. A client retry triggered by a flaky network — or an automatic retry from the HTTP infrastructure — will cause a second OTP message to be sent to the user, which is annoying at best and can trigger upstream provider throttling/abuse detection at worst.
violations.fixPrompt: Add deduplication to `request_otp`. Track the timestamp of the last OTP request per `(session, method)` in memory or the DB and short-circuit (returning the cached prior response) if a request was issued within a short window (e.g., 30–60 seconds). Alternatively, accept and honor an `Idempotency-Key` header so retries of the same logical request never deliver a second message.

violations.title: `send_partition_command` arms/disarms with no idempotency protection
violations.content: `send_partition_command` dispatches `arm_away`, `arm_stay`, or `disarm` to a security alarm partition with no idempotency key and no check that the partition is not already in the requested state. While arming an already-armed partition is usually a no-op upstream, this is a security-critical mutation that frequently triggers audible chimes, push notifications, and audit-log entries on the alarm provider's side. If the request times out and is retried, the user receives duplicate notifications and the alarm audit log shows duplicate state-change attempts, which can mask real activity.
violations.fixPrompt: Make `send_partition_command` retry-safe. Either accept an `Idempotency-Key` header and cache the response keyed by it for a short window, or fetch the partition's current state before issuing the command and short-circuit (returning the cached current state) when it already matches the requested `arm_away`/`arm_stay`/`disarm` target.

violations.title: `import_alexa_mac_addresses` external API calls lack retry logic
violations.content: `import_alexa_mac_addresses` in `routes/alexa.py` calls `alexa_client.get_all_device_macs()` and `alexa_client.get_echo_devices_web()` against the external Alexa Web API. On a transient failure the function catches the exception and proceeds with `device_macs = []`, silently producing an empty import result instead of retrying. Given this is a manual user-initiated operation and the API is known to be flaky, transient failures should retry with exponential backoff before falling through to the empty-result path.
violations.fixPrompt: Wrap `alexa_client.get_all_device_macs()` and `alexa_client.get_echo_devices_web()` in retry logic with exponential backoff (2-3 attempts) for transient errors. Only fall through to the empty-result branch after retries are exhausted.

violations.title: `identify_complete` Deco API call lacks retry logic
violations.content: `identify_complete` in `routes/alexa.py` calls `deco_client.get_client_list_local` (an HTTP call to the local Deco router API) without retry. Any transient network error causes an immediate 500 response, requiring the user to restart the entire identify flow (which has a 5-minute snapshot window). Local-router API calls commonly experience transient failures and should retry with brief backoff.
violations.fixPrompt: Add retry logic (2-3 attempts with short exponential backoff) around the `await loop.run_in_executor(None, deco_client.get_client_list_local)` call in `identify_complete` to handle transient failures from the Deco local API.

violations.title: `import_alexa_mac_addresses` keeps iterating Alexa API on failure
violations.content: `import_alexa_mac_addresses` calls `alexa_client.get_all_device_macs()` which internally iterates `devices-v2` and calls `/api/device-wifi-details` for every device. There is no circuit breaker or maximum-failure threshold: if Amazon returns errors for many devices in sequence (e.g. cookie expiry, rate limiting, regional outage), the loop continues hammering the upstream endpoint and only catches a single top-level `Exception`. This can exhaust the shared `requests.Session` connection pool and amplify a partial Alexa outage into a full request stall on this route.
violations.fixPrompt: Add a circuit breaker / failure-budget around the Alexa MAC enumeration in `backend/services/alexa_client.py:get_all_device_macs` (or wrap it in `routes/alexa.py:import_alexa_mac_addresses`). After N consecutive `device-wifi-details` failures or a configurable error rate, abort the iteration early and return a partial result with an explicit `circuit_open` status so callers fail fast instead of continuing to call the failing endpoint.

violations.title: `_identify_snapshots` dict grows unbounded across `identify_start` calls
violations.content: The module-level `_identify_snapshots: Dict[str, Dict]` cache at line 960 stores a full Deco client-list snapshot (every online MAC + name + IP) per `entity_id` whenever `POST /smart-home/{entity_id}/identify/start` is called (line 990). Entries are only removed in two places: when `identify_complete` runs successfully (line 1064), and when `identify_complete` detects a stale snapshot (line 1019). There is no background sweep, no `__len__` cap, no LRU eviction, and the staleness check only fires when `identify_complete` is invoked. A client that repeatedly calls `/identify/start` with different `entity_id` values (or the same one without ever calling `/identify/complete`) will accumulate per-entity snapshots indefinitely. Each snapshot scales with the number of online network clients (potentially hundreds), so under abuse or buggy clients the dict can grow without bound and exhaust memory.
violations.fixPrompt: Add a bound on `_identify_snapshots` in `backend/routes/alexa.py`. Options: (1) enforce a maximum size (e.g. `MAX_IDENTIFY_SNAPSHOTS = 32`) and evict the oldest entry by `ts` before inserting in `identify_start`; (2) proactively prune entries older than 300s on every `identify_start` call rather than only inside `identify_complete`; (3) replace the raw dict with a TTL-bounded structure such as `cachetools.TTLCache(maxsize=N, ttl=300)`. Whichever approach you choose, ensure both stale-time AND maximum-cardinality limits are enforced regardless of which endpoint is called.

violations.title: Module-level discovery/state caches define `CACHE_TTL` but never enforce it
violations.content: The module declares in-memory caches `_discovery_cache`/`_state_cache` along with `_discovery_cache_time`/`_state_cache_time` timestamps and a `CACHE_TTL = 300` constant, but `CACHE_TTL` is never referenced anywhere else in the file. `_refresh_state_cache` (lines 1551-1609) writes to `_state_cache` and updates `_state_cache_time`, yet no reader compares `time.time() - _state_cache_time` against `CACHE_TTL` to expire entries, and there is no invalidation when underlying Deco/Chester state changes (e.g., when a node is added/removed, when WiFi is toggled via the API, or when credentials are updated). If the Lambda endpoints at lines 1539-1548 and 1675-1678 are ever re-enabled, callers would receive indefinitely stale endpoint and state data.
violations.fixPrompt: In `backend/routes/alexa.py`, either remove the unused `_discovery_cache`, `_state_cache`, `_discovery_cache_time`, `_state_cache_time`, and `CACHE_TTL` symbols (lines 30-35) if the disabled Lambda routes are not coming back, or wire up real invalidation: (1) add a helper `_cache_is_fresh(ts)` that returns `time.time() - ts < CACHE_TTL` and have any reader (including a re-enabled `lambda_discover`/`lambda_get_state`) call `_refresh_state_cache` / discovery rebuild when the cache is stale or empty; (2) call an invalidation function that clears `_state_cache`/`_discovery_cache` whenever Deco WiFi, node, or Chester state is mutated via the existing routes (`/api/deco/...`, `/api/chester/...`, settings updates) so source-of-truth changes do not leave clients reading 5+ minute old data.

violations.title: `optimize_network` triggers external mesh optimization without idempotency key
violations.content: The `optimize_network` endpoint calls `deco_service.deco_client.optimize_network()` which triggers an actual network-wide optimization pass on the Deco mesh (channel reassignment, band steering, client re-association). The endpoint accepts no idempotency key and performs no deduplication. Alternatively, enforce a minimum interval between optimization runs (e.g. 30s) and return the prior result if called again within that window.

async def optimize_network() -> Dict[str, Any]:
    """Trigger Deco mesh network optimization.
    Re-evaluates channel assignments, band steering, and client-node associations.
    """
    if deco_service is None or deco_service.deco_client is None:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=503, detail="Deco service not available")
    try:
        result = deco_service.deco_client.optimize_network()
        error_code = result.get("error_code", -1)
        perf = result.get("performance", {})
        client_count = result.get("client_count", 0)
        cpu = perf.get("cpu_usage", "?")
        mem = perf.get("mem_usage", "?")
        return {
            "success": error_code == 0,
            "error_code": error_code,
            "message": f"Network refreshed — {client_count} clients, CPU: {cpu}%, Mem: {mem}%",
            "performance": perf,
            "client_count": client_count,
        }
    except Exception as e:
        logger.error(f"Failed to optimize network: {e}")
        raise HTTPException(status_code=500, detail=f"Failed to optimize network: {str(e)}")

Several mutation endpoints in this same file change data that appears in the topology response — `rename_deco_client` (writes new device/node names), `update_wifi_config` (changes SSID/band settings), `optimize_network` (re-evaluates mesh associations), and `refresh_deco_nodes` (explicitly intended to bypass cache). Even `/nodes/refresh`, whose entire purpose is to bypass the cache, only clears `deco_service.clear_cache()` while leaving the route-level topology cache stale. Users who rename a client or run "Optimize Network" will see no immediate effect in the topology view.

Call it at the end of `refresh_deco_nodes`, `rename_deco_client`, `update_wifi_config`, `optimize_network`, `set_client_mesh`, `auto_name_deco_nodes`, `import_deco_client_names`, and `sync_deco_names_from_alexa` so the next read rebuilds the cache instead of returning stale data.

violations.title: No error-monitoring SDK initialized in FastAPI backend
violations.content: The FastAPI entry point `backend/main.py` imports `fastapi`, `uvicorn`, `logging`, and the application's own modules but does not initialize any error-monitoring SDK (no `sentry_sdk`, `bugsnag`, `ddtrace`, or `opentelemetry` imports anywhere in the backend). All error handling routes through `logger.error(...)` only — see `routes/deco.py`, `routes/alexa.py`, `routes/events.py`, `services/digest_service.py`, `services/health_service.py`, `services/retention_scheduler.py`, etc. There is no global exception handler that ships unhandled exceptions to an external service, and no Express/FastAPI middleware that captures stack traces. Background tasks like `services/polling_service.py`, `services/hiboost_scheduler.py`, and `services/speedtest_scheduler.py` swallow errors with `logger.error(str(e))`, meaning failures in long-running async loops will only surface in local logs.
violations.fixPrompt: Add `sentry-sdk[fastapi]` (or an equivalent) to `requirements.txt`, initialize it at the top of `backend/main.py` using `sentry_sdk.init(dsn=os.getenv('SENTRY_DSN'), integrations=[FastApiIntegration(), AsyncioIntegration()])` guarded by the env var, and ensure background scheduler tasks (`hiboost_scheduler`, `speedtest_scheduler`, `retention_scheduler`, `polling_service`) report exceptions via `sentry_sdk.capture_exception(e)` in their error branches.

violations.title: No HTTP/DB performance metrics instrumentation in FastAPI app
violations.content: `backend/main.py` configures CORS, static files, and routers but never installs any performance-metrics middleware. There is no import of `prometheus_client`, `prometheus-fastapi-instrumentator`, `statsd`, `opentelemetry`, or similar across the backend. As a result, HTTP request latency, status-code distributions, and throughput per route (`/api/devices`, `/api/sse`, `/api/speedtest`, etc.) are not measured. SQLite query duration in `db.py` is unmeasured, and queue-style components like the SSE subscriber list in `routes/sse.py` (`_subscribers`, `asyncio.Queue`) and the background pollers in `services/polling_service.py`, `services/hiboost_scheduler.py`, `services/speedtest_scheduler.py` expose no depth/processing-rate gauges. Without metrics, regressions in scan time, speed-test cadence, or SSE backpressure will only be noticed when users complain.
violations.fixPrompt: Install `prometheus-fastapi-instrumentator` and in `backend/main.py` add: `from prometheus_fastapi_instrumentator import Instrumentator; Instrumentator().instrument(app).expose(app, endpoint='/metrics')`. Wrap key SQLite calls in `db.py` (or a thin helper) with a `Histogram('homesentinel_db_query_seconds', ['op'])` timer. Add gauges for SSE subscriber count in `routes/sse.py` (`Gauge('sse_subscribers').set(len(_subscribers))`) and for queue depths / last-run-age in `polling_service.py`, `hiboost_scheduler.py`, and `speedtest_scheduler.py`.

violations.title: No correlation/trace ID middleware registered in FastAPI app
violations.content: `backend/main.py` imports `fastapi.middleware.cors` and `middleware.auth` but registers no request-ID/correlation middleware. None of the route handlers (`get_devices`, `get_events`, `get_alerts`, `trigger_manual_scan`, `update_device`, etc.) accept a `Request` object to extract or generate a correlation ID, and there is no module-level extraction visible. Although `services.correlation_service` is imported, the absence of a global middleware means HTTP requests are not tagged with a trace ID that can propagate to logs, inter-service calls (`deco_client`, `chester_client`, `alexa_client`, `alarm_com_client`, `hiboost_client`), or SSE events.
violations.fixPrompt: Add a request-correlation middleware in `backend/main.py` (or `backend/middleware/`) that, for every incoming request: (1) reads `X-Request-Id`/`X-Correlation-Id` headers or generates a UUID, (2) stores it in a `contextvars.ContextVar` consumed by logging filters, (3) attaches it to the response as `X-Request-Id`. Register it via `app.add_middleware(...)` before CORS. Propagate the correlation ID into outbound client calls (`deco_client`, `chester_client`, `alexa_client`, etc.) via headers, and include it in log statements using a `logging.Filter` that injects `correlation_id` into each `LogRecord`.

violations.title: `create_device_group` is non-idempotent — retries create duplicate groups
violations.content: `create_device_group` is a POST endpoint that generates a fresh `uuid.uuid4()` server-side on every invocation and calls `group_repo.create_group` without checking for an existing group with the same `name`, and without accepting an idempotency key from the client. If the client (or any intermediate proxy/network layer) retries the request after a transient failure or timeout, a duplicate group will be created with a new ID but identical user-visible name. The frontend cannot safely retry a failed group creation without risking duplicate rows.
violations.fixPrompt: Make `create_device_group` idempotent. Either (a) accept an `Idempotency-Key` header, store the resulting `group_id` in a short-lived cache keyed by header value, and return the same response for repeated keys; or (b) enforce a unique constraint on the group `name` (per tenant) at the DB level and return the existing record's ID on conflict instead of creating a duplicate.

violations.content: `publish_event(event_type: str, data: dict)` in `backend/routes/sse.py` publishes events to subscribers without accepting or attaching the originating request's correlation/trace ID. The `_event_generator` and `sse_events` handler likewise lack request-context identifiers in their stream payloads.

violations.title: `authorize` issues a new auth code on every call with no idempotency
violations.content: The OAuth `authorize` endpoint generates a fresh `code` via `secrets.token_urlsafe(32)` and stores it in `_auth_codes` on every invocation. There is no idempotency key, no deduplication by `(client_id, state)` tuple, and no rate limiting. While OAuth spec permits issuing new codes per request, the combination here — auto-approve with no consent gate and unbounded code issuance — means a retried or replayed authorize request will silently grow `_auth_codes` and produce divergent redirect URLs the client must reconcile. For a personal skill this is low blast radius, but on retry the second code supersedes the first, which can produce confusing auth failures if the first redirect actually completed.
violations.fixPrompt: In `backend/routes/oauth.py`, deduplicate authorization codes within a short window: if an authorize call arrives with the same `(client_id, redirect_uri, state)` as a recent (<60s) request, return the existing code rather than minting a new one. Also add a periodic pruning step or TTL-based cleanup for `_auth_codes` to prevent unbounded growth on retry storms.

async def authorize(
    client_id: str,
    response_type: str,
    redirect_uri: str,
    state: str = "",
    scope: str = "",
):
    """OAuth authorization endpoint — shows consent page and redirects with auth code."""
    if client_id != CLIENT_ID:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail="Invalid client_id")
    if response_type != "code":
        raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail="Only 'code' response_type supported")

    # Generate auth code
    code = secrets.token_urlsafe(32)
    _auth_codes[code] = {
        "redirect_uri": redirect_uri,
        "expires": time.time() + 300,  # 5 min
        "client_id": client_id,
    }

    logger.info("OAuth authorize: issuing code for redirect to %s", redirect_uri)

    # Auto-approve (personal skill — no login needed)
    # Build redirect with code and state
    separator = "&" if "?" in redirect_uri else "?"
    redirect_url = f"{redirect_uri}{separator}{urlencode({'code': code, 'state': state})}"

    return RedirectResponse(url=redirect_url)

violations.title: `token` refresh_token grant issues new access token on every retry
violations.content: The `refresh_token` grant branch in `token` mints a brand-new `access_token` on every call (line 129) and stores it in `_access_tokens` without any idempotency check. A retried token-refresh request — common on flaky network connections from Alexa/Lambda — will produce multiple valid access tokens for the same refresh, bloating `_access_tokens` and making session revocation/auditing impossible. There is no idempotency key support and no dedup of in-flight refreshes for the same refresh token.
violations.fixPrompt: In the `refresh_token` branch of `token` in `backend/routes/oauth.py`, track recent refreshes keyed by the refresh token string with a short TTL (e.g. 10 seconds). If the same refresh token is presented within the window, return the previously issued access token instead of minting a new one. Alternatively, accept an `Idempotency-Key` header and cache the response by that key.

violations.title: Unbounded in-memory OAuth token stores
violations.content: The module-level dicts `_auth_codes`, `_access_tokens`, and `_refresh_tokens` accumulate entries indefinitely with no size limit or eviction policy. `_auth_codes` is popped on successful redemption but unredeemed codes remain forever; `_access_tokens` and `_refresh_tokens` are never cleaned up at all — every call to `/oauth/token` adds new entries (e.g., refresh-token grants in lines 129-133 add a new access token without removing the old one). Under sustained load — for example, an Alexa skill or attacker repeatedly hitting `/oauth/authorize` and `/oauth/token` — these dicts will grow without bound, eventually causing OOM. Expired entries are detected only when explicitly looked up, never proactively reaped.
violations.fixPrompt: In `backend/routes/oauth.py`, add a periodic cleanup task (e.g., a background asyncio task started at app startup) that walks `_auth_codes`, `_access_tokens`, and `_refresh_tokens` and removes entries whose `expires` timestamp is in the past. Alternatively, replace the raw dicts with a TTL-aware structure (e.g., `cachetools.TTLCache`) sized to a reasonable maximum to bound memory even under abuse. When issuing a refresh-token grant, also evict any prior access token associated with the same refresh token.

violations.title: `run_speedtest` mutation endpoint lacks idempotency key
violations.content: The `run_speedtest` endpoint triggers a side-effecting operation (SSH into the Chester router and execute a speed test) on every invocation without accepting an idempotency key or checking for an in-flight test. If a client or proxy retries due to a transient network error or timeout, the handler will SSH in and run another full speed test, consuming bandwidth, contending for the router's SSH session, and producing duplicate rows in the speed test history plus duplicate insight generation. There is no deduplication window, no lock against concurrent invocations, and no idempotency-key-based replay of the prior result.
violations.fixPrompt: Add idempotency support to `run_speedtest` in `backend/routes/speedtest.py`. Accept an optional `Idempotency-Key` header; if a recent (e.g., within the last few minutes) test was executed with the same key, return the cached result rather than running a new speed test. Additionally, guard against concurrent invocations with an in-flight flag or asyncio lock so that a retry while a test is in progress returns the in-progress result instead of starting a second SSH speed test.

violations.title: `generate_insights` mutation endpoint is not idempotent
violations.content: The `generate_insights` endpoint manually triggers insight generation from accumulated test data without an idempotency key or deduplication check. Each call invokes `speedtest_service.generate_insights`, which produces and persists insights. Retries (from clients, proxies, or browser refreshes) will run insight generation repeatedly, likely producing duplicate or near-duplicate insight rows for the same underlying data window. The handler returns `generated: len(insights)` but does not dedupe against insights already produced for the same observation window.
violations.fixPrompt: Add idempotency to `generate_insights` in `backend/routes/speedtest.py`. Either accept an `Idempotency-Key` header and cache the response for that key, or have `speedtest_service.generate_insights` deduplicate based on the observation window / content hash so repeated calls within the same period return the existing insights rather than creating new ones. Also consider using a lock to serialize concurrent generations.

violations.title: `request_otp` sends an OTP notification with no deduplication
violations.content: `request_otp` calls `alarm_com_client.request_otp(body.method)` which causes Alarm.com to deliver a one-time password to the user via app push, email, or SMS. There is no idempotency key, no rate-limiting, and no deduplication of recent OTP requests for the same `(user, method)` pair. A client retry triggered by a flaky network — or an automatic retry from the HTTP infrastructure — will cause a second OTP message to be sent to the user, which is annoying at best and can trigger upstream provider throttling/abuse detection at worst.
violations.fixPrompt: Add deduplication to `request_otp`. Track the timestamp of the last OTP request per `(session, method)` in memory or the DB and short-circuit (returning the cached prior response) if a request was issued within a short window (e.g., 30–60 seconds). Alternatively, accept and honor an `Idempotency-Key` header so retries of the same logical request never deliver a second message.

violations.title: `send_partition_command` arms/disarms with no idempotency protection
violations.content: `send_partition_command` dispatches `arm_away`, `arm_stay`, or `disarm` to a security alarm partition with no idempotency key and no check that the partition is not already in the requested state. While arming an already-armed partition is usually a no-op upstream, this is a security-critical mutation that frequently triggers audible chimes, push notifications, and audit-log entries on the alarm provider's side. If the request times out and is retried, the user receives duplicate notifications and the alarm audit log shows duplicate state-change attempts, which can mask real activity.
violations.fixPrompt: Make `send_partition_command` retry-safe. Either accept an `Idempotency-Key` header and cache the response keyed by it for a short window, or fetch the partition's current state before issuing the command and short-circuit (returning the cached current state) when it already matches the requested `arm_away`/`arm_stay`/`disarm` target.

Inter-service calls without a forwarded correlation ID make it impossible to trace an Alexa voice command from Lambda invocation through backend state lookups to device-control responses.
violations.fixPrompt: Update the Alexa Lambda handlers in `backend/routes/alexa.py` to accept a `Request` parameter, extract the correlation ID from headers such as `X-Amzn-Trace-Id` or `X-Request-Id` (fallback to UUID), and store it on a context var. violations.title: `import_alexa_mac_addresses` external API calls lack retry logic

On a transient failure the function catches the exception and proceeds with `device_macs = []`, silently producing an empty import result instead of retrying. Given this is a manual user-initiated operation and the API is known to be flaky, transient failures should retry with exponential backoff before falling through to the empty-result path.

violations.content: `identify_complete` in `routes/alexa.py` calls `deco_client.get_client_list_local` (an HTTP call to the local Deco router API) without retry. Any transient network error causes an immediate 500 response, requiring the user to restart the entire identify flow (which has a 5-minute snapshot window). Local-router API calls commonly experience transient failures and should retry with brief backoff.

violations.title: `import_alexa_mac_addresses` keeps iterating Alexa API on failure
violations.content: `import_alexa_mac_addresses` calls `alexa_client.get_all_device_macs()` which internally iterates `devices-v2` and calls `/api/device-wifi-details` for every device. There is no circuit breaker or maximum-failure threshold: if Amazon returns errors for many devices in sequence (e.g. cookie expiry, rate limiting, regional outage), the loop continues hammering the upstream endpoint and only catches a single top-level `Exception`. This can exhaust the shared `requests.Session` connection pool and amplify a partial Alexa outage into a full request stall on this route.
violations.fixPrompt: Add a circuit breaker / failure-budget around the Alexa MAC enumeration in `backend/services/alexa_client.py:get_all_device_macs` (or wrap it in `routes/alexa.py:import_alexa_mac_addresses`). After N consecutive `device-wifi-details` failures or a configurable error rate, abort the iteration early and return a partial result with an explicit `circuit_open` status so callers fail fast instead of continuing to call the failing endpoint.

violations.title: `_identify_snapshots` dict grows unbounded across `identify_start` calls
violations.content: The module-level `_identify_snapshots: Dict[str, Dict]` cache at line 960 stores a full Deco client-list snapshot (every online MAC + name + IP) per `entity_id` whenever `POST /smart-home/{entity_id}/identify/start` is called (line 990). Entries are only removed in two places: when `identify_complete` runs successfully (line 1064), and when `identify_complete` detects a stale snapshot (line 1019). There is no background sweep, no `__len__` cap, no LRU eviction, and the staleness check only fires when `identify_complete` is invoked. A client that repeatedly calls `/identify/start` with different `entity_id` values (or the same one without ever calling `/identify/complete`) will accumulate per-entity snapshots indefinitely. violations.title: `optimize_network` triggers external mesh optimization without idempotency key
violations.content: The `optimize_network` endpoint calls `deco_service.deco_client.optimize_network()` which triggers an actual network-wide optimization pass on the Deco mesh (channel reassignment, band steering, client re-association). The endpoint accepts no idempotency key and performs no deduplication. If a client or proxy retries this request on timeout/transient failure, the underlying mesh optimization will run multiple times — each pass can transiently disrupt client connectivity, so duplicate executions amplify user-visible disruption. There is also no rate limiting visible on this route.
violations.fixPrompt: Add idempotency support to `optimize_network` in `backend/routes/deco.py`. Accept an optional `Idempotency-Key` header, and use an in-memory or DB-backed short-lived cache (e.g. keyed by the header value with a 60-second TTL) to return the cached prior response on retry instead of re-invoking `deco_service.deco_client.optimize_network()`. Alternatively, enforce a minimum interval between optimization runs (e.g. 30s) and return the prior result if called again within that window.
violations.snippet:
async def optimize_network() -> Dict[str, Any]:
    """Trigger Deco mesh network optimization.
    Re-evaluates channel assignments, band steering, and client-node associations.
    """
    if deco_service is None or deco_service.deco_client is None:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=503, detail="Deco service not available")
    try:
        result = deco_service.deco_client.optimize_network()
        error_code = result.get("error_code", -1)
        perf = result.get("performance", {})
        client_count = result.get("client_count", 0)
        cpu = perf.get("cpu_usage", "?")
        mem = perf.get("mem_usage", "?")
        return {
            "success": error_code == 0,
            "error_code": error_code,
            "message": f"Network refreshed — {client_count} clients, CPU: {cpu}%, Mem: {mem}%",
            "performance": perf,
            "client_count": client_count,
        }
    except Exception as e:
        logger.error(f"Failed to optimize network: {e}")
        raise HTTPException(status_code=500, detail=f"Failed to optimize network: {str(e)}")

violations.title: Topology route cache lacks event-based invalidation on mutations
violations.content: The module-level caches `_topology_json_cache` and `_topology_svg_cache` use only a 60-second TTL (`TOPOLOGY_ROUTE_CACHE_TTL`) for invalidation. Several mutation endpoints in this same file change data that appears in the topology response — `rename_deco_client` (writes new device/node names), `update_wifi_config` (changes SSID/band settings), `optimize_network` (re-evaluates mesh associations), and `refresh_deco_nodes` (explicitly intended to bypass cache). None of these call any invalidation routine on `_topology_json_cache` / `_topology_svg_cache`, so `GET /topology` and `GET /topology-graph` can serve stale data for up to 60 seconds after a user-initiated change. Even `/nodes/refresh`, whose entire purpose is to bypass the cache, only clears `deco_service.clear_cache()` while leaving the route-level topology cache stale. Users who rename a client or run "Optimize Network" will see no immediate effect in the topology view.

Call it at the end of `refresh_deco_nodes`, `rename_deco_client`, `update_wifi_config`, `optimize_network`, `set_client_mesh`, `auto_name_deco_nodes`, `import_deco_client_names`, and `sync_deco_names_from_alexa` so the next read rebuilds the cache instead of returning stale data.

violations.title: `authorize` issues a new auth code on every call with no idempotency
violations.content: The OAuth `authorize` endpoint generates a fresh `code` via `secrets.token_urlsafe(32)` and stores it in `_auth_codes` on every invocation. There is no idempotency key, no deduplication by `(client_id, state)` tuple, and no rate limiting. While OAuth spec permits issuing new codes per request, the combination here — auto-approve with no consent gate and unbounded code issuance — means a retried or replayed authorize request will silently grow `_auth_codes` and produce divergent redirect URLs the client must reconcile. For a personal skill this is low blast radius, but on retry the second code supersedes the first, which can produce confusing auth failures if the first redirect actually completed.
violations.fixPrompt: In `backend/routes/oauth.py`, deduplicate authorization codes within a short window: if an authorize call arrives with the same `(client_id, redirect_uri, state)` as a recent (<60s) request, return the existing code rather than minting a new one. Also add a periodic pruning step or TTL-based cleanup for `_auth_codes` to prevent unbounded growth on retry storms.
violations.snippet:
async def authorize(
    client_id: str,
    response_type: str,
    redirect_uri: str,
    state: str = "",
    scope: str = "",
):
    """OAuth authorization endpoint — shows consent page and redirects with auth code."""
    if client_id != CLIENT_ID:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail="Invalid client_id")
    if response_type != "code":
        raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail="Only 'code' response_type supported")

    # Generate auth code
    code = secrets.token_urlsafe(32)
    _auth_codes[code] = {
        "redirect_uri": redirect_uri,
        "expires": time.time() + 300,  # 5 min
        "client_id": client_id,
    }

    logger.info("OAuth authorize: issuing code for redirect to %s", redirect_uri)

    # Auto-approve (personal skill — no login needed)
    # Build redirect with code and state
    separator = "&" if "?" in redirect_uri else "?"
    redirect_url = f"{redirect_uri}{separator}{urlencode({'code': code, 'state': state})}"

    return RedirectResponse(url=redirect_url)

violations.title: `token` refresh_token grant issues new access token on every retry
violations.content: The `refresh_token` grant branch in `token` mints a brand-new `access_token` on every call (line 129) and stores it in `_access_tokens` without any idempotency check. A retried token-refresh request — common on flaky network connections from Alexa/Lambda — will produce multiple valid access tokens for the same refresh, bloating `_access_tokens` and making session revocation/auditing impossible. There is no idempotency key support and no dedup of in-flight refreshes for the same refresh token.
violations.fixPrompt: In the `refresh_token` branch of `token` in `backend/routes/oauth.py`, track recent refreshes keyed by the refresh token string with a short TTL (e.g. 10 seconds). If the same refresh token is presented within the window, return the previously issued access token instead of minting a new one. Alternatively, accept an `Idempotency-Key` header and cache the response by that key.

violations.title: Unbounded in-memory OAuth token stores
violations.content: The module-level dicts `_auth_codes`, `_access_tokens`, and `_refresh_tokens` accumulate entries indefinitely with no size limit or eviction policy. `_auth_codes` is popped on successful redemption but unredeemed codes remain forever; `_access_tokens` and `_refresh_tokens` are never cleaned up at all — every call to `/oauth/token` adds new entries (e.g., refresh-token grants in lines 129-133 add a new access token without removing the old one). Under sustained load — for example, an Alexa skill or attacker repeatedly hitting `/oauth/authorize` and `/oauth/token` — these dicts will grow without bound, eventually causing OOM. Expired entries are detected only when explicitly looked up, never proactively reaped.
violations.fixPrompt: In `backend/routes/oauth.py`, add a periodic cleanup task (e.g., a background asyncio task started at app startup) that walks `_auth_codes`, `_access_tokens`, and `_refresh_tokens` and removes entries whose `expires` timestamp is in the past. Alternatively, replace the raw dicts with a TTL-aware structure (e.g., `cachetools.TTLCache`) sized to a reasonable maximum to bound memory even under abuse. When issuing a refresh-token grant, also evict any prior access token associated with the same refresh token.

violations.title: `run_speedtest` mutation endpoint lacks idempotency key
violations.content: The `run_speedtest` endpoint triggers a side-effecting operation (SSH into the Chester router and execute a speed test) on every invocation without accepting an idempotency key or checking for an in-flight test. If a client or proxy retries due to a transient network error or timeout, the handler will SSH in and run another full speed test, consuming bandwidth, contending for the router's SSH session, and producing duplicate rows in the speed test history plus duplicate insight generation. There is no deduplication window, no lock against concurrent invocations, and no idempotency-key-based replay of the prior result.
violations.fixPrompt: Add idempotency support to `run_speedtest` in `backend/routes/speedtest.py`. Accept an optional `Idempotency-Key` header; if a recent (e.g., within the last few minutes) test was executed with the same key, return the cached result rather than running a new speed test. Additionally, guard against concurrent invocations with an in-flight flag or asyncio lock so that a retry while a test is in progress returns the in-progress result instead of starting a second SSH speed test.

violations.title: `generate_insights` mutation endpoint is not idempotent
violations.content: The `generate_insights` endpoint manually triggers insight generation from accumulated test data without an idempotency key or deduplication check. Each call invokes `speedtest_service.generate_insights`, which produces and persists insights. Retries (from clients, proxies, or browser refreshes) will run insight generation repeatedly, likely producing duplicate or near-duplicate insight rows for the same underlying data window. The handler returns `generated: len(insights)` but does not dedupe against insights already produced for the same observation window.
violations.fixPrompt: Add idempotency to `generate_insights` in `backend/routes/speedtest.py`. Either accept an `Idempotency-Key` header and cache the response for that key, or have `speedtest_service.generate_insights` deduplicate based on the observation window / content hash so repeated calls within the same period return the existing insights rather than creating new ones. Also consider using a lock to serialize concurrent generations.

async def generate_insights() -> Dict[str, Any]:
    """Manually trigger insight generation from accumulated test data."""
    if speedtest_service is None:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=500, detail="Speed test service not initialized")

    import asyncio
    loop = asyncio.get_event_loop()
    insights = await loop.run_in_executor(None, speedtest_service.generate_insights)
    return {
        "generated": len(insights),
        "insights": insights,
    }

violations.title: `request_otp` sends an OTP notification with no deduplication
violations.content: `request_otp` calls `alarm_com_client.request_otp(body.method)` which causes Alarm.com to deliver a one-time password to the user via app push, email, or SMS. There is no idempotency key, no rate-limiting, and no deduplication of recent OTP requests for the same `(user, method)` pair. A client retry triggered by a flaky network — or an automatic retry from the HTTP infrastructure — will cause a second OTP message to be sent to the user, which is annoying at best and can trigger upstream provider throttling/abuse detection at worst.
violations.fixPrompt: Add deduplication to `request_otp`. Track the timestamp of the last OTP request per `(session, method)` in memory or the DB and short-circuit (returning the cached prior response) if a request was issued within a short window (e.g., 30–60 seconds). Alternatively, accept and honor an `Idempotency-Key` header so retries of the same logical request never deliver a second message.

violations.title: `send_partition_command` arms/disarms with no idempotency protection
violations.content: `send_partition_command` dispatches `arm_away`, `arm_stay`, or `disarm` to a security alarm partition with no idempotency key and no check that the partition is not already in the requested state. While arming an already-armed partition is usually a no-op upstream, this is a security-critical mutation that frequently triggers audible chimes, push notifications, and audit-log entries on the alarm provider's side. If the request times out and is retried, the user receives duplicate notifications and the alarm audit log shows duplicate state-change attempts, which can mask real activity.
violations.fixPrompt: Make `send_partition_command` retry-safe. Either accept an `Idempotency-Key` header and cache the response keyed by it for a short window, or fetch the partition's current state before issuing the command and short-circuit (returning the cached current state) when it already matches the requested `arm_away`/`arm_stay`/`disarm` target.

violations.title: Alexa Lambda integration handlers do not propagate a correlation ID
violations.content: The Alexa Lambda bridge handlers (`lambda_discover`, `lambda_refresh_cache`, `lambda_get_state`, `lambda_command`, `lambda_store_token`, `lambda_accept_grant`) in `backend/routes/alexa.py` cross a service boundary (AWS Lambda → backend) but the imports list shows no `correlation_service` and the function signatures do not include `Request` for header extraction. Inter-service calls without a forwarded correlation ID make it impossible to trace an Alexa voice command from Lambda invocation through backend state lookups to device-control responses.
violations.fixPrompt: Update the Alexa Lambda handlers in `backend/routes/alexa.py` to accept a `Request` parameter, extract the correlation ID from headers such as `X-Amzn-Trace-Id` or `X-Request-Id` (fallback to UUID), and store it on a context var. In `lambda/lambda_function.py`, generate and forward a request ID header when calling the backend. Use the same ID in all `logger` calls within these handlers and include it in the response body's `event.header` for Alexa-side correlation.

violations.title: `import_alexa_mac_addresses` external API calls lack retry logic
violations.content: `import_alexa_mac_addresses` in `routes/alexa.py` calls `alexa_client.get_all_device_macs()` and `alexa_client.get_echo_devices_web()` against the external Alexa Web API. On a transient failure the function catches the exception and proceeds with `device_macs = []`, silently producing an empty import result instead of retrying. Given this is a manual user-initiated operation and the API is known to be flaky, transient failures should retry with exponential backoff before falling through to the empty-result path.
violations.fixPrompt: Wrap `alexa_client.get_all_device_macs()` and `alexa_client.get_echo_devices_web()` in retry logic with exponential backoff (2-3 attempts) for transient errors. Only fall through to the empty-result branch after retries are exhausted.

violations.title: `identify_complete` Deco API call lacks retry logic
violations.content: `identify_complete` in `routes/alexa.py` calls `deco_client.get_client_list_local` (an HTTP call to the local Deco router API) without retry. Any transient network error causes an immediate 500 response, requiring the user to restart the entire identify flow (which has a 5-minute snapshot window). Local-router API calls commonly experience transient failures and should retry with brief backoff.
violations.fixPrompt: Add retry logic (2-3 attempts with short exponential backoff) around the `await loop.run_in_executor(None, deco_client.get_client_list_local)` call in `identify_complete` to handle transient failures from the Deco local API.

violations.title: `import_alexa_mac_addresses` keeps iterating Alexa API on failure
violations.content: `import_alexa_mac_addresses` calls `alexa_client.get_all_device_macs()` which internally iterates `devices-v2` and calls `/api/device-wifi-details` for every device. There is no circuit breaker or maximum-failure threshold: if Amazon returns errors for many devices in sequence (e.g. cookie expiry, rate limiting, regional outage), the loop continues hammering the upstream endpoint and only catches a single top-level `Exception`. This can exhaust the shared `requests.Session` connection pool and amplify a partial Alexa outage into a full request stall on this route.
violations.fixPrompt: Add a circuit breaker / failure-budget around the Alexa MAC enumeration in `backend/services/alexa_client.py:get_all_device_macs` (or wrap it in `routes/alexa.py:import_alexa_mac_addresses`). After N consecutive `device-wifi-details` failures or a configurable error rate, abort the iteration early and return a partial result with an explicit `circuit_open` status so callers fail fast instead of continuing to call the failing endpoint.

violations.title: `_identify_snapshots` dict grows unbounded across `identify_start` calls
violations.content: The module-level `_identify_snapshots: Dict[str, Dict]` cache at line 960 stores a full Deco client-list snapshot (every online MAC + name + IP) per `entity_id` whenever `POST /smart-home/{entity_id}/identify/start` is called (line 990). Entries are only removed in two places: when `identify_complete` runs successfully (line 1064), and when `identify_complete` detects a stale snapshot (line 1019). There is no background sweep, no `__len__` cap, no LRU eviction, and the staleness check only fires when `identify_complete` is invoked. A client that repeatedly calls `/identify/start` with different `entity_id` values (or the same one without ever calling `/identify/complete`) will accumulate per-entity snapshots indefinitely. Each snapshot scales with the number of online network clients (potentially hundreds), so under abuse or buggy clients the dict can grow without bound and exhaust memory.
violations.fixPrompt: Add a bound on `_identify_snapshots` in `backend/routes/alexa.py`. Options: (1) enforce a maximum size (e.g. `MAX_IDENTIFY_SNAPSHOTS = 32`) and evict the oldest entry by `ts` before inserting in `identify_start`; (2) proactively prune entries older than 300s on every `identify_start` call rather than only inside `identify_complete`; (3) replace the raw dict with a TTL-bounded structure such as `cachetools.TTLCache(maxsize=N, ttl=300)`. Whichever approach you choose, ensure both stale-time AND maximum-cardinality limits are enforced regardless of which endpoint is called.

violations.title: Module-level discovery/state caches define `CACHE_TTL` but never enforce it
violations.content: The module declares in-memory caches `_discovery_cache`/`_state_cache` along with `_discovery_cache_time`/`_state_cache_time` timestamps and a `CACHE_TTL = 300` constant, but `CACHE_TTL` is never referenced anywhere else in the file. `_refresh_state_cache` (lines 1551-1609) writes to `_state_cache` and updates `_state_cache_time`, yet no reader compares `time.time() - _state_cache_time` against `CACHE_TTL` to expire entries, and there is no invalidation when underlying Deco/Chester state changes (e.g., when a node is added/removed, when WiFi is toggled via the API, or when credentials are updated). If the Lambda endpoints at lines 1539-1548 and 1675-1678 are ever re-enabled, callers would receive indefinitely stale endpoint and state data.
violations.fixPrompt: In `backend/routes/alexa.py`, either remove the unused `_discovery_cache`, `_state_cache`, `_discovery_cache_time`, `_state_cache_time`, and `CACHE_TTL` symbols (lines 30-35) if the disabled Lambda routes are not coming back, or wire up real invalidation: (1) add a helper `_cache_is_fresh(ts)` that returns `time.time() - ts < CACHE_TTL` and have any reader (including a re-enabled `lambda_discover`/`lambda_get_state`) call `_refresh_state_cache` / discovery rebuild when the cache is stale or empty; (2) call an invalidation function that clears `_state_cache`/`_discovery_cache` whenever Deco WiFi, node, or Chester state is mutated via the existing routes (`/api/deco/...`, `/api/chester/...`, settings updates) so source-of-truth changes do not leave clients reading 5+ minute old data.

violations.title: No error-monitoring SDK initialized in FastAPI backend
violations.content: The FastAPI entry point `backend/main.py` imports `fastapi`, `uvicorn`, `logging`, and the application's own modules but does not initialize any error-monitoring SDK (no `sentry_sdk`, `bugsnag`, `ddtrace`, or `opentelemetry` imports anywhere in the backend). All error handling routes through `logger.error(...)` only — see `routes/deco.py`, `routes/alexa.py`, `routes/events.py`, `services/digest_service.py`, `services/health_service.py`, `services/retention_scheduler.py`, etc. There is no global exception handler that ships unhandled exceptions to an external service, and no Express/FastAPI middleware that captures stack traces. Background tasks like `services/polling_service.py`, `services/hiboost_scheduler.py`, and `services/speedtest_scheduler.py` swallow errors with `logger.error(str(e))`, meaning failures in long-running async loops will only surface in local logs.
violations.fixPrompt: Add `sentry-sdk[fastapi]` (or an equivalent) to `requirements.txt`, initialize it at the top of `backend/main.py` using `sentry_sdk.init(dsn=os.getenv('SENTRY_DSN'), integrations=[FastApiIntegration(), AsyncioIntegration()])` guarded by the env var, and ensure background scheduler tasks (`hiboost_scheduler`, `speedtest_scheduler`, `retention_scheduler`, `polling_service`) report exceptions via `sentry_sdk.capture_exception(e)` in their error branches.

violations.title: No HTTP/DB performance metrics instrumentation in FastAPI app
violations.content: `backend/main.py` configures CORS, static files, and routers but never installs any performance-metrics middleware. There is no import of `prometheus_client`, `prometheus-fastapi-instrumentator`, `statsd`, `opentelemetry`, or similar across the backend. As a result, HTTP request latency, status-code distributions, and throughput per route (`/api/devices`, `/api/sse`, `/api/speedtest`, etc.) are not measured. SQLite query duration in `db.py` is unmeasured, and queue-style components like the SSE subscriber list in `routes/sse.py` (`_subscribers`, `asyncio.Queue`) and the background pollers in `services/polling_service.py`, `services/hiboost_scheduler.py`, `services/speedtest_scheduler.py` expose no depth/processing-rate gauges. Without metrics, regressions in scan time, speed-test cadence, or SSE backpressure will only be noticed when users complain.
violations.fixPrompt: Install `prometheus-fastapi-instrumentator` and in `backend/main.py` add: `from prometheus_fastapi_instrumentator import Instrumentator; Instrumentator().instrument(app).expose(app, endpoint='/metrics')`. Wrap key SQLite calls in `db.py` (or a thin helper) with a `Histogram('homesentinel_db_query_seconds', ['op'])` timer. Add gauges for SSE subscriber count in `routes/sse.py` (`Gauge('sse_subscribers').set(len(_subscribers))`) and for queue depths / last-run-age in `polling_service.py`, `hiboost_scheduler.py`, and `speedtest_scheduler.py`.

violations.title: No correlation/trace ID middleware registered in FastAPI app
violations.content: `backend/main.py` imports `fastapi.middleware.cors` and `middleware.auth` but registers no request-ID/correlation middleware. None of the route handlers (`get_devices`, `get_events`, `get_alerts`, `trigger_manual_scan`, `update_device`, etc.) accept a `Request` object to extract or generate a correlation ID, and there is no module-level extraction visible. Although `services.correlation_service` is imported, the absence of a global middleware means HTTP requests are not tagged with a trace ID that can propagate to logs, inter-service calls (`deco_client`, `chester_client`, `alexa_client`, `alarm_com_client`, `hiboost_client`), or SSE events.
violations.fixPrompt: Add a request-correlation middleware in `backend/main.py` (or `backend/middleware/`) that, for every incoming request: (1) reads `X-Request-Id`/`X-Correlation-Id` headers or generates a UUID, (2) stores it in a `contextvars.ContextVar` consumed by logging filters, (3) attaches it to the response as `X-Request-Id`. Register it via `app.add_middleware(...)` before CORS. Propagate the correlation ID into outbound client calls (`deco_client`, `chester_client`, `alexa_client`, etc.) via headers, and include it in log statements using a `logging.Filter` that injects `correlation_id` into each `LogRecord`.

violations.title: `create_device_group` is non-idempotent — retries create duplicate groups
violations.content: `create_device_group` is a POST endpoint that generates a fresh `uuid.uuid4()` server-side on every invocation and calls `group_repo.create_group` without checking for an existing group with the same `name`, and without accepting an idempotency key from the client. If the client (or any intermediate proxy/network layer) retries the request after a transient failure or timeout, a duplicate group will be created with a new ID but identical user-visible name. The frontend cannot safely retry a failed group creation without risking duplicate rows.
violations.fixPrompt: Make `create_device_group` idempotent. Either (a) accept an `Idempotency-Key` header, store the resulting `group_id` in a short-lived cache keyed by header value, and return the same response for repeated keys; or (b) enforce a unique constraint on the group `name` (per tenant) at the DB level and return the existing record's ID on conflict instead of creating a duplicate.

violations.title: `optimize_network` triggers external mesh optimization without idempotency key
violations.content: The `optimize_network` endpoint calls `deco_service.deco_client.optimize_network()` which triggers an actual network-wide optimization pass on the Deco mesh (channel reassignment, band steering, client re-association). The endpoint accepts no idempotency key and performs no deduplication. If a client or proxy retries this request on timeout/transient failure, the underlying mesh optimization will run multiple times — each pass can transiently disrupt client connectivity, so duplicate executions amplify user-visible disruption. violations.title: `authorize` issues a new auth code on every call with no idempotency
violations.content: The OAuth `authorize` endpoint generates a fresh `code` via `secrets.token_urlsafe(32)` and stores it in `_auth_codes` on every invocation. There is no idempotency key, no deduplication by `(client_id, state)` tuple, and no rate limiting. While OAuth spec permits issuing new codes per request, the combination here — auto-approve with no consent gate and unbounded code issuance — means a retried or replayed authorize request will silently grow `_auth_codes` and produce divergent redirect URLs the client must reconcile. For a personal skill this is low blast radius, but on retry the second code supersedes the first, which can produce confusing auth failures if the first redirect actually completed.
violations.fixPrompt: In `backend/routes/oauth.py`, deduplicate authorization codes within a short window: if an authorize call arrives with the same `(client_id, redirect_uri, state)` as a recent (<60s) request, return the existing code rather than minting a new one. Also add a periodic pruning step or TTL-based cleanup for `_auth_codes` to prevent unbounded growth on retry storms.

async def authorize(
    client_id: str,
    response_type: str,
    redirect_uri: str,
    state: str = "",
    scope: str = "",
):
    """OAuth authorization endpoint — shows consent page and redirects with auth code."""
    if client_id != CLIENT_ID:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail="Invalid client_id")
    if response_type != "code":
        raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail="Only 'code' response_type supported")

    # Generate auth code
    code = secrets.token_urlsafe(32)
    _auth_codes[code] = {
        "redirect_uri": redirect_uri,
        "expires": time.time() + 300,  # 5 min
        "client_id": client_id,
    }

    logger.info("OAuth authorize: issuing code for redirect to %s", redirect_uri)

    # Auto-approve (personal skill — no login needed)
    # Build redirect with code and state
    separator = "&" if "?" in redirect_uri else "?"
    redirect_url = f"{redirect_uri}{separator}{urlencode({'code': code, 'state': state})}"

    return RedirectResponse(url=redirect_url)

violations.title: `token` refresh_token grant issues new access token on every retry
violations.content: The `refresh_token` grant branch in `token` mints a brand-new `access_token` on every call (line 129) and stores it in `_access_tokens` without any idempotency check. A retried token-refresh request — common on flaky network connections from Alexa/Lambda — will produce multiple valid access tokens for the same refresh, bloating `_access_tokens` and making session revocation/auditing impossible. There is no idempotency key support and no dedup of in-flight refreshes for the same refresh token.
violations.fixPrompt: In the `refresh_token` branch of `token` in `backend/routes/oauth.py`, track recent refreshes keyed by the refresh token string with a short TTL (e.g. 10 seconds). If the same refresh token is presented within the window, return the previously issued access token instead of minting a new one. Alternatively, accept an `Idempotency-Key` header and cache the response by that key.

violations.title: Unbounded in-memory OAuth token stores
violations.content: The module-level dicts `_auth_codes`, `_access_tokens`, and `_refresh_tokens` accumulate entries indefinitely with no size limit or eviction policy. `_auth_codes` is popped on successful redemption but unredeemed codes remain forever; `_access_tokens` and `_refresh_tokens` are never cleaned up at all — every call to `/oauth/token` adds new entries (e.g., refresh-token grants in lines 129-133 add a new access token without removing the old one). Under sustained load — for example, an Alexa skill or attacker repeatedly hitting `/oauth/authorize` and `/oauth/token` — these dicts will grow without bound, eventually causing OOM. Expired entries are detected only when explicitly looked up, never proactively reaped.
violations.fixPrompt: In `backend/routes/oauth.py`, add a periodic cleanup task (e.g., a background asyncio task started at app startup) that walks `_auth_codes`, `_access_tokens`, and `_refresh_tokens` and removes entries whose `expires` timestamp is in the past. Alternatively, replace the raw dicts with a TTL-aware structure (e.g., `cachetools.TTLCache`) sized to a reasonable maximum to bound memory even under abuse. When issuing a refresh-token grant, also evict any prior access token associated with the same refresh token.

violations.title: `publish_event` does not attach correlation/trace ID to SSE messages
violations.content: `publish_event(event_type: str, data: dict)` in `backend/routes/sse.py` publishes events to subscribers without accepting or attaching the originating request's correlation/trace ID. Downstream consumers receiving these events cannot correlate them to the HTTP request, background scan, or scheduler tick that produced them. This violates the rule that event/message publishing must carry the originating request ID for cross-boundary tracing. The `_event_generator` and `sse_events` handler likewise lack request-context identifiers in their stream payloads.
violations.fixPrompt: Update `publish_event` in `backend/routes/sse.py` to accept an optional `correlation_id: Optional[str] = None` parameter and inject it into the event payload (e.g., `{"correlation_id": cid, "type": event_type, "data": data}`). At each call site (device scanner, polling service, deco service, alexa service, etc.), propagate the correlation ID from the originating request context (use `contextvars.ContextVar` populated by a FastAPI middleware that reads `X-Request-Id`/`X-Correlation-Id` headers or generates a UUID). Ensure the SSE generator emits the `correlation_id` field so frontend listeners can tie events back to triggering requests.

violations.title: `run_speedtest` mutation endpoint lacks idempotency key
violations.content: The `run_speedtest` endpoint triggers a side-effecting operation (SSH into the Chester router and execute a speed test) on every invocation without accepting an idempotency key or checking for an in-flight test. If a client or proxy retries due to a transient network error or timeout, the handler will SSH in and run another full speed test, consuming bandwidth, contending for the router's SSH session, and producing duplicate rows in the speed test history plus duplicate insight generation. There is no deduplication window, no lock against concurrent invocations, and no idempotency-key-based replay of the prior result.
violations.fixPrompt: Add idempotency support to `run_speedtest` in `backend/routes/speedtest.py`. Accept an optional `Idempotency-Key` header; if a recent (e.g., within the last few minutes) test was executed with the same key, return the cached result rather than running a new speed test. Additionally, guard against concurrent invocations with an in-flight flag or asyncio lock so that a retry while a test is in progress returns the in-progress result instead of starting a second SSH speed test.

violations.title: `generate_insights` mutation endpoint is not idempotent
violations.content: The `generate_insights` endpoint manually triggers insight generation from accumulated test data without an idempotency key or deduplication check. Each call invokes `speedtest_service.generate_insights`, which produces and persists insights. Retries (from clients, proxies, or browser refreshes) will run insight generation repeatedly, likely producing duplicate or near-duplicate insight rows for the same underlying data window. The handler returns `generated: len(insights)` but does not dedupe against insights already produced for the same observation window.
violations.fixPrompt: Add idempotency to `generate_insights` in `backend/routes/speedtest.py`. Either accept an `Idempotency-Key` header and cache the response for that key, or have `speedtest_service.generate_insights` deduplicate based on the observation window / content hash so repeated calls within the same period return the existing insights rather than creating new ones. Also consider using a lock to serialize concurrent generations.

async def generate_insights() -> Dict[str, Any]:
    """Manually trigger insight generation from accumulated test data."""
    if speedtest_service is None:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=500, detail="Speed test service not initialized")

    import asyncio
    loop = asyncio.get_event_loop()
    insights = await loop.run_in_executor(None, speedtest_service.generate_insights)
    return {
        "generated": len(insights),
        "insights": insights,
    }

violations.title: `_create_session` configures retries without a circuit breaker
violations.content: `_create_session` builds a `requests.Session` with a `Retry` strategy (`total=3`, `backoff_factor=1`) for the Deco API but has no circuit breaker. Every call to a failing Deco endpoint will go through the full retry cycle, holding connections and threads. If the Deco router is consistently unreachable, the system will keep hammering it instead of failing fast, which can exhaust connection pools and cascade slowness to the entire backend (device polling, topology refreshes, schedulers).
violations.fixPrompt: Wrap the `requests.Session` returned by `_create_session` (or the call sites in `_local_encrypted_request` / `_cloud_request`) with a circuit breaker (e.g. `pybreaker.CircuitBreaker`) that opens after N consecutive failures, returns fast for a cooldown window, then half-opens to probe recovery. Track failure counts at the host/endpoint level so a failing Deco device doesn't block unrelated calls.
violations.snippet:
def _create_session(self) -> requests.Session:
        session = requests.Session()
        retry_strategy = Retry(
            total=3,
            status_forcelist=[429, 500, 502, 503, 504],
            allowed_methods=["HEAD", "GET", "POST", "PUT", "DELETE"],
            backoff_factor=1,
        )
        adapter = HTTPAdapter(max_retries=retry_strategy)
        session.mount("http://", adapter)
        session.mount("https://", adapter)
        return session

violations.title: `_local_encrypted_request` re-authenticates and recurses without a failure threshold
violations.content: `_local_encrypted_request` makes HTTP calls to the local Deco API and, on 403 / empty-data / AES-decrypt failure, calls `self.authenticate()` then recursively retries. There is no circuit breaker tracking how often the Deco API is failing across calls — if the router is down or rejecting sessions persistently, every caller (`get_device_list`, `get_client_list`, `get_topology_local`, `optimize_network`, scheduler polls) will keep re-authenticating and re-trying, on top of the underlying `Retry(total=3)` adapter. There is no fail-fast path and no global failure-rate gate, which means one failing dependency can stall the polling scheduler and cascade slowness.
violations.fixPrompt: Introduce a circuit breaker around `_local_encrypted_request` (e.g. `pybreaker` or a small counter of consecutive failures with timestamped open/half-open state). Once N consecutive failures occur within a window, raise `APIConnectionError` immediately without performing the HTTP call, authentication, or retry recursion. Reset on a successful call after the cooldown.

violations.title: `get_client_list` iterates devices calling cloud API without a failure threshold
violations.content: The cloud branch of `get_client_list` loops over every device returned by `get_device_list` and issues a `_cloud_request("passthrough", ...)` for each. Failures are caught per-device with `logger.warning` and the loop continues, but there is no shared failure counter or circuit breaker — if the regional cloud endpoint is degraded, every device call will hit the timeout/retry path, multiplied by the device count, on every poll cycle. A circuit breaker would let the method fail fast and skip the remaining devices once a failure rate threshold is exceeded.
violations.fixPrompt: Track consecutive `_cloud_request` failures within the loop (or via a shared breaker on `_cloud_request`). After M consecutive failures inside one invocation, break out of the loop early and return what has been collected so far. Additionally, gate `_cloud_request` itself with a circuit breaker so subsequent polls fail fast while the cloud is unhealthy.

violations.title: `get_topology_local` loops over nodes calling Deco API without a failure threshold
violations.content: `get_topology_local` iterates over each Deco node and issues an `admin/client?form=client_list` request per node via `_local_encrypted_request`. Per-node failures are swallowed with `logger.warning`, but there is no failure-rate tracking — if the local API is unresponsive, every node call will go through its own retry/auth cycle on every topology refresh, blocking the request thread for an extended period. There is no fast-fail path once the dependency is clearly unhealthy.
violations.fixPrompt: Add a per-call failure counter inside the loop: if K consecutive node requests fail, abort the remaining iterations and return partial results (or raise). Better, share a circuit breaker with `_local_encrypted_request` so once it opens, subsequent node calls return immediately without I/O.

    def get_topology_local(self) -> Dict[str, Any]:
        """Get node list and per-node client mappings via local Deco API.

        Returns:
            Dict with 'nodes' (list of node dicts) and 'node_clients' (node_mac -> list of clients)
        """
        if not HAS_CRYPTO:
            raise APIConnectionError("pycryptodome required for local API")

        # Return cached data if fresh enough
        global _topology_cache, _topology_cache_time
        import time
        now = time.time()
        if _topology_cache and _topology_cache_time and (now - _topology_cache_time) < TOPOLOGY_CACHE_TTL:
            logger.debug("Returning cached topology data")
            return _topology_cache

        with _local_api_lock:
            # Double-check cache after acquiring lock (another thread may have filled it)
            now = time.time()
            if _topology_cache and _topology_cache_time and (now - _topology_cache_time) < TOPOLOGY_CACHE_TTL:
                return _topology_cache

            logger.info("Creating temporary local DecoClient for topology fetch")
            local_client = DecoClient(
                local_endpoint=self.local_endpoint,
                use_cloud=False,
                verify_ssl=False,
            )
            local_client.username = "admin"
            local_client.password = self.password

            try:
                local_client.authenticate()

                # Get all nodes
                node_result = local_client._local_encrypted_request(
                    "admin/device?form=device_list",
                    json.dumps({"operation": "read"})
                )
                nodes = node_result.get("device_list", [])
                logger.info(f"Local API returned {len(nodes)} nodes")

                # Get per-node clients
                node_clients = {}
                for node in nodes:
                    node_mac = node.get("mac", "")
                    try:
                        result = local_client._local_encrypted_request(
                            "admin/client?form=client_list",
                            json.dumps({"operation": "read", "params": {"device_mac": node_mac}})
                        )
                        clients = result.get("client_list", [])
                        node_clients[node_mac] = clients
                        logger.debug(f"Node {node_mac}: {len(clients)} clients")
                    except Exception as e:
                        logger.warning(f"Failed to get clients for node {node_mac}: {e}")
                        node_clients[node_mac] = []

                result = {"nodes": nodes, "node_clients": node_clients}
                _topology_cache = result
                _topology_cache_time = time.time()
                return result
            except Exception as e:

violations.title: `HiBoost` client session has no retry strategy
violations.content: The `HiBoostClient.__init__` creates a bare `requests.Session()` at line 102 without mounting a `Retry`/`HTTPAdapter` strategy. Subsequent HTTP calls to the external HiBoost API (auth, RF parameter polling, etc.) over this session will fail permanently on the first transient network error (timeouts, 5xx, connection resets). Contrast with `DecoClient._create_session` (lines 175-186) which mounts a `Retry(total=3, status_forcelist=[429, 500, 502, 503, 504], backoff_factor=1)` adapter for the same kind of external integration. Given the HiBoost API is a remote third-party service and the client runs on a periodic poller, transient failures are likely and should be retried with exponential backoff.

Use `total=3`, `status_forcelist=[429, 500, 502, 503, 504]`, `allowed_methods=["HEAD", "GET", "POST", "PUT", "DELETE"]`, and `backoff_factor=1`, mirroring `DecoClient._create_session`. Mount the adapter on both `http://` and `https://`.

violations.title: `HiBoostClient.__init__` creates a `requests.Session` with no circuit breaker for the HiBoost API
violations.content: `HiBoostClient` initializes a bare `requests.Session` with a 15s timeout for calls to the HiBoost cloud API but never configures a circuit breaker (and does not even configure retry/backoff). The HiBoost scheduler polls this external service every `HIBOOST_POLL_INTERVAL` seconds; if the upstream API degrades or hangs near the timeout, every poll will pay the full timeout cost, tying up worker threads. Without a circuit breaker the service has no way to back off and fail fast when HiBoost is unhealthy.

When the breaker is open, raise immediately so the scheduler skips the poll cycle instead of waiting on timeouts. Optionally pair it with a `urllib3.util.Retry` adapter for short-lived transient errors, but ensure the breaker — not retries — governs sustained outages.
